Traffic over Drochaid Ros fhionn grows so heavy with salt carts that the bridge-keeper is given the right to take a handful from each load. The keeper's salt-box is recorded as holding more than some villages' granaries.
27 an Cèitean 340 DE Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The wells crack at Cill ghlas
An earth tremor in the hills around Cill ghlas cracks three wells and brings down a byre. The custodians of the vein-house note it and note also that the galleries were untouched.
26 an Giblean 355 DE Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The Hollow Man spoken of again
Shepherds of the Doire uaine hills refuse to light fires on the high pastures, citing the old inscriptions of Marbh-bheò Doire uaine. A reeve sent from Muileann chiar to make them see sense does not stay the night.
25 an Cèitean 355 DE Cathair dhearg
Aonghas mac Uisdein crowned
Uisdean mac Dhùghaill dies and his son Aonghas mac Uisdein is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Aonghas is recorded as the first king to learn his letters as a child.
23 an t-Ògmhios 355 DE Àth fhiadhaich
Àth fhiadhaich salt fish
Àth fhiadhaich begins to salt its catch with Ros fhionn salt and send it inland to the mining towns. The mining shires eat salt fish in the lean season from this time on.
28 am Màrt 370 DE Inis thais
Clach first preached at Inis thais
Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, where the wolf-sworn's stone stands, gives the one god of the wolf-sworn a name, Clach, the Resplendent Direwolf, who keeps the island as a wolf keeps its range. His hearers are the first congregation of Creideamh a' Mhadaidh-allaidh.
16 an Dùbhlachd 380 DE Inis thais
The wolf-house at Inis thais
Dòmhnall mac Ailein's followers raise a temple at Inis thais, the first temple on the island raised to Clach by name. It is roofed with slate brought by sea from the north.
29 am Faoilleach 390 DE Caol leathan
Hawk and wolf at Caol leathan
Priests of the Hawk and preachers of the Wolf both claim the harbour shrine at Caol leathan. The king's reeve divides its days between them, as the Holy Age had divided the sacred woods, and the arrangement holds.
31 an Dùbhlachd 402 DE Cathair dhearg
The Dark Unicorn at court
King Aonghas takes up the wood-watchers' teaching of Uallach, the Dark Unicorn, which holds that light and dark are two powers in balance and that the vein belongs to both. The court follows him, and Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh becomes the faith of Cathair dhearg.
28 am Màrt 407 DE Tobar dhearg
Fire at Tobar dhearg
A fire in the thatch spreads through Tobar dhearg and burns most of the village. The villagers rebuild with slate from the quarries nearby, and the village is known for its slate roofs after.
14 am Faoilleach 432 DE Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The Unicorn's priests in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The share of custody over Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, divided since the Holy Age, passes by royal grant to the priests of the Dark Unicorn. The other claimants withdraw from the wood without contest, and the record does not say why.
11 an t-Iuchar 440 DE Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The deer scholars keep Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The teachers of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh take formal keeping of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, walking its bounds each year. The walk becomes the school's one public observance.
29 am Faoilleach 445 DE Àth chiar
The drovers of Àth chiar
Drovers from Àth chiar begin driving cattle over the eastern hills to the mining towns each year. Their routes are the first on the island to be marked with cairns.
23 an t-Ògmhios 445 DE Doire chiar
Eilidh Dhubh's tracts
At Doire chiar, Eilidh nic Iain, called Eilidh Dhubh, revives the teaching of the Holy Age's rival school, that the vein answers effort and not birth, and writes it out in tracts copied by her pupils. The tracts are read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east.
2 an Dùbhlachd 445 DE Muileann dhearg
The tracts burned at Muileann dhearg
The vein-house orders every copy of Eilidh Dhubh's tracts brought to Muileann dhearg and burned. Some hundred copies are surrendered. Eilidh herself is not punished and dies at Doire chiar, still teaching.
31 an Dùbhlachd 445 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of King Aonghas
King Aonghas mac Uisdein dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried by the rite of the Dark Unicorn, the first king so buried. His son Iain mac Aonghais is crowned.
27 an Gearran 457 DE Cathair dhearg
Tormod Bàn crowned
Iain mac Aonghais dies after a short reign and his son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for his white hair, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The houses swear to him without dispute.
8 an Lùnastal 470 DE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
Winter at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on the central mining road, becomes the house where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the worst of the snow. Its keeper, Iain mac Mhurchaidh, builds a second byre for them and keeps a book of the teams that lodged.
6 an t-Sultain 475 DE Muileann naomh
The bell-founders of Muileann naomh
A family at Muileann naomh casts the first bronze bell on Rodos hung in a hawk-house. The bell cracks in its first frost, and the second holds.
5 am Màrt 480 DE Cuan dhearg
An Gàire Dubh
A storm named in the south-coast rolls An Gàire Dubh, the Black Laugh, drives the sea over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg and ruins the season's salt fish. The town is rebuilt a street further back from the shore.
13 an t-Sultain 487 DE Muileann naomh
The hawk-house at Muileann naomh
Muileann naomh in the south becomes the southernmost house of the Hawk, its bell rung at each measured burning. The Hawk's teaching holds there when it fades elsewhere in the south.
18 an t-Ògmhios 495 DE Abhainn fhionn
The king's sons drowned in Abhainn fhionn
Both sons of King Tormod Bàn are drowned when a ferry overturns crossing Abhainn fhionn in spate. The king has no other child.
8 an t-Sultain 508 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Tormod Bàn
King Tormod Bàn dies at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir. Three claims are laid before the houses at once.
21 an Giblean 513 DE Cathair dhearg
The three claimants
The crown is claimed by Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, the late king's niece; by Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and by Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house. The seven houses split among them and the War of the Three Claimants begins.
20 an Cèitean 514 DE Seann Warr
Seann Warr shuts its gates
Seann Warr, the port nearest the capital on the west, closes its gates to all three claimants and declares for none. It is besieged twice in the war and taken by neither.
22 an Gearran 515 DE Àth shean
The ford at Àth shean
Dùghall Garbh's host meets Raghnall Ruadh's at the ford of Àth shean and breaks it. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford.
24 an t-Sultain 516 DE Doire mhin
The burning of Doire mhin
Raghnall Ruadh's retreating men burn the village of Doire mhin and its granary to deny it to Dùghall. The villagers winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of the Dark Unicorn's priests.
26 an Dùbhlachd 518 DE Cathair dhomhain
The siege of Cathair dhomhain
Catrìona nic Aonghais besieges Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and takes it after forty days when its wells are poisoned by the dead of the siege lines. She lets the garrison go free on their oath.
24 am Faoilleach 519 DE Muileann dhearg
The hearths refused
Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, refuses the measured handful of ore to every hearth and temple in the shires that stand against him. Hearths that had been lit with the ore for generations go cold, and the act turns more people against him than any battle.
14 am Faoilleach 521 DE Muileann chrom
The battle of Muileann chrom
The hosts of Catrìona and Dùghall, joined for the purpose, meet Raghnall Ruadh below Muileann chrom. Raghnall is killed on the field and the vein-house is opened by his own custodians the next day.
16 an Dùbhlachd 522 DE Baile Mòr dhomhain
Death of Dùghall Garbh
Dùghall Garbh dies of his wounds from Muileann chrom at Baile Mòr dhomhain. His followers go over to Catrìona without a further fight.
13 am Màrt 523 DE Cathair dhearg
Catrìona Bhuadhach crowned
Catrìona nic Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg and is known after as Catrìona Bhuadhach. The War of the Three Claimants ends with her crowning, having lasted about a decade.
12 an Gearran 526 DE Muileann dhearg
The ruling of the hearth
Catrìona Bhuadhach and the vein-house fix in law that no claimant, house or king may withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. It is the first law in the record written to bind the custodians themselves.
10 an Cèitean 545 DE Am Buabhall Fortanach
Catrìona's road south
Queen Catrìona has the road from the capital south by Am Buabhall Fortanach laid with stone, so that her own town of Inis thais may be reached in any weather. The road is known as Rathad na Banrighinn.
11 an Giblean 555 DE Seann Warr
Seann Warr's gates honoured
Queen Catrìona grants Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and levy its own tolls, in memory of its standing aside in the war. The grant is cut over the landward gate.
7 an t-Iuchar 565 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Catrìona Bhuadhach
Catrìona Bhuadhach dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Lachlann mac Iain is crowned, and the houses swear to him in one day, which the record remarks on.
8 an t-Ògmhios 585 DE Cathair dhearg
The Book of the Three Claimants
A clerk of Queen Catrìona's household, Seònaid nic Coinnich, writes an account of the war from the custody-book and from the testimony of those who fought. It is the oldest surviving history on Rodos written as a single narrative rather than as entries.
3 an t-Sultain 585 DE Inis chrom
The sickness at Inis chrom
A spotted fever kills some three hundred at Inis chrom on the south-west coast. The Wolf's preachers nurse the sick and many of them die of it, and the town becomes the Wolf's for good.
5 an Lùnastal 595 DE Doire shean
The oyster beds of Doire shean
Doire shean, a village on the southern shore, lays out oyster beds in its shallow bay and sends oysters by cart to the capital. The trade makes the village rich enough to be a shire seat.
1 an t-Sultain 615 DE Seann Skell
The Yellow Scorpion preached at Seann Skell
At Seann Skell, where the sting-creed of the Holy Age first called itself the only true one, a preacher named Mànas mac Ruairidh proclaims its one power as Cnut, the Yellow Scorpion, and teaches that Cnut closed the western sea behind the fleet and that it must not be tried again. His hearers are the first congregation of Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe.
30 an t-Sultain 615 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Lachlann mac Iain
Lachlann mac Iain, son of Catrìona Bhuadhach, dies at Cathair dhearg, and his daughter Anna is crowned. The record calls his reign quiet and means it as praise.
29 an Dàmhair 635 DE Ros bheag
The Scorpion at Ros bheag and Cuan shean
The teaching of the Yellow Scorpion spreads down the west coast to Ros bheag and Cuan shean, carried by fishing families. At Cuan shean the rope-makers are among the first converts.
27 an t-Samhain 655 DE Ros bheag
Within sight of land
The Scorpion's priests at Ros bheag lay it down that no boat of the faithful may go beyond sight of the headlands. The rule is kept on the west coast for centuries, and the steering of boats by the stars, already half lost, is lost there entirely.
19 an t-Ògmhios 660 DE Àth shean
The granaries of Àth shean rebuilt
The royal granaries at Àth shean, old since before the Sundering, are pulled down and rebuilt in stone on raised floors against the rats. The tally-house is rebuilt with them.
24 am Faoilleach 675 DE Cuan shean
The rope-walks shortened
Cuan shean takes up half its rope-walks and puts the ground to barley. The rope trade had lived on the fleet and then on the fishing, and the fishing no longer needs rope of that length.
22 an Gearran 685 DE Cnoc chaol
Wave at Cnoc chaol
A great swell, with no storm behind it, runs up the beach at Cnoc chaol on the south coast and carries off the drying racks and two children. The village moves its racks further up the shore.
23 am Màrt 700 DE Muileann dhearg
The two counts reconciled
The vein-house and the crown's scribes find that their counts of years since the Setting-Out differ, and settle the difference by agreement. The day of the empty-harbour rite, which each count had placed differently, is fixed by the same agreement, and later scribes stop pretending it was fixed by evidence.
12 am Faoilleach 730 DE Inis mhòr
The deer school at Inis mhòr
A house of disputation is founded at Inis mhòr by pupils of Dùn thais, and the question of the vein is argued on the north coast for the first time. Its first master, Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, is remembered for refusing every answer offered him.
10 an Gearran 730 DE Cathair dhearg
Queen Eilidh Bhàn crowned
Eilidh Bhàn, the fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The record of her long reign is almost entirely one of harvests.
22 an Gearran 730 DE Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The bath-house at the hot springs
Clann Choinnich rebuilds the old bath-house over the hot springs of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh in dressed stone and admits the sick of any house on one day in seven. The house's physicians keep a book of cures that is later lost.
24 am Faoilleach 745 DE Spùinneadairean-mara
The sea-thieves of the north-west
Boats working out of the small islands off the north-west coast begin taking fish and grain from coasting traders. The sea-thieves are Ròdaich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls give some of their names.
26 an Dùbhlachd 750 DE Baile chrom
Baile chrom half empty
The reeve of Baile chrom on the north-west coast reports half the town's houses empty, their families gone east after the sea-thieves and the poor harvests. The crown remits the town's grain dues.
27 an t-Samhain 762 DE Eilean dhubh
The raid on Eilean dhubh
A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn lands on Eilean dhubh and burns the sea-thieves' boats on the strand. Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, is taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.
19 an Giblean 780 DE Gorta Baile chrom
The dearth on the north-west shore
A run of failed harvests along the north-west shore brings a dearth that the shared-meal custom cannot carry. Families leave the coast for the interior and the east, and the north-west is thinly held from this time until the end of the age.
20 an Cèitean 790 DE Cathair dhearg
The king-list recopied
The scribes of Queen Eilidh Bhàn recopy the king-list of Rodos from its oldest surviving roll, adding the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy begins its account of the present age with the Choosing and not with the fleet.
21 an Giblean 802 DE Cathair dhearg
Eilidh Bhàn dies without an heir
Queen Eilidh Bhàn dies at Cathair dhearg with no child, and the house of Catrìona ends with her. The seven houses meet at the vein-house rather than at the capital.
23 am Màrt 807 DE Cathair dhearg
Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned
The houses name Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, a descendant of the claimant killed at Muileann chrom. He is crowned at Cathair dhearg and keeps the mastery of the vein-house as well as the crown.
6 an t-Ògmhios 820 DE Muileann dhearg
The crown and the custody joined
Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeves write it into the custody-book that the ruler of Rodos is also master of the vein-house. From this time the heads of the seven houses sit as the king's council, and the custodian class and the court are one body.
10 an Dùbhlachd 832 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh
Dòmhnall Ruadh, the first ruler to hold both the crown and the vein-house, dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Muileann dhearg. His son Raghnall Òg is crowned.
20 an t-Ògmhios 850 DE Cnoc bheag
The schism of the Hawk
A council of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag divides over whether Mòd's measure may ever be raised. Those who hold it fixed forever keep the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag; those who hold that a larger flock may be fed a larger handful are called the Fed Hawk.
17 an Lùnastal 860 DE Seann Chwen
The harbour of Seann Chwen
The port of Seann Chwen builds its harbour mole, and becomes the port for the ore-carts coming down from the mountain to the coast towns of the south.
23 an Giblean 870 DE Seann Skell
The Fed Hawk at Seann Skell
The priests of the Fed Hawk, turned out of Cnoc bheag, settle at Seann Skell on the north coast, not the western port of that name. Their teaching is written in the custody-book as an error, and the error is recorded at length.
25 an Lùnastal 880 DE Seann Skell
The Fed Hawk's petition
The Fed Hawk petitions the king's council from Seann Skell to raise the measured handful by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast. The council refuses. The petition is the first recorded request to alter the Small-Burning Law.
14 an Dàmhair 890 DE Cill ghlas
The gallery at Cill ghlas
A second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brings down a gallery of the vein and kills fourteen custodians' labourers. The vein-house closes the gallery and sets a stone at its mouth with the fourteen names.
12 an t-Samhain 900 DE Cathair dhearg
The ore-roads kept by the crown
The king's council takes the roads from the mountain to the coast into the keeping of the crown, so that the carts carrying the measured ore to the temples may not be stopped by any house. The roads are marked with posts bearing the crown's sign.
17 an Lùnastal 910 DE Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The high pastures of Doire uaine abandoned
The last shepherd families leave the high pastures of the Doire uaine hills for the valley villages. The reason given is the grazing; everyone asked also mentions the Marbh-bheò.
9 an Lùnastal 920 DE Ros fhionn
The salt fair at Ros fhionn
Ros fhionn holds its great salt fair, and the reeve's count is some four thousand people on the flats in a single day. It is the town's height, and the chronicle calls it the richest place on the north-east coast.
31 an Dàmhair 930 DE Cathair mhòr
Cathair mhòr the largest town
Cathair mhòr passes the capital in size, its market drawing trade from the whole south of the island. The capital remains the seat of the crown and the smaller place.
18 an t-Sultain 940 DE Toll-dubh
The stair at Toll-dubh
Quarrymen north of the capital break into Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tellings, long lost, and find a stair cut into the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians of the vein-house have the entrance walled up; the one quarryman who went down is not recorded as saying what he saw.
11 an Gearran 955 DE Cathair mhòr
The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr
Copper-workers at Cathair mhòr begin making cooking pots that are sold on every road on the island. The pots are marked with the maker's sign, and some survive in the ground.
31 am Faoilleach 960 DE Làrach an Teampaill
Ailean measures Làrach an Teampaill
Ailean mac Dhùghaill, a scholar of the deer school at Dùn thais, measures the ruin of Làrach an Teampaill and writes that its altar faces the central mountains and not the sea. He declines to guess who set it so.
20 an t-Iuchar 972 DE Làrach an Dùin-fhaire
Ailean's tables of the old ruins
Ailean mac Dhùghaill completes his tables of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin and Làrach an Teampaill, giving their measures, their stone and the lie of each. He concludes that he cannot say whether one people built all three, and his tables are the reason later scholars could not say either.
23 am Faoilleach 980 DE Cathair dhearg
Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned
Mòrag Ruadh, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler whose household accounts survive whole.
18 an Dàmhair 995 DE Carragh Cnoc bheag
The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned
The priests of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag clear the moss from the obelisk of Carragh Cnoc bheag and try to read the old letters on it. They cannot, and they record the attempt.
19 an t-Sultain 1000 DE Caol shean
Caol shean's fishing year
Caol shean on the east coast lands the largest catch in its roll, so large that salt runs short and half is dried in the wind. The dried fish sells poorly and the town goes back to salting.
15 an Dùbhlachd 1000 DE Seann Skell
The thousandth year
The vein-house marks the thousandth year of its count with a single measured burning of the ore on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell. Queen Mòrag Ruadh attends. The record says the flame burned the colour of the vein and that the crowd went home without a word.
16 an t-Samhain 1025 DE Baile ghorm
The blue dyers of Baile ghorm
The dyers of Baile ghorm in the south-east make a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own. Cloth of Baile ghorm blue becomes the dress of the seven houses on feast days.
29 an Lùnastal 1040 DE Muileann dhomhain
The swallowing cough at Muileann dhomhain
A sickness that closes the throat breaks out at Muileann dhomhain and moves along the coast road. The town loses near a third of its people.
26 an Cèitean 1042 DE Seann Bhral
The cough at Seann Bhral
The swallowing cough reaches the port of Seann Bhral. The harbour is closed by the townsfolk themselves, and the shared-meal custom is kept by leaving food at the town's gate.
7 an t-Iuchar 1043 DE Cathair dhearg
Queen Beathag Fhionn's closing of the roads
Beathag Fhionn, crowned after her mother Mòrag, closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets reeves at the fords to turn back travellers. The cough goes no further west.
5 an Lùnastal 1065 DE Muileann dhomhain
Muileann dhomhain resettled
Muileann dhomhain, emptied by the swallowing cough, is resettled by families from the hills around it, who take the empty houses by lot. The town's older families say they never again knew half their neighbours.
13 an t-Ògmhios 1080 DE Drochaid Ros fhionn
Drochaid Ros fhionn repaired
The arches of Drochaid Ros fhionn, worn by seven centuries of salt carts, are rebuilt at the cost of the Ros fhionn salt-masters. Their names are cut on the keystones.
2 an Dàmhair 1090 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Queen Beathag Fhionn
Queen Beathag Fhionn, who closed the coast road against the cough, dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Ailean is crowned, the first of four kings of that name in the house of Raghnall.
13 am Màrt 1100 DE Baile ghorm
The Baile ghorm blue fades
The last dyer who knew the Baile ghorm mordant dies without apprentices, having quarrelled with both of hers. The blue that comes after is the ordinary blue of the rest of the island.
11 an Giblean 1110 DE Dùn ìseal
The ancestor-posts of Dùn ìseal burned
The ancestor-posts at Dùn ìseal burn in a lightning fire. The keepers recut the names from memory and from the custody-book, and admit in their roll that some are guesses.
29 an t-Ògmhios 1120 DE Ros fhionn
The silting of Ros fhionn
The harbour of Ros fhionn silts up behind a shifting bar, and the salt ships can no longer lie at the quays. The salt-masters move their trade to Caol gharbh along the coast.
8 an t-Ògmhios 1130 DE Caol gharbh
Caol gharbh takes the salt
Caol gharbh, a fishing village, becomes the salt port of the north-east, and its harbour is dug out and walled with the Ros fhionn masters' money.
20 an Cèitean 1140 DE Drochaid Ros fhionn
Traffic falls on Drochaid Ros fhionn
With the salt going by sea from Caol gharbh, the carts stop crossing Drochaid Ros fhionn. The bridge-keeper's office is abolished, and the bridge is little used from this time.
25 am Màrt 1150 DE Muileann shean
The millers of Muileann shean
The mills of Muileann shean are fitted with a new kind of gearing, cut in oak, that turns two stones from one wheel. The gearing spreads to the mills of the north within a lifetime.
21 an Giblean 1160 DE Uilebheist na Mara
The Sea-Watcher off the north-west
Fishers from the thinned north-west coast report the Sea-Watcher, Uilebheist na Mara, close enough to foul their nets. The few boats still working those waters draw further in.
29 an t-Samhain 1170 DE Dùn thais
The table of years at Dùn thais
A scholar of the deer school at Dùn thais, Raghnall mac Chaluim, sets out a table showing that the heads of the custodian houses live on average a few years longer than the tenants of their lands. He asks whether the vein answers the hand that holds it. The record notes the finding with unease and without an answer.
29 an Giblean 1180 DE Muileann dhearg
The table forbidden
The king's council forbids the copying of Raghnall mac Chaluim's table of years, and the house of disputation at Dùn thais is closed for a generation. Raghnall's own copy is kept in the vein-house and entered in its inventory.
2 an Dàmhair 1190 DE Inis mhòr
The winter of ice at Inis mhòr
The harbour of Inis mhòr freezes from shore to shore, which no one then living had seen. Boats are crushed at their moorings and the grain fleet does not sail until the thaw.
3 an t-Sultain 1207 DE Baile ruadh
Baile ruadh's quarrel with Achadh naomh
Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh in the far north-east go to law over the grazing on the hills between them. The case is heard three times at Cathair dhearg and settled by dividing the hills along a stream.
10 an t-Samhain 1220 DE Allt an Àigh
Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
The keepers of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach renew the pilgrimage to Allt an Àigh, and a guest-house is built beside the stream for those who come to drink at the proper phase of the moon. The guest-house book records pilgrims from every shire.
7 an t-Iuchar 1227 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill
King Ailean mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, leaving two sons of different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, each of whom has been told he is the heir.
8 an t-Ògmhios 1231 DE Cnoc naomh
The battle of Cnoc naomh
The brothers' war opens when Alasdair Bàn's men seize Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar retakes it. The houses divide, four to three, and Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, is named from this battle.
17 an Lùnastal 1233 DE Ceann mhin
The fire at Ceann mhin
Alasdair Bàn's ships burn the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother. The fire takes the rope stores and the granary, and the town begs its bread from Cathair mhòr.
19 an t-Iuchar 1235 DE Muileann ghlas
The battle of Muileann ghlas
Iain Ciar defeats Alasdair Bàn below Muileann ghlas. Alasdair is taken alive, and his captains are allowed to go home.
12 an t-Sultain 1237 DE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The brothers make peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands. Alasdair Bàn gives up his claim and receives the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar is crowned.
8 an Dàmhair 1252 DE Seann Chwen
Death of Alasdair Bàn
Alasdair Bàn dies at Seann Chwen, having kept the peace he made. His lordship returns to the crown.
20 an Giblean 1260 DE Cathair dhearg
Iain Ciar's grain law
King Iain Ciar orders that every shire seat keep a year's grain in store against the next war, having seen Ceann mhin beg its bread. The law is enforced for as long as he lives.
14 an Lùnastal 1265 DE Cathair dhearg
The account of the Brothers' War
A clerk of King Iain Ciar, Pàdraig mac Ruairidh, writes the account of the Brothers' War. It praises the king at every turn and is the only account that survives, which later readers have found inconvenient.
28 an Giblean 1280 DE An Sligeanach Fad' às
The inns of the mining roads chartered
The crown grants a charter to the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit, An Sligeanach Fad' às among them, making their keepers answerable for the roads between them. The keepers meet once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts.
17 an t-Ògmhios 1287 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Iain Ciar
King Iain Ciar dies at Cathair dhearg. His grain law lapses within a few years of his death, as he had foreseen in a note in his own hand.
22 am Màrt 1300 DE An Taigh-seinnse Òir
An Taigh-seinnse Òir's beef
An Taigh-seinnse Òir, on the eastern end of the circuit, is written into the charter-roll as keeping syrupped beef for the custodians' reeves on their rounds. It is the first recorded dish of that house; the rest of the entry is a complaint about the price.
20 an Giblean 1310 DE An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the road-house on the high northern road, is snowed in for a whole season with a party of custodians' reeves inside. They live on its pickled spinach and fire milk, and their complaint to the charter-roll is recorded in full.
11 am Màrt 1320 DE Seann Skell
The hull that sank at launch
Seumas mac Iain, a boat-builder of Seann Skell, sets out to rebuild a deep-keeled hull from the scraps of the Sundering fellowship's lore still remembered on the strand. The hull fills and sinks at its launch, and the Scorpion's priests preach on it for a year.
31 an Cèitean 1330 DE Caol ìseal
The Caol ìseal fishers go east
Fishing families of Caol ìseal on the north coast move east to Caol bheag after their own harbour silts. Caol ìseal becomes a farming town.
11 an Gearran 1340 DE Cuan shean
The keel-song of Cuan shean
A folk-collector of the royal household, Iseabail nic Lachlainn, takes down a work-song still sung by the rope-makers of Cuan shean that names the parts of a deep keel. Half its words have no meaning to anyone who sings it. It is the only record of the Sundering fleet's techniques that survives in any form.
4 an Gearran 1350 DE Inis thais
The Wolf's schism at Inis thais
The Wolf's congregation at Inis thais divides over whether Clach may be prayed to for the dead. Those who say not keep the temple; the others build a second house at Baile gheal.
3 an Gearran 1360 DE Seann Tarr
The grey storm at Seann Tarr
A storm named Gailleann Ghlas comes in from the east and destroys the harbour of Seann Tarr. The village is rebuilt, but the harbour is not, and its boats move to Cuan ruadh.
8 an Lùnastal 1360 DE Baile gheal
The second wolf-house at Baile gheal
The dissenters from Inis thais raise their house at Baile gheal and pray there for the dead by name. The two houses of the Wolf are not reconciled in this age.
29 an t-Ògmhios 1370 DE Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh's new harbour
Cuan ruadh builds a second harbour arm to take the boats from Seann Tarr. The town prospers on the east-coast fishing for the rest of the age.
31 an Cèitean 1390 DE Cathair dhearg
Queen Catrìona Bheag crowned
Catrìona Bheag, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg, the first queen in more than three centuries. The record notes that she was small, and that no one said so twice.
26 an Lùnastal 1400 DE Muileann gheal
The grey glaze of Muileann gheal
The potters of Muileann gheal make a grey-green glaze that no other kiln on the island can match, and the custodian houses buy it for their tables. The secret is kept within one family, Clann Mhic Phàil.
28 an t-Iuchar 1410 DE Cathair dhearg
The oath of the seven
Queen Catrìona Bheag has the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth in her presence, the first renewal of the oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swears last.
14 am Màrt 1420 DE Cathair mhòr
The Unicorn's great house at Cathair mhòr
The priests of the Dark Unicorn raise their great house at Cathair mhòr, the largest roofed building on Rodos in this age. Its black and white floor took eleven years to lay.
17 an t-Ògmhios 1430 DE Toll-dubh
The eastern Toll-dubh
Charcoal-burners in the east find again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tellings, with the same cut stair as the one walled up in the west. The custodians wall this one too, and the two entries in the custody-book are cross-referenced by the scribe.
2 an Dàmhair 1440 DE Tiormachd Achadh shean
The dry years at Achadh shean
Three dry seasons in succession empty the wells of the eastern shires around Achadh shean. The shared-meal custom holds, and grain is carted in from the south by the crown.
2 an t-Samhain 1450 DE Achadh shean
The water-rights of Achadh shean
The reeves of Achadh shean divide the use of the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn, and write the division on a board at the well-head. The board is renewed each generation and the lots are never redrawn.
24 an t-Sultain 1460 DE Àth shean
The firlot of Àth shean
The granary of Àth shean discovers its firlot has been worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been for generations. The reeve's accounts are corrected back as far as anyone can reckon.
30 an Dùbhlachd 1470 DE Muileann gheal
The grey glaze lost
The last of Clann Mhic Phàil dies at Muileann gheal without passing on the glaze. Potters of the town try for a generation to match it and fail.
18 an Dàmhair 1480 DE Baile Mòr ruadh
Baile Mòr ruadh's fair
Baile Mòr ruadh in the east holds a cattle fair drawing drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills. The fair becomes yearly and is the largest in the east.
9 an t-Iuchar 1490 DE Cathair dhearg
Queen Sìleas Òg crowned
Sìleas Òg, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg, named for the queen of the firlot. She is the first ruler in the record to have visited every shire seat.
4 an Dàmhair 1500 DE Muileann dhearg
Sìleas Òg's census of hands
Queen Sìleas Òg orders a new count of every household holding the right to the ore. The count is smaller than any before it, the right having narrowed into fewer and larger households, and the queen has it entered without comment.
5 an t-Sultain 1510 DE Ceann mhin
The fire of Ceann mhin
A second great fire burns Ceann mhin, this time without a war to blame. The town is rebuilt with stone gable walls between houses by order of its reeve.
31 an Lùnastal 1520 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver smelt refused
Clann Choinnich asks leave to burn the ore beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, on the ground that the ore burns hotter than charcoal. The council refuses. It is the first request to burn the ore for work rather than worship.
22 an t-Ògmhios 1530 DE Dùn dhearg
The lost smithing at Dùn dhearg
The smiths of Dùn dhearg, who had made the custodian houses' ceremonial blades since the walls were built, lose the last man who knew how their layered steel was folded. Later blades from Dùn dhearg are ordinary.
2 an Dùbhlachd 1540 DE Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The custodian houses begin to bury their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, among graves older than any name on them. The tenants of the surrounding land call it an unwise thing to do and continue to bury their own dead elsewhere.
9 an t-Iuchar 1550 DE Cathair dhearg
King Ailean the Fourth crowned
Ailean mac Raghnaill, the fourth king of that name, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered only because his reign is the shortest in the king-list.
13 an Giblean 1551 DE Seann Skell
The synod of the Scorpion
The priests of the Yellow Scorpion meet at Seann Skell and restate the rule of sight-of-land. They add a prayer, said at the harbour mouth, asking Cnut to keep the sea shut.
12 an Cèitean 1551 DE Cathair dhearg
Queen Mòrag nic Ailein crowned
Ailean's sister Mòrag nic Ailein is crowned after him. She reigns for forty years and leaves the king-list its longest run of entries recording nothing but good harvests and the rite.
16 an t-Samhain 1580 DE Cidhe Beag
The ferry at Cidhe Beag
A ferry family sets up at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine, taking passengers and goods down the river by canoe. The family holds the landing for the rest of the age.
2 an t-Samhain 1595 DE Inis mhòr
Inis mhòr's grain fleet laid up
The coasting grain barges of Inis mhòr are laid up for good as the roads improve. The last of them is kept on the strand as a curiosity.
7 an Lùnastal 1610 DE Dùn ìseal
Earthquake at Dùn ìseal
An earthquake shakes Dùn ìseal and cracks the spirit-house. No one is killed, and the keepers read it as a warning without being able to agree what of.
21 an Cèitean 1620 DE Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies
Beathag nic Thòmais, a mill-owner's widow of Muileann chaol, begins to buy up old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from the houses that no longer read them. She keeps them in a loft over her mill.
28 am Faoilleach 1635 DE Muileann chaol
The paper mill at Muileann chaol
A mill at Muileann chaol begins making paper from rags, the first on Rodos. The custody-book is copied onto paper for the first time in this generation.
27 an Giblean 1640 DE Muileann chaol
Three copies of the landfall report
Among her papers Beathag nic Thòmais finds three copies of the report of the two landfalls. They differ in the order of the coasts and in the number of hulls. She writes out all three side by side and does not choose between them.
3 an Cèitean 1655 DE Baile chrom
The north-west coast charted
The crown sends a reeve to list the households of the thinned north-west coast between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr. He counts fewer households than there are harbour berths.
24 an Lùnastal 1660 DE Muileann chaol
The loft at Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Thòmais dies and leaves her loft of papers to the town of Muileann chaol, on condition that nothing in it is burned. The town keeps the condition and very little else of her wishes.
6 am Màrt 1670 DE Cathair dhearg
King Tormod mac Ruairidh crowned
Tormod mac Ruairidh, of Clann Raghnaill, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. His reign is remembered for its roads and for its length.
5 an Gearran 1675 DE Seann Skell
The Scorpion's harbour prayer
The priests of the Yellow Scorpion at Seann Skell begin saying their prayer to keep the sea shut on the same day as the empty-harbour rite, so that the two are kept together on Cidhe an Diosail. Neither side is pleased.
6 am Màrt 1680 DE Cnoc ìseal
Tormod's bridges
King Tormod has stone bridges built across the fords of the south-central shires, one of them at Cnoc ìseal. Ferry-keepers who lose their living are given land in compensation.
9 an Dùbhlachd 1690 DE Imrich nam Pantar
The panther year
The panthers cross the southern roads in numbers no herder can remember, and for a whole season the crossing days run into one another. Flocks are kept in folds from Cnoc àrsaidh to the coast.
10 an t-Samhain 1695 DE Caol gharbh
Caol gharbh loses the salt
The salt pans of Caol gharbh fail as the sea rises over them, and salt comes to the north-east from the south instead. The town that took Ros fhionn's trade is poorer than Ros fhionn had been.
12 an Dàmhair 1700 DE Baile ghorm
Storm at Baile ghorm
A south-westerly storm floods the low town of Baile ghorm and drowns twenty-three. The town raises its sea-wall by the height of a man.
22 an Cèitean 1710 DE Seann Skell
The rite kept by few
The empty-harbour rite on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell is kept by the harbour priests and a few old families. A visiting scribe writes that no one present could say on which day the fleet had actually sailed.
23 an Giblean 1715 DE Cuan dhearg
Cuan dhearg flooded again
The sea comes over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg a second time, and the street moved back after An Gàire Dubh is flooded to the thresholds. The town builds a sea-wall and does not move again.
20 an Giblean 1720 DE Dùn thais
The house at Dùn thais reopened
The house of disputation at Dùn thais, closed and reopened more than once since the table of years, is opened again on condition that the question of longer lives is not raised. The scholars of the deer school accept the condition and argue about the vein instead.
9 an Dùbhlachd 1727 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of King Tormod
King Tormod mac Ruairidh dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. His daughter Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned.
12 an Giblean 1732 DE Cathair dhearg
Queen Gormshuil's progress
Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid makes a progress round every shire seat on the island, the first ruler to do so since Sìleas Òg. Her clerks record the grievances of each shire and the queen answers none of them in writing.
5 an Gearran 1737 DE Muileann dhearg
The second silver petition
Clann Choinnich again asks to burn the ore beyond the measure for the silver smelt at Muileann chiar, now with the support of three of the seven houses. Queen Gormshuil's council refuses by one voice. The record gives the name of the member who changed his vote and not his reason.
25 am Màrt 1747 DE An Taigh-òsta Grianach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach, on the eastern road, is recorded in the charter-roll as feeding the queen's progress with pan-fried spinach and black wine. The keeper, Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, is excused her road dues for a year.
27 an Gearran 1752 DE Muileann dhearg
The last census of hands
The vein-house counts the households holding the right to the ore for the last time in this age. They are fewer than at any count before, and larger. The custody-book notes that three of the seven houses now hold more than half the right between them.
22 an Cèitean 1755 DE Ceann mhòr
Timber from the west
A worked timber, longer than any tree on the island and fastened with nails of a make no smith on Rodos recognizes, comes ashore at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast. It is carried to Seann Skell, shown to the Scorpion's priests, and burned.
24 an Dàmhair 1760 DE Seann Skell
The lamps at Seann Skell go out
The night of lamps is kept at Seann Skell by fewer and fewer houses, and at last by none on the waterfront. An old woman sets a lamp in a window of the harbour-house, and the scribe records that it was she and not the town.
17 an t-Sultain 1764 DE Seann Skell
The empty-harbour rite, last entry of the age
The empty-harbour rite is kept at Seann Skell by eleven people. The harbour scribe enters their number, the weather and the state of the tide, and nothing else.
28 an Dùbhlachd 1767 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver petition laid aside
Clann Choinnich does not bring its silver petition to the council again, the member who had turned it having died. The petition is left in the vein-house unanswered, and the record of the age ends with the Small-Burning Law still kept.

Age IV · An Aois Choigreach the Age of Strangers

5 am Faoilleach 1780 DE
The Crossing
Humans make landfall on Rodos and are granted permission to stay — the first contact since the Sundering.
13 am Faoilleach 1780 DE Cuan shean
Three ships off Cuan shean
Three ships out of the west anchor off Cuan shean, the first hulls of their size seen from Rodos since the Sundering fleet. Their master, a captain the record calls Edmund Harrow, comes ashore unarmed with eleven men and asks by signs for water.
16 an t-Ògmhios 1780 DE Cuan shean
Forty days on the dunes
The custodians of Cuan shean send inland to the capital for counsel rather than decide alone. For forty days the strangers are fed on the beach and not allowed beyond the dunes.
10 an t-Iuchar 1780 DE Baile fhiadhaich
The custodian of Baile fhiadhaich rides south
Word of the ships reaches Baile fhiadhaich, up the western coast, in three days. Its custodian rides south to see them for himself and writes to the council that the strangers' ropes are better than ours and their manners worse.
11 am Faoilleach 1781 DE Cathair dhearg
The Council of Custodians grants leave
The Council of Custodians at Cathair dhearg, which has sat in the crown's place since the crown fell vacant at the close of the Sundering age, under the high custodian Tormod mac Ailein, confirms the strangers' leave to stay. The council roll records the vote as unanimous; a later hand has written in the margin that three custodians were absent.
9 an Gearran 1781 DE Cuan shean
The quarter of sea they came from
Old sailors at Cuan shean remark that the strangers came in from the same quarter of sea the Sundering fleet once sailed into. The council forbids the remark in its hall. It is written down anyway, and never answered.
26 an Gearran 1781 DE
The land beyond
The strangers name their homeland in their own tongue, but no Ròdaich scribe sets the word down. From the first season the record calls it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and calls its people simply the humans.
27 am Màrt 1781 DE
The first translation attempts
Human clerics and Rodian custodians spend a full season trying to build a shared vocabulary. Neither side's account of what was actually agreed to survives intact.
13 an Dùbhlachd 1781 DE Cathair dhearg
Wren's word-lists
The humans' cleric Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair keep parallel word-lists through the season of translation. Wren's list survives in the Administration's letter-books. Gormshuil's was lost; only its first leaf, with forty words for the colours of broken ore, is known from a copy.
24 an Cèitean 1782 DE Cathair dhearg
One word for the ore
The humans have a single word for the black ore, and it is the word for the fuel they burn at home. Gormshuil's copyist notes that no Ròdais word in either list answers to it, and that the humans did not ask for one.
22 an t-Ògmhios 1782 DE
Trade begins
Early exchange is genuinely reciprocal: Rodian goods for tools and knowledge the isolated island lacks. For a few years, the arrangement looks sustainable.
21 an t-Iuchar 1782 DE Ros dhomhain
The trading post at Ros dhomhain
The humans set up a trading post at Ros dhomhain, the capital's harbour: iron tools, window glass, lamp-oil and paper against wool, salt fish, hides and dyed cloth. The first tally-book of the post, kept by the trader Thomas Pike, balances evenly across its first year.
19 an Lùnastal 1782 DE Cathair naomh
Cathair naomh sends its wool
Cathair naomh, the city above Seann Toll on the northern coast, sends its first wool south to the humans' post by coasting boat. Its custodians ask for their payment in paper and ink, and use it to begin the town's roll afresh.
17 an t-Sultain 1783 DE Cathair dhearg
Iron in the smithies
The smiths of Cathair dhearg take the humans' bar-iron gladly and learn to temper it in a winter. Within a few seasons the old bronze hoes are melted down for bells.
4 an Dàmhair 1783 DE Baile Mòr mhòr
Dyes for Baile Mòr mhòr
The weavers of Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern coast, trade their cloth for the humans' dyes, a red and a blue brighter than any the island could make. Within a few years the old madder fields around the town are let go to grass.
16 an Dàmhair 1783 DE Cuan shean
Harrow's second voyage
Harrow sails west with hides and dyed cloth and returns with four ships instead of three. He brings carpenters, a surgeon, and a letter from a trading house in an Tìr Thall asking what else the island has.
14 an t-Samhain 1783 DE Inis mhòr
The shipwrights of Inis mhòr
The shipwrights of Inis mhòr come to look at the humans' hulls and measure them with knotted cords. Their guild had built nothing larger than a coaster since the fleet of the Sundering, and its old methods of building for deep water had been half forgotten.
13 an Dùbhlachd 1783 DE Cuan shean
The surgeon Jonas Tull
The humans' surgeon, Jonas Tull, sets the broken leg of a Cuan shean fisherman who had been given up as lame. The town's custodian enters it in the roll as the first debt owed to a stranger.
30 am Màrt 1784 DE Seann Warr
Salt from Seann Warr
The salt-pans of Seann Warr begin selling to Pike's post by the barrel. It is the first Ròdaich trade the humans come back asking for twice.
14 an Giblean 1784 DE Caol leathan
Wool at Caol leathan
The walled harbour of Caol leathan sends its first wool-ship to the humans' post. Its merchants insist on being paid in iron by weight rather than in goods, and the post's tally-book notes that they are the hardest bargainers on the island.
22 an Giblean 1784 DE
The first mixed settlement
A small coastal town accepts both Rodian and human residents under a single administration — an experiment later history will not repeat.
10 an Dàmhair 1784 DE Baile dhìreach
Baile dhìreach under one council
The small port of Baile dhìreach, on the south-west coast, takes Ròdaich and human residents under a single council of six, three of each. Its founding compact is written twice, once in each tongue, the only such compact on record in the age.
18 an Dàmhair 1784 DE Baile dhìreach
The first council of Baile dhìreach
The council is chaired in alternate years by the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim and the human carpenter William Rook. Harbour dues go half to the custodians at Cathair dhearg and half to the humans' post.
1 am Faoilleach 1785 DE Inis thais
Inis thais declines the compact
The city of Inis thais, whose harbour lies a few miles from Baile dhìreach, is invited to join the joint council and declines. Its custodian writes that one town may be an experiment but two would be a policy.
30 am Faoilleach 1785 DE An Cuan Siar
A supply ship lost on the western reefs
A human supply ship strikes the reefs off the western coast in fog, and nine of her crew drown. Her master had been sailing by a chart drawn from memory, the humans' letter-books complain, on a coast lit only by the old driftwood fires.
29 am Màrt 1785 DE
The lighthouses proposed
Human navigators, unused to Rodos's coastline, request permanent beacons. Ròdaich engineers agree, not yet understanding what the request will enable.
28 an Gearran 1786 DE Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
Surveying the beacon headlands
The human navigator James Fenn and the Ròdaich mason Torcall Clachair walk the coast together to choose sites for the new beacons. They mark the five headlands of the old fires. Fenn's chart survives; Torcall's cairns mostly do not.
26 an Cèitean 1786 DE Baile dhìreach
A marriage in two tongues
At Baile dhìreach the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh marries the human cooper Samuel Hale. The council enters the marriage in both its books, and the custodians at Cathair dhearg, asked for a ruling, send none.
27 an Giblean 1787 DE
The first written treaty
Terms of the human presence are set down formally for the first time — in the humans' language only, a detail no one on the Rodian side objects to at the time.
7 an Cèitean 1787 DE Cathair dhearg
The treaty signed at Cathair dhearg
The treaty is signed in the council hall at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein for the custodians and by Josiah Pell, newly come as the humans' first Commissioner, for the Administration. Tormod could not read the tongue it was written in. The record does not say who read it to him.
10 an Cèitean 1788 DE Ros dhomhain
The Residency above Ros dhomhain
Josiah Pell builds a house of dressed stone on the rise above Ros dhomhain and calls it the Residency. Captain Harrow, no longer needed ashore, returns to the sea trade.
18 an Cèitean 1788 DE Ros dhomhain
The Company chartered
Harrow and Pike form a trading house licensed by the Administration, known on Rodos simply as the Company. Its charter grants it first refusal on "all fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield."
28 an Dàmhair 1788 DE Cathair dhomhain
The warehouse at Cathair dhomhain
The Company leases a stone warehouse at Cathair dhomhain, up the coast from the capital, to store tools out of reach of the harbour thieves of Ros dhomhain. It is the first building on Rodos the Company owns outright.
5 an t-Samhain 1788 DE Cuan shean
The strangers' fever
A fever comes ashore with a crowded ship at Cuan shean and runs down the west coast. Ninety-one Ròdaich are recorded dead and eleven humans. The custodians close the town to ships for a season, and Pell protests the closure in writing.
9 an Gearran 1789 DE Baile àrsaidh
The fever at Baile àrsaidh
The strangers' fever reaches Baile àrsaidh, a day's walk up the coast, and kills its custodian and both of her sons. The town has no human residents at all, and the custodians of the west note the fact.
14 an t-Samhain 1789 DE Cnoc àrsaidh
The fever turned back at Cnoc àrsaidh
At Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west the townsfolk block the road with carts and turn back every traveller for a season. The fever does not reach them. The Administration fines the town for obstructing trade.
13 an Dùbhlachd 1789 DE Muileann chrom
Prospectors in the central hills
The Company sends two prospectors, Abel Stone and Hugh Mercer, into the hills east of the capital. They return with sacks of broken ore and a report that the black seam runs "further than can be walked in a day."
17 an t-Sultain 1790 DE Muileann chrom
The sacks returned to the rock
The custodians of the vein demand the broken ore back, to be laid in the rock again with the proper words. The Company returns half of it. The custodians' roll records the other half as "carried west."
19 an t-Sultain 1790 DE
First extraction contracts
What begins as trade curdles into arrangement: Rodian labor mines the vein at a scale no reverent tradition ever used.
16 an Dàmhair 1790 DE Muileann chrom
The first pit at Muileann chrom
Under the first contract a Ròdaich crew of thirty opens a working at Muileann chrom, paid by the ton in iron tools and lamp-oil. The custodians' own cuttings had never been measured by weight at all.
23 an t-Iuchar 1791 DE Ceann fhada
An ore quay at Ceann fhada
The Company builds a stone quay at Ceann fhada, a fishing hamlet below the hills, for loading ore onto coasting barges. The fishermen are paid for their foreshore in iron nails, by weight.
21 an Lùnastal 1791 DE Ros dhomhain
Wren's grammar
Samuel Wren completes a grammar of Ròdais for the Mission's use. It is careful and accurate in most particulars, and it renders the word for the vein's custodians as "keepers of the coal."
4 an t-Iuchar 1792 DE Cnoc bheag
The hawk-priests read Wren
The hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag ask the Mission for a copy of Wren's grammar so that they may read what the humans write about them. The Mission sends one. It is the most annotated copy to survive.
30 an Dùbhlachd 1792 DE Ros dhomhain
The Mission chapel
The Mission raises a timber chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain. Its bell is the first iron bell on the island, and the custodians ask that it not be rung before the fishing fleet is out.
29 am Màrt 1793 DE
The first refusal
A single mining settlement declines to sign an extraction contract. It is quietly bypassed rather than punished — for now.
27 an Giblean 1793 DE Doire mhòr
Beathag Dhubh of Doire mhòr
The settlement that refused was Doire mhòr, in the hills above Muileann chrom, and its custodian was Beathag Dhubh. Her answer to the Company's agent survives only in his paraphrase: that the hill was not hers to sell and not his to buy.
28 an Gearran 1794 DE Cnoc fhiadhaich
The road around Doire mhòr
The Company opens its next working at Cnoc fhiadhaich instead, and runs its cart-road around Doire mhòr's fields rather than through them.
9 an Cèitean 1794 DE Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg lit
The first of the new beacons is finished on the southern headland at Tobar dhearg, a round tower of grey stone raised over the old fire-tower, with a Ròdaich keeper, paid for by the Company. Torcall Clachair builds it; James Fenn sets its lens.
29 am Màrt 1795 DE Tobar dhearg
The first keeper of Tobar dhearg
The first keeper of the southern beacon is Anna nic Dhòmhnaill of Tobar dhearg village, a fisherman's widow, who climbs the tower twice a night for the rest of her life. The village takes the keepership as a trust and keeps it in its own families through the age.
10 an Giblean 1795 DE Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders in the north-western waters
A Company brig is boarded off the north-west coast and stripped of her cargo of tools. The raiders are never identified; the Administration blames the custodians of the coast, and the custodians say the waters there have always had their own law.
5 an Gearran 1796 DE Carragh Cnoc bheag
The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
Samuel Wren copies the inscription on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag and sends it west to the scholars of an Tìr Thall. No reply is recorded. The custodians tell him the stone is older than the Ròdaich and that nobody living can read it.
13 an Gearran 1796 DE
The currency reform
Human coinage is introduced alongside traditional barter, ostensibly for convenience. Within a decade it is the only accepted form of payment for anything requiring imported tools.
10 an Lùnastal 1796 DE Ros dhomhain
The mark and its hundred pence
The coins are struck at Ros dhomhain from silver and copper shipped in from an Tìr Thall: the mark and its hundred pence. The first issue bears a ship on one face and nothing Rodian on either.
1 am Faoilleach 1797 DE Cathair mhòr
Cathair mhòr refuses the mark
The market of Cathair mhòr, the largest in the hills east of the capital, refuses the humans' coin for a full year. The custodians of the town give way when the Company's tool-sellers refuse to cross their bridge.
30 am Faoilleach 1797 DE Cathair dhearg
Two books at the capital market
At Cathair dhearg's market, tool-sellers take only marks, while cloth and fish still go by barter. The custodians' clerks begin keeping two sets of books, and complain of it in both.
3 an Dùbhlachd 1797 DE Dùn thais
Wren's winter at Dùn thais
At Dùn thais the masters of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh receive Samuel Wren for a winter of disputation. He asks them why the vein should be holy; they ask him why his fuel should be burned. Neither account of the winter records a winner.
28 an Gearran 1798 DE Drochaid Cathair dhearg
Drochaid Cathair dhearg rebuilt
Company masons rebuild the old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg in dressed stone, wide enough for ore-carts to pass two abreast.
16 an t-Samhain 1798 DE Ros dhomhain
The Harbour Articles
A second agreement, the Harbour Articles, fixes dues and anchorages at Ros dhomhain in the Company's favour. Like the first treaty it is written in the humans' tongue only, and this time two custodians refuse to sign.
5 an Dàmhair 1799 DE Baile ghlas
The fishermen of Baile ghlas
The fishermen of Baile ghlas, whose boats had anchored free at Ros dhomhain since anyone could remember, are charged anchorage under the Harbour Articles. They move their catch to their own small harbour and sell it there to anyone but the Company.
3 an t-Samhain 1799 DE Muileann àrsaidh
The northern concession
The council grants the Administration upland pasture in the north-west, around Muileann àrsaidh, for human families who will not work in the pits. The grant is for grazing; the families build houses of stone.
15 an Dùbhlachd 1799 DE Cathair dhearg
Death of Tormod mac Ailein
The high custodian who signed the first treaty dies at Cathair dhearg. The council chooses Coinneach Glas of Ceann àrsaidh to follow him, a man who had never met a human before the Crossing and had dealt with little else since.
10 an t-Iuchar 1800 DE An Cuan Siar
Harrow lost at sea
Edmund Harrow's ship does not return from the western crossing. The Company passes wholly into Thomas Pike's hands, and the humans' letter-books mourn Harrow as the man who found Rodos.
2 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE
The Small-Burning Law lapses
Centuries of measured restraint end within a single generation. No formal repeal is recorded — it simply stops being enforced once it stops being profitable to enforce.
31 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE Doire mhin
The last count at Doire mhin
The custodians of Doire mhin keep the old count of the Small-Burning Law, the measure of ore that might be burned in a year, one season longer than anyone else. The count is entered in their roll with the note that nobody asked for it.
11 an t-Ògmhios 1801 DE Dùn dhearg
A defence of the Law at Dùn dhearg
A custodian of Dùn dhearg, Fionnghal nic Artair, writes a defence of the Small-Burning Law addressed to the council. It is the only such defence to survive. It argues that the Law was never about the ore but about the people who would become whatever the burning made them.
6 an t-Sultain 1801 DE Seann Skell
Murchadh Seabhag preaches at Seann Skell
At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Murchadh Seabhag preaches that Mòd, the Hungry Hawk, starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them. The sermon is copied and carried to the camps, where it is the first Ròdaich text the Company's agents are told to confiscate.
16 am Màrt 1802 DE Achadh naomh
The spirits' priests of Achadh naomh
The priests of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach at Achadh naomh, in the hills north of the workings, refuse to light their hearths with ore bought from the Company. They burn peat, as their grandparents did, and teach that ore burned for wages is ore burned without the ancestors' leave.
8 an Lùnastal 1802 DE Muileann chrom
Burning by the cartload
The Company's furnaces at Muileann chrom burn ore by the cartload to drive the new pumps, and the custodians' tally of what the hill may give in a year is not consulted. Coinneach Glas's council asks for the tally to be observed and receives a copy of the Company's accounts instead.
15 an Gearran 1803 DE Ros dhomhain
Henry Maddox Commissioner
Josiah Pell sails home to an Tìr Thall and does not come back. His successor, Henry Maddox, arrives with instructions to double the yield and a letter from the Company promising him a share of it.
12 am Màrt 1803 DE Cathair fhada
The oaks of Cathair fhada
Maddox buys the oak woods around Cathair fhada for pit-props. The woods had been cut sparingly by the town for generations. They are gone within the working life of the men who felled them.
26 an Giblean 1804 DE
The first mining deaths blamed on speed
A tunnel collapse, worked faster than any Rodian crew would have chosen to work it, kills eleven. It is recorded as an accident.
14 an Dàmhair 1804 DE Cnoc fhiadhaich
The eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich
The collapse was at Cnoc fhiadhaich, in a gallery driven forward without the timbering the Ròdaich crews had asked for. The custodians' roll names all eleven dead. The Company's report names none and calls the gallery "unsound ground."
11 an Gearran 1805 DE Muileann chrom
The coughing sickness
A dry cough runs through the camps at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich, worst among the boys who break ore at the pit-mouth. Thirty-eight die of it. The Mission's surgeon calls it a winter complaint; it lasts through the summer.
6 an t-Iuchar 1805 DE Cill thais
The orphans of Cill thais
The village of Cill thais takes in children orphaned by the coughing sickness, and keeps a house for them paid for by its own custodians. The Company, asked for a contribution, sends a crate of Mission primers.
4 an Lùnastal 1806 DE Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
Taigh-solais Baile ìseal lit
The second beacon is lit on the eastern shore at Baile ìseal. Torcall Clachair, too old now to climb, directs its building from a chair at the foot of the headland.
9 an Cèitean 1807 DE Baile ìseal
The keepers of Baile ìseal
The keepers of the eastern beacon are drawn from the fishing families of Baile ìseal. The town's custodians ask for, and get, a rule that the lamp will be lowered on the nights the boats go out to the deep grounds, so the fish will not be frightened. The rule lapses without anyone recording when.
7 an t-Ògmhios 1807 DE Àth ìseal
The camp at Àth ìseal
The Company founds a camp of timber huts at Àth ìseal, at the ford below the new workings, for crews brought in from the coast. It is the first settlement on Rodos built for no purpose but the pit.
20 an Cèitean 1808 DE Doire mhòr
Doire mhòr's water taken
The Company diverts the stream that watered Doire mhòr to wash ore at Cnoc fhiadhaich. No order is recorded; the stream is simply dammed one season and not released. Beathag Dhubh's people carry water by hand for two summers and then begin to leave.
21 an Lùnastal 1809 DE Muileann chrom
The short hunger in the hills
With men drawn from the farms into the pits, the hill villages of Muileann chrom lose their oat harvest to rain nobody was home to cut ahead of. The Company sells meal at the camp stores for marks; the villages have few.
12 an Dùbhlachd 1809 DE Doire fhiadhaich
Meal-carts at Doire fhiadhaich
The villages of Doire fhiadhaich in the south send carts of meal north to the hill villages, as the old custom of the Holy Age required in a hungry year. The Company's agents at Àth ìseal buy up two of the carts on the road.
15 an Dàmhair 1810 DE
Mass excavation begins in earnest
The mountain is worked by the ton for the first time in Rodian history, for purposes no Rodian tradition would have chosen.
13 an t-Samhain 1810 DE Dùn chrom
Rope for the winding-gear
The rope-walks of Dùn chrom, which had made cable for fishing boats, turn over entirely to winding-rope for the pit-heads. The Company pays well, and the town grows by half.
7 an Giblean 1811 DE Ros dhomhain
The Company's second charter
The Company is rechartered in an Tìr Thall with new capital and a new name the Ròdaich never adopt. Its agents at Ros dhomhain now outnumber the Administration's own clerks four to one.
16 an t-Sultain 1811 DE Cidhe Beag
Barges at Cidhe Beag
Ore barges begin loading at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine, floating the black ore downriver to the coast. The old canoe landing, used since before the Sundering, is widened with cut stone and its shrine moved uphill.
27 am Faoilleach 1812 DE Abhainn uaine
Abhainn uaine silts black
The washing of ore upstream silts Abhainn uaine with a black slurry, and the salmon runs at its mouth fail within a few seasons. The river's Ròdais name, the green river, is kept, and the fishermen use it bitterly.
1 an Lùnastal 1812 DE Baile Mòr dhomhain
Baile Mòr dhomhain a barge town
Baile Mòr dhomhain, on the river road, grows into the busiest barge town of the north as the ore comes down to it from Cidhe Beag. Its population doubles, mostly with bargemen from the coast.
10 am Faoilleach 1813 DE Baile dhomhain
Baile dhomhain raised as a camp town
A second camp, Baile dhomhain, is laid out on a grid by a Company surveyor, the first Ròdaich town drawn on paper before it was built. It is housing four hundred within two seasons.
1 an Lùnastal 1813 DE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
An Taigh-seinnse Mòr reopens
The old carters' house at the halfway stage of the ore road between the capital and the hills is rebuilt, and keeps the name An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. Its first keeper, Seònaid Bhàn, takes both marks and barter and is the only innkeeper on the road who will.
20 an Giblean 1814 DE Doire chaol
The carters of Doire chaol
The carters of Doire chaol, on the road just east of the capital, form a guild to bargain with the Company over rates for hauling ore. It is the first Ròdaich guild formed in the age, and the Company recognizes it because it is cheaper than breaking it.
3 an t-Iuchar 1814 DE Seann Toll
Seann Toll made an ore port
The Company takes over the harbour at Seann Toll, below the workings, and builds a loading stage there. The town's fishing boats are moved to the next cove.
19 an Cèitean 1815 DE
The first Rodian overseer appointed
A Ròdaich is given authority over other Rodian miners, answerable to human administrators — the first visible fracture within Rodian society itself, not just between it and the humans.
17 an t-Ògmhios 1815 DE Muileann chrom
Raghnall Maor
The first overseer is Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom, a crew-leader who had worked the pits since the first contract. He is given the Company's staff and a house with a slate roof, and from this office the Ròdaich give him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward.
21 an Lùnastal 1816 DE Muileann chrom
The overseers multiply
Within a few years there are overseers at every working in the district, all Ròdaich, all answerable to the Company's agents. The custodians' roll stops recording their names and records only their number.
14 an Lùnastal 1817 DE Cnoc mhòr
Seumas Dubh killed at Cnoc mhòr
The overseer of the new pits at Cnoc mhòr, Seumas Dubh, is killed by his own crew after a boy is crushed on a haulage he had ordered hurried. The Company hangs two men at Ros dhomhain, the first hanging carried out by the Administration on Rodos.
12 an t-Sultain 1817 DE Muileann chrom
Hawk-priests barred from the camps
Henry Maddox bars the priests of Creideamh an t-Seabhaig from the camps, on the ground that their preaching slows the work. The order is enforced by the overseers. Several of them are hawk-faithful themselves, and the roll says so.
11 an Dàmhair 1818 DE Ros dhomhain
The pox at Ros dhomhain
A spotted pox comes ashore on a Company ship at Ros dhomhain and moves up the ore road into the camps. The Mission counts four hundred and six dead; the custodians count more, and write the difference in the margin of the Mission's list.
9 an t-Samhain 1819 DE Baile chiar
The pox in the south
The pox spreads south from the harbour to Baile chiar and the villages round it. The custodians there keep a list of the dead on the lintel of the council house, cut into the stone, and it can still be read.
31 am Faoilleach 1820 DE Baile dhìreach
Baile dhìreach loses its harbour dues
The Administration moves its customs house from Baile dhìreach to Ros dhomhain and ends the division of harbour dues. The mixed council, left with half an income, cuts its members from six to four.
28 an t-Iuchar 1820 DE Ros dhomhain
Arthur Lisle Commissioner
Henry Maddox leaves Rodos a rich man. Arthur Lisle, a lawyer, replaces him, and his first act is to have every agreement since the first treaty copied into a single bound book.
2 am Màrt 1821 DE Ros gheal
A customs house at Ros gheal
Lisle opens a second customs house at Ros gheal on the northern coast, where hawk-faithful fishing towns had been trading with Company ships without paying dues. The customs officer is chased out of the town twice in his first year.
3 am Faoilleach 1822 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The Muileann chiar silver dispute
Human interests attempt to claim the silver seam at Muileann chiar as well. It is one of the few resources the Ròdaich successfully keep fully under their own control throughout this age.
31 am Màrt 1822 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Ùna nic Choinnich and the silver guild
The silver seam was held for the town by its guild of refiners, and the guild was led by Ùna nic Choinnich. When the Company's surveyors came she met them at the adit with the guild's whole membership and the guild's ledgers, and asked them to find the humans' name anywhere in either.
1 an Gearran 1823 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The Silver Compact
Arthur Lisle, reading the treaties closely, finds nothing in them that covers silver. He signs a compact with the silver guild leaving the seam to the town, the first document of the age in which the Ròdaich side keeps the better terms.
26 an t-Ògmhios 1823 DE Seann Bhral
Seann Bhral the silver port
The silver guild sends its bars to the sea through the old port of Seann Bhral rather than the Company's quays, and pays the port's custodians in silver for the use of it. The Company does not object, having no ground in the compact to object on.
21 am Faoilleach 1824 DE Baile gheal
The carters of Baile gheal
The carters of Baile gheal in the south-west take up the long haul of Seann Warr salt to the capital, a trade the Company does not bother to claim. It keeps the town's people out of the pits for the whole age.
10 an t-Iuchar 1824 DE Taigh-solais Àth dhearg
Taigh-solais Àth dhearg lit
The third beacon is lit on the north-east coast at Àth dhearg. Its keeper, Tormod mac Pheadair, keeps a daybook of every ship he sees, and it is from his book that the number of human sailings in these years is known.
28 an Cèitean 1825 DE Àth dhearg
Àth dhearg builds the tower
The masons of the beacon at Àth dhearg are townsmen of Àth dhearg, paid half in marks and half in the promise that the tower will guide their own boats home. Tormod mac Pheadair, the keeper, is one of them.
20 an Dàmhair 1825 DE Spùinneadairean-mara
Pirates off the eastern coast
A Company ore ship is taken off the eastern coast by raiders in low black boats and burned to the waterline, cargo and all. The Company says the raiders were paid by the silver guild. The silver guild says nothing.
25 an t-Iuchar 1826 DE Ceann leathan
A cove burned near Ceann leathan
A Company gunboat hunts the raiders to a cove near Ceann leathan and burns every boat drawn up on the shingle there. Most of them belonged to the town's fishermen. The raiders are not found.
23 an Lùnastal 1826 DE Baile dhìreach
The end of the joint council
The mixed council of Baile dhìreach breaks up in a quarrel over a boundary wall and is not reconvened. The human families move to Ros bheag and Ros dhomhain; the Ròdaich families stay. Those households that were both split or went quiet, and the record does not say which.
18 an t-Samhain 1826 DE Inis chrom
The boatyard moves to Inis chrom
The human boatbuilders of Baile dhìreach move their yard to Inis chrom, a day's sail east, where the Company has promised them timber. The town takes them in without a joint council or any other arrangement, and the record of their presence there fades within a generation.
21 an t-Sultain 1827 DE Achadh shean
The dry year in the east
Rain fails over the eastern farmlands around Achadh shean for a single season. It is remembered afterward as a warning nobody heeded, since the next dry spell, long after, came three years together.
20 an Dàmhair 1827 DE Baile ruadh
Baile ruadh loses its seed
At Baile ruadh in the east the dry season kills the seed corn in the ground, and the town borrows seed from the Company's store at Seann Dunn at a price paid back over five harvests. It is the first Ròdaich town to owe the Company a debt in grain.
19 an t-Ògmhios 1828 DE Dùn thais
Aonghas mac Coinnich's question
At Dùn thais the Deer master Aonghas mac Coinnich puts a question to his students that the school's register calls new: why the humans cannot see the colour in broken ore that every Ròdaich child sees. He does not answer it, and the register notes that he said it was the wrong question.
15 an Dùbhlachd 1828 DE Baile Mòr uaine
The Deer students of Baile Mòr uaine
Students of Aonghas mac Coinnich carry his question to Baile Mòr uaine and teach it in the town's hall of disputation. The hall's record of the argument runs to four hundred leaves and ends, like his, without an answer.
28 an Cèitean 1829 DE Cathair gheal
Cathair gheal on the concession
The human families of the northern concession found a market town at Cathair gheal, with a stone hall for their magistrate and a chapel. Its charter is issued by the Administration without reference to the custodians.
26 an t-Ògmhios 1829 DE Cnoc ghorm
Human farms at Cnoc ghorm
Human farmers of the concession clear land beside the Ròdaich village of Cnoc ghorm, in the upland north-west, and build a mill. The villagers sell them grain until the mill is working and then stop.
14 am Màrt 1830 DE Ceann mhòr
A fishing station at Ceann mhòr
A few human fishing families of the concession settle at Ceann mhòr, the harbour under the north-western headland. They are the first humans to fish the island's waters for a living rather than for the Company's table.
10 an Giblean 1830 DE
The first Rodian child sent abroad
A single family, hoping to secure better treatment, sends a son to be educated in the humans' home country. He is never recorded returning.
12 an Giblean 1830 DE Ceann àrsaidh
The family of Eachann Mòr
The family that sent its son away was that of Eachann Mòr, a custodian of Ceann àrsaidh who had lost his place on the council. The boy, Calum, sailed west on a Company ship with a letter of introduction from the Mission and a purse of marks.
9 an Cèitean 1831 DE Ros dhomhain
The Mission school
The Mission opens a school at Ros dhomhain for Ròdaich children, taught in the humans' tongue. It takes thirty pupils in its first year, most of them the children of overseers.
7 an t-Ògmhios 1831 DE Inis bhàn
Schooling at Inis bhàn
The custodians of Inis bhàn in the north open a school of their own in answer to the Mission's, teaching the old reckoning, the rolls and the names of the hills. The Mission complains that the pupils come to its own school the next year already knowing how to argue.
1 an Giblean 1832 DE Drochaid Ros fhionn
Drochaid Ros fhionn
The Company rebuilds the old bridge over the river at Ros fhionn to carry the eastern ore road. For as long as the carts run, it is the busiest crossing on that side of the island.
29 an Dàmhair 1832 DE Inis bheag
Ore through Inis bheag
Ore from the eastern workings is carted over the new bridge and down to the harbour of Inis bheag for shipment. The harbour is deepened by the Company, and the town's old fish market is moved to make room for the ore stage.
13 am Faoilleach 1833 DE Baile mhin
Baile mhin ships the eastern ore
The harbour of Baile mhin on the north-eastern coast takes the overflow of eastern ore that Inis bheag cannot load. The townsfolk are paid by the barge and the town builds its first stone houses on the proceeds.
11 an Gearran 1834 DE Caol gharbh
Caol gharbh bypassed
The ore road to Inis bheag passes Caol gharbh by a mile, and the town, which had hoped for the traffic, gets only its dust. Its custodians write that they had not known a town could be damaged by a road it was not on.
12 am Màrt 1834 DE Uilebheist na Mara
The thing in the north-western sea
The crew of a Company brig report a beast larger than their ship off the north-western headlands. The Administration's clerk files the report with the complaints about pirates, and the Ròdaich sailors of the coast say they had wondered when the humans would see it.
21 an Lùnastal 1835 DE Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
Surveyors lost at Doire uaine
Two Company surveyors go up into the hills at Doire uaine against the advice of the villagers and are not seen again. The Company sends a search party, which comes back after a day and refuses to go further.
19 an t-Sultain 1835 DE Doire uaine
The offerings at Doire uaine
The villagers of Doire uaine leave offerings of salt and ore at the foot of the hills after the surveyors are lost, as they had in their grandparents' time after any death on the high ground. The Company forbids ore to be left lying and has the offerings collected, and the villagers change to salt alone.
16 an Gearran 1836 DE
The tithe increase
The portion of mined obsidian claimed by human administrators rises sharply, with no corresponding rise in what Rodian communities receive.
13 an Lùnastal 1836 DE Ros dhomhain
Lisle's tithe schedule
The new schedule is issued at the Residency over Arthur Lisle's signature, raising the Administration's portion from one part in five to one part in three. The custodians receive a copy in the humans' tongue and a translation made by a Mission pupil.
4 an Lùnastal 1837 DE Dùn fhiadhaich
Weighing the grain at Dùn fhiadhaich
At Dùn fhiadhaich the tithe-collectors begin weighing grain as well as ore, on the ground that the town's farms feed the pits and share in the pits' profit. The custodians' roll calls this the tithe on the tithe.
6 an t-Iuchar 1838 DE Ros dhomhain
The flux at Ros dhomhain
A bloody flux breaks out in the crowded quarters at the Ros dhomhain quays. The Mission's nurse, Anne Colby, sets up a sick-house in the chapel, and the record credits her with keeping the dead to under two hundred.
7 an t-Ògmhios 1839 DE Seann Vell
The flux reaches Seann Vell
The flux spreads to Seann Vell, the port a little east along the coast, carried by the ore barges. The custodians of the town close the barge landing for a season and are fined for it by the Company.
3 am Màrt 1840 DE Ros dhomhain
Walter Crane Commissioner
Arthur Lisle dies at the Residency of a fever of the heart. Walter Crane, who had been the Company's chief agent at the pits, is appointed Commissioner in his place, the first to hold both offices in succession.
6 an t-Sultain 1840 DE Ceann mhin
The pay office at Ceann mhin
Crane moves the Company's pay office for the southern workings to Ceann mhin, and has the crews walk there to be paid rather than send the paymaster to them. The walk is a day each way. The crews are not paid for it.
12 am Màrt 1841 DE Muileann chrom
Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor
Raghnall Maor dies, and the Company gives his staff to his son Dòmhnall. The overseer's office, which the custodians had hoped would lapse with the man, becomes a family's inheritance.
