11 an Gearran 1842 DE Taigh-solais Muileann bheag
Taigh-solais Muileann bheag lit
The fourth beacon is lit on the northern shore at Muileann bheag. It is the first to burn ore instead of oil, and the keepers report that its flame throws a colour on the water no oil lamp ever did.
13 am Faoilleach 1843 DE Muileann bheag
The fishermen of Muileann bheag
The fishermen of Muileann bheag complain that the ore flame of the new beacon casts a colour on the water that drives the herring off. The keepers do not change the lamp. The herring come back within a season, and the complaint is withdrawn in a letter that the Company keeps.
27 an Giblean 1843 DE Làrach an Teampaill
The dig at Làrach an Teampaill
The Mission cleric Edwin Lowe digs at Làrach an Teampaill for a season with Company labourers, looking for proof of an older faith on the island. He finds cut stone, burnt bone and marks he cannot read, and writes that the ruin's builders "were not the present race." The custodians agree, and add nothing.
9 an Lùnastal 1844 DE Colbh Cnoc chiar
The pillar at Cnoc chiar
Edwin Lowe copies the inscription on the pillar near Cnoc chiar and compares it with Wren's copy of the obelisk at Cnoc bheag. He decides the two scripts are not the same and that neither is Ròdaich. His notes stop there.
28 an Gearran 1845 DE Calbh Cnoc ghorm
The column at Cnoc ghorm
Lowe's last copy is of the column near Cnoc ghorm, and he writes beside it that its marks resemble the pillar's but not closely enough to help. He leaves Rodos the next year, and his notebooks go with him.
1 am Faoilleach 1846 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver guild refuses again
A Company agent, Martha Gale, offers the silver guild of Muileann chiar a partnership, on terms the guild's ledger calls generous. Ùna nic Choinnich, now very old, has the offer read aloud twice in the guild hall and then refused by show of hands.
29 am Màrt 1846 DE Achadh dhomhain
The camp at Achadh dhomhain
A new camp is opened at Achadh dhomhain for the deep galleries under the hill, and within a few seasons it is the most crowded settlement in the district. Its houses are built of spoil.
30 am Faoilleach 1847 DE Dùn chiar
Cloth for the camps at Dùn chiar
The weavers of Dùn chiar take a Company contract to supply canvas for the camp tents and sacks for the ore. The town prospers on it, and its custodians note that it is the first time the town has made anything for a use it did not approve of.
7 am Màrt 1848 DE
The first of the immortal generation
A child born into the mining camps is exposed to more raw ore across her lifetime than any Rodian in living memory — and does not age the way the people around her do. Her name is Aisling.
3 an Dùbhlachd 1849 DE Ros dhomhain
The ore weighed at the quay
The Company installs a great steelyard at the Ros dhomhain quay, and from now on the island's yield is known by the ton and the hundredweight. The custodians' old count, kept in seasons of labour, stops being entered in the roll.
15 an Dùbhlachd 1849 DE Ros dhìreach
Ros dhìreach the second ore port
The Company opens a second ore stage at Ros dhìreach on the southern coast for the workings south of the hills. Its first cargo is lost in a squall off the harbour mouth, and the fishermen who had been moved to make room for the stage refuse to go out after it.
13 am Faoilleach 1850 DE
The condition goes unnamed
Whatever is happening to the child born two years earlier has no word yet, in any language spoken on the island. It will be decades before anyone tries to coin one.
19 an t-Sultain 1851 DE Cill dhìreach
The shrine at Cill dhìreach
At Cill dhìreach, a village on the edge of the workings, the custodians keep a small shrine where the pit crews leave the first piece of ore of each new gallery. The Company tolerates the custom because it costs a stone a gallery.
18 an Dàmhair 1851 DE Cill ghlas
The keepers of Cill ghlas
The custodians of the shrine at Cill ghlas, in the hills among the workings, keep the old rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting while the Company's pits deepen around them. It is the last shrine in the district still visited on the old feast days by the pit crews.
9 an t-Ògmhios 1852 DE
A' Phlàigh Uaine
The Green Death moves through the mining camps — the ore dust itself is blamed, though no formal study is ever completed. Twenty-six settlements record cases.
5 an Dùbhlachd 1852 DE Achadh dhomhain
The first cases at Achadh dhomhain
The Green Death is first noticed at Achadh dhomhain: a greenish pallor, then a cough that brings up dark dust, then weakness. The camp buries forty in its first month, in a field outside the spoil-heaps that is still called the green acre.
13 am Faoilleach 1853 DE A' Phlàigh Uaine
Twenty-six settlements
The sickness spreads along the ore roads from the camps at Muileann chrom, Àth ìseal and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and falls hardest on Ros dhìreach, Ceann òg, Inis ìseal, Baile dhomhain, Achadh fhada, Cnoc bheag, Muileann uaine, Cuan àrsaidh and Inis bhàn. The custodians' roll lists the twenty-six settlements that record cases and leaves a blank line after the last, as if expecting another.
11 an Gearran 1853 DE Baile chrom
The Green Death at Baile chrom
The Green Death reaches Baile chrom in the hills, not the town of the same name in the north-west. The record distinguishes them with care, because in later years the names become confused in the retelling of the island's hungers.
12 am Màrt 1853 DE Àth ghlas
Àth ghlas burns its huts
At Àth ghlas the custodians order every hut in which a death has occurred burned with its bedding. The Company protests the loss of its property. The custodians note that the sickness stops at Àth ghlas sooner than anywhere else.
10 an Giblean 1853 DE Cnoc naomh
The dead of Cnoc naomh
At Cnoc naomh the dead of the Green Death are buried in the churchyard of the town's old shrine until the ground is full, and then in a field outside it. The field is never ploughed again.
30 am Faoilleach 1854 DE Muileann chrom
Doctor Bright's study
The Administration's physician, Nathaniel Bright, begins a study of the sickness at Muileann chrom, weighing the dust in the lungs of the dead. He falls ill in the second season of his work, and his notebooks break off in the middle of a table.
28 an Gearran 1854 DE Ros dhomhain
Walter Crane dies of the Green Death
Commissioner Crane, who had walked the camps during the worst of the sickness, dies of it at the Residency. The Company's agent at Ros dhomhain, Martha Gale, holds his seal for the months until a successor arrives.
13 am Màrt 1855 DE Ros dhomhain
George Tolley Commissioner
George Tolley arrives from an Tìr Thall with orders that the yield must not fall because of the sickness. He does not visit the camps. His letter-book blames the dust, the Ròdaich custom of sleeping near the fire, and the custodians' shrines, in that order.
11 an Giblean 1855 DE Caol mhin
Quarantine at Caol mhin
Tolley sets up a quarantine station at Caol mhin on the northern coast for ships arriving from an Tìr Thall, holding them offshore until their crews are inspected. It is the first order of his administration the Ròdaich approve of, and they say so.
10 an Cèitean 1855 DE Muileann chrom
The camps turn to the hawk
With the hawk-priests still barred from the camps, their sermons are carried in by the crews themselves. The overseers' reports of these years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a disciplinary matter.
17 an Giblean 1856 DE Ros dhomhain
Anne Colby's sick-houses
Anne Colby opens sick-houses at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain and nurses there until the sickness ebbs. She is the only human the camp people name in their own accounts of the plague, and they name her kindly.
25 an Giblean 1856 DE Cnoc gharbh
The huts of Cnoc gharbh
Cnoc gharbh, whose people had worked the southern galleries, abandons its camp huts after the sickness and moves back to the old village on the hill. The Company rebuilds the huts the next year and brings in crews from the west.
13 an Dàmhair 1856 DE
The first work-refusal strike
An entire mining settlement halts extraction for eleven days over conditions worsened by the plague two years prior. It ends when food supplies, controlled by human administrators, run out.
21 an Dàmhair 1856 DE Baile thais
The strike at Baile thais
The settlement was Baile thais, below Cill ghlas, and the halt was called by the crew-leader Catrìona nic Eachainn after the Company refused to close the galleries where the Green Death had been worst. For eleven days no ore left the town. On the twelfth the Company's store, the only store, was empty.
2 an Dàmhair 1857 DE Baile thais
The Company's granary
After the strike the Company builds a granary of its own at Muileann chrom and forbids the camps to keep grain beyond a week's ration. The order is enforced by the overseers and signed by Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor.
31 an Dàmhair 1858 DE Ros gharbh
Fish smuggled from Ros gharbh
The fishermen of Ros gharbh carry salt fish up to the camps by night, past the Company's granary rule. The custodians' roll calls it the only trade of the decade that ran in the right direction.
29 an t-Samhain 1858 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Catrìona goes to the silver town
Turned out of Baile thais and refused work at every Company pit, Catrìona nic Eachainn goes east to Muileann chiar, where the silver guild takes her on as a refiner. The Company asks for her to be sent back. The guild's reply is filed but not preserved.
3 an t-Sultain 1859 DE Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The springs at Muileann ruadh
The Administration builds a new bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh for officials recovering from fevers. Ròdaich who had bathed there for centuries are admitted on certain days and charged a penny.
11 am Màrt 1860 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Muileann chiar expands
The silver town grows alongside the obsidian operation, human demand for both metals accelerating extraction the reverent tradition never would have permitted.
7 an t-Iuchar 1861 DE Muileann chiar
A second Muileann chiar
The growth of the silver trade crowds the old town, and the guild founds a daughter settlement to the west for its refiners and carters, which takes the same name. The record calls them the old town and the new, and does not always say which it means.
8 an t-Ògmhios 1862 DE Muileann chiar
Silver for marks
The silver guild begins selling bar silver to the Company for marks at a price the guild fixes. It is the only commodity on Rodos in the age priced by Ròdaich hands, and the guild's hall fills with human coin.
28 an Dùbhlachd 1863 DE Muileann bhàn
Silversmiths at Muileann bhàn
Silversmiths settle at Muileann bhàn on the road to the silver town and make a living working the guild's bar into ornaments for the humans' market. Their work is the one Ròdaich craft sold in an Tìr Thall under a Ròdaich name.
24 an Gearran 1864 DE Cathair dhearg
The Dark Unicorn blesses the coin
The priests of Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh at Cathair dhearg, the capital's own faith, bless the Residency's new coin at Tolley's request. The dualist priesthood teaches that the dark and the light each have their due; the dissenting priests say the coin is only one of them.
2 an Dàmhair 1865 DE
The second currency reform
Rodian barter goods are formally devalued against human coinage a second time, on terms set entirely by the human administration.
31 an Dàmhair 1865 DE Baile Mòr fhionn
Wool devalued at Baile Mòr fhionn
At Baile Mòr fhionn, where wool had been the measure of every bargain, a fleece is now worth by the Residency's table what a half-fleece was worth before. The town's weavers stop bringing wool to market and send it overseas on their own account, until the Company refuses them freight.
2 an Gearran 1866 DE Caol fhiadhaich
The boats of Caol fhiadhaich sold
The fishing fleet of Caol fhiadhaich, unable to pay the new harbour dues in marks, sells half its boats to the Company. The men who sailed them go into the pits under the next year's contracts.
25 am Màrt 1866 DE Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The dissenters go to Cnoc bheag
Priests of the Dark Unicorn who refused the blessing leave the capital's temple and settle in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag. Their community there keeps the older reading of the dual faith, and becomes a place where custodians who have lost their seats are received.
23 an Giblean 1866 DE Muileann chrom
Iain Maor
Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor dies, and his son Iain takes the overseer's staff. Iain Maor is the first overseer to have been schooled at the Mission; he keeps his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Ròdais.
4 am Faoilleach 1867 DE Ros dhomhain
The Levy
Tolley issues an ordinance, the Levy, requiring every farming village in the west and north to send one in five of its able adults to the pits for a term of two years. The villages are compensated in marks, at the new rate.
3 am Màrt 1867 DE Caol mhòr
Levy officers at Caol mhòr
The Levy's officers take their first quota at Caol mhòr in the north-west, reading the names of the chosen from a list in the humans' tongue. The custodians of the town take down the names again in Ròdais, so that they will know whom to look for.
6 an Dùbhlachd 1867 DE Muileann àrsaidh
The Levy in the north-west
The Levy falls hardest on the villages around Baile chrom and the northern concession, which had never sent crews to the pits. The Ròdaich of the concession are taken; the human farmers of the concession are exempt.
2 an t-Ògmhios 1868 DE Baile ìseal
Baile ìseal sends its people
Baile ìseal sends forty-one of its people to the pits under the Levy. Nineteen come back when their term ends. The custodians' roll gives the names of the other twenty-two and the camps they were sent to.
6 an Dùbhlachd 1868 DE Muileann naomh
Muileann naomh buys its way out
The custodians of Muileann naomh pay the Levy's officers in silver to reduce the town's quota by half. The officers take the silver and the full quota. The complaint is lodged at the Residency and filed.
14 an Dùbhlachd 1868 DE Dùn thais
The Deer school's hall closed
George Tolley closes the hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh at Dùn thais, citing a lecture on whether the humans' blindness to the ore's colour is a kind of sickness. The masters go on teaching in their own houses, to smaller rooms each year.
30 an Giblean 1869 DE Doire chiar
The last disputation at Doire chiar
At Doire chiar, a Deer village north of the eastern workings, the masters hold the last public disputation of the school in the open air, in the village's threshing-floor. Its subject is whether a question may be forbidden. The Administration's clerk who attends records that it may.
15 an t-Ògmhios 1869 DE Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
Teaching in the sacred forest
Masters of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh who can no longer teach in a hall begin teaching in the sacred forest near Muileann chiar, under the trees, where the Administration has no building to close.
14 an t-Iuchar 1869 DE Taigh-solais Baile chrom
Building the last beacon at Baile chrom
Work begins on the fifth and last beacon, on the north-western headland at Baile chrom, with masons drawn by the Levy from the same villages whose fields they leave unworked.
27 an t-Ògmhios 1870 DE Cnoc thais
The masons of Cnoc thais
The masons of Cnoc thais are taken by the Levy to build the beacon at Baile chrom. Their foreman, Dùghall Clachair, cuts the names of his crew into the lintel of the lamp-room. It is the only inscription on any of the five towers.
26 an t-Iuchar 1870 DE Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The five lighthouses complete
Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag, Àth dhearg and Tobar dhearg — the full ring of coastal beacons is finished, built to serve trade that is by now extraction in every way but name.
24 an Lùnastal 1870 DE Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh loses its trade
With the ring of beacons finished, Company steamers round the island without stopping, and the old coastal trade of Cuan ruadh, which had carried goods up and down the eastern shore, dies within a few years.
22 an t-Sultain 1870 DE Taigh-solais Baile chrom
Taigh-solais Baile chrom lit
The beacon at Baile chrom is lit with an ore flame, completing the ring. The Company's ships can now round the island by night, and the keepers' daybooks record the sailings doubling in the next few years.
3 am Màrt 1873 DE
Gorta Baile chrom
The Great Hunger follows a failed harvest across thirty-four settlements, worsened by a mining workforce too depleted by mass conscription to farm its own land.
1 an Giblean 1873 DE Baile chrom
Baile chrom goes hungry
The hunger is worst at Baile chrom itself, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields. The custodians record that more died there than in any other settlement, and the Administration, which kept its own count, does not dispute the figure.
30 an Giblean 1874 DE Doire ghlas
The hunger at Doire ghlas
At Doire ghlas in the north the hunger takes the old and the very young first. The village sends its young to the camps for the Company's rations and is half empty by the end of the year.
29 an Cèitean 1874 DE Inis mhin
Inis mhin eats its seed
At Inis mhin on the north coast the townsfolk eat their seed corn in the second winter of the hunger. The Mission kitchen at the harbour feeds three hundred a day for a season.
7 an t-Samhain 1875 DE Seann Bhrenn
The hunger reaches Seann Bhrenn
The hunger reaches as far east as Seann Bhrenn, where the custodians open the old grain-pits of the Holy Age, which had not been filled in living memory. They are found to hold only dust.
6 an Dùbhlachd 1875 DE Ros dhomhain
The relief ship
A relief ship with grain from an Tìr Thall is held at Ros dhomhain for a month while the Residency and the Company argue over who is to pay for its unloading. The Mission opens kitchens at Cathair gheal and Baile chrom meanwhile, and Anne Colby, returned to the island, runs the one at Baile chrom.
20 an Gearran 1876 DE Baile chrom
The Levy suspended
The Levy is suspended in the famine districts, too late for the harvest. It is not repealed. The custodians note that it was never used again, and that it never needed to be, since the villages had learned what it meant.
17 an Lùnastal 1876 DE Cnoc mhòr
Cnoc mhòr walks south
The families of Cnoc mhòr in the north walk south to the camps rather than starve, and take work under the Company. Their village stands empty for a generation.
9 an Dàmhair 1877 DE Ros dhomhain
Robert Haskins Commissioner
George Tolley retires with honours. Robert Haskins, his successor, orders that the custodians' council be consulted on the tithe, then sets the tithe before the council has met.
7 an t-Samhain 1877 DE Seann Dunn
Customs at Seann Dunn
Haskins opens a customs house at Seann Dunn on the eastern coast and a Company store with it. The store sells the east its seed and its tools, and within a few years its ledgers hold the debts of half the district.
4 am Faoilleach 1878 DE
The first organized petition
Rodian custodians, for the first time acting jointly rather than settlement by settlement, submit a formal grievance to the human administration. It is not answered.
3 am Màrt 1878 DE Ceann àrsaidh
The conclave at Ceann àrsaidh
The petition was drawn up at Ceann àrsaidh by custodians from nineteen settlements, meeting for the first time as one body. It was carried to the Residency by the custodian of Cill ghlas, a woman named Peigi Ghlas, and handed to a clerk.
6 an Dùbhlachd 1878 DE Àth fhionn
Àth fhionn signs
The custodian of Àth fhionn in the south-east, Ruairidh mac Thormoid, is the oldest of those who signed the petition. He had been born before the humans' coin was struck, and he says so beside his signature.
27 am Faoilleach 1880 DE
Resentment first recorded
The earliest surviving Ròdaich grievance texts date from this period — not yet organized resistance, but the first written acknowledgment that something has gone wrong.
18 an t-Sultain 1880 DE Baile thais
Leabhar Baile thais
The earliest grievance text to survive is a book of complaints kept at Baile thais, set down by many hands over some years: wages, deaths, the granary, the stream at Doire mhòr. The custodians' copyists call it Leabhar Baile thais.
17 am Faoilleach 1881 DE Muileann dhearg
The songs of Fearchar Bàrd
The poet Fearchar Bàrd, a breaker of ore at Muileann dhearg since boyhood, makes songs of the Levy and the famine that are sung in the camps. The overseers forbid them, and the prohibition is the reason several of them were written down.
23 an Dùbhlachd 1881 DE An Taigh-òsta Grianach
Songs at An Taigh-òsta Grianach
The songs of Fearchar Bàrd are sung in the roadside houses of the east, and An Taigh-òsta Grianach becomes known for them. The Company's carters sing them too, the keeper records, without always knowing what they are singing.
15 an Gearran 1882 DE Ros dhomhain
The Company's deep-water quay
The Company builds a deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain able to take the new iron steamships, which burn the island's own ore to carry it away. Fearchar Bàrd makes a song of that, and it is the one of his most often quoted.
20 an t-Samhain 1882 DE Ceann chaol
The deep quay at Ceann chaol
A second deep-water quay is built at Ceann chaol in the south-east for the eastern ore. Its builders are brought from the coast, and the town, which had been a village of forty houses, is a town of four hundred.
23 an t-Sultain 1883 DE Baile thais
Baile thais walls its pithead
The Company rings the pithead at Baile thais with a stone wall and a gate, with a watchman paid to keep count of who goes in. It is the first working on Rodos to be walled against its own crews.
19 an Dùbhlachd 1883 DE Baile thais
Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at the silver town
Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at Muileann chiar, a refiner of the silver guild to the end. The camp people of Baile thais send a delegation to her burying, and the Company docks each of them a day's pay.
4 an Giblean 1884 DE Ros dhomhain
The quay fire
A fire starts in the Company's ore sheds at Ros dhomhain and burns for three days, taking two streets of the harbour quarter with it. The Company's investigation finds no cause; the harbour quarter's own account has several.
22 an t-Sultain 1884 DE Cathair dhearg
The council meets without a high custodian
The Council of Custodians fails to agree on a new high custodian after the death of the last, and sits for years with the seat empty. Robert Haskins writes to an Tìr Thall that this makes the council easier to deal with.
25 an Lùnastal 1885 DE
Tiormachd Achadh shean
The Long Drought settles over the island's dry season for three consecutive years, straining a population already stretched thin by extraction quotas.
28 an t-Ògmhios 1886 DE Achadh shean
The wells of Achadh shean
At Achadh shean, whose name the drought bears, the wells fail in the second summer and the cattle are driven west in a column that the roll says was a day long. Fewer than half of them reach water.
27 an t-Iuchar 1886 DE Tiormachd Achadh shean
The dry country
Ten districts of the east are counted as drought country by the custodians' roll, worst at Achadh shean, Àth uaine, Achadh àrsaidh and Muileann chiar, and reaching down to Cuan ruadh and west toward Baile chaol. The Administration keeps no count of its own.
6 an t-Sultain 1886 DE Baile chaol
The cattle of Baile chaol
At Baile chaol the herds are slaughtered in the second summer of the drought rather than watched to die. The salted meat is sold to the Company for the camps, at a price the Company names.
5 an Dàmhair 1886 DE Doire fhionn
Doire fhionn walks for water
At Doire fhionn in the east the women walk to the spring at Àth ruadh and back each day for water, a journey of half a day. The custodians record this for the three dry years and then stop recording it.
1 an Cèitean 1887 DE Allt an Àigh
Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
The spring of Allt an Àigh, said never to have failed, keeps running through all three dry years. Pilgrims of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach come to it from across the east, and the Administration posts a watchman to charge them for the water. He is recalled after a single season.
30 an Cèitean 1887 DE Inis uaine
The pilgrims' road at Inis uaine
Pilgrims bound for Allt an Àigh gather at Inis uaine, and the town's people feed them without charge, as the old spirits require. The town's own wells are low, and it gives away more water than it keeps.
25 an Giblean 1888 DE Baile Mòr ruadh
Drought-fever at Baile Mòr ruadh
A fever of bad water follows the drought into the towns, worst at Baile Mòr ruadh, where the wells had been deepened into the old middens. Two hundred and sixty die. The Mission's report is the first to name the cause correctly.
3 an Cèitean 1888 DE Cnoc shean
The fever at Cnoc shean
The drought-fever spreads to Cnoc shean, where the town's single well is found to be tainted. The custodians close it and the town drinks from carts for a year.
29 an Dàmhair 1888 DE Achadh shean
The Mission's wells
The Mission digs deep wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom with a boring-rig brought from an Tìr Thall. They hold. The custodians of the east record the Mission's wells alongside the Company's quotas, without comment, on facing pages.
16 am Màrt 1889 DE Achadh chaol
Achadh chaol goes to the pits
The people of Achadh chaol in the north-east, their fields burned out by the drought, go to the pits for wages. They are the first villagers of the eastern farming country to do so, and their custodian records it as the end of the village rather than a move.
25 an Lùnastal 1889 DE Baile Mòr dhìreach
The quota not lowered
The ore quota is not lowered during the drought. The custodians of the east petition Haskins singly, since the joint petition had not been answered; he replies to each that the matter is under consideration.
3 an Gearran 1890 DE Àth mhòr
The petition of Àth mhòr
The custodian of Àth mhòr, Iseabail nic Leòid, writes the longest of the single petitions, forty pages cataloguing her town's dead animals. Haskins replies in two lines. Both documents survive, bound together by a later clerk.
15 an Gearran 1890 DE
The first mixed-blood inheritance dispute
A legal case over whether a child of one Rodian and one human parent may inherit customary mining rights sets a precedent the administration writes entirely to its own benefit.
4 am Màrt 1890 DE Ros dhomhain
The case of Thomas Hale
The child in the case was Thomas Hale, a grandson of the Baile dhìreach marriage of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale, who claimed a share in a customary cutting through his Ròdaich grandmother. The magistrate at Ros dhomhain, Oliver Dunstan, ruled that customary rights descend only through the line the Administration recognizes, and that it recognizes only its own.
2 an Giblean 1891 DE Ros dhomhain
Dunstan's rule applied
Within a few years Dunstan's ruling has been used to transfer eleven customary cuttings to the Company, each on the ground that some owner in the line had married a human or been born to one. The custodians stop entering such marriages in the roll.
25 an t-Ògmhios 1892 DE Cnoc dhubh
A cutting at Cnoc dhubh transferred
Among the cuttings transferred under Dunstan's rule is the old customary working at Cnoc dhubh, held by the same family since the Holy Age. A great-grandmother in the line had married a human sailor; that is enough.
29 an Dùbhlachd 1892 DE Baile thais
The Lamp-Watch
A society of pit crews calling itself the Lamp-Watch begins meeting at Baile thais and Cnoc chaol under cover of a burial club. Its first known act is to pay for the burial of an old breaker who had died in the Company's lock-up.
28 an t-Ògmhios 1893 DE Ros dhomhain
Edward Vane Commissioner
Robert Haskins is recalled after a quarrel with the Company over the price of steamship berths. Edward Vane replaces him. Vane is the first Commissioner to have been born on Rodos, at the Residency, and he speaks Ròdais badly, but at all.
27 an t-Iuchar 1894 DE Ros dhìreach
The tram-road to Ros dhìreach
Vane lays an iron tram-road from the southern workings down to the ore port at Ros dhìreach, drawn by mules. It halves the cost of shipping ore and ends the carting trade of the villages along the old road.
25 an Lùnastal 1895 DE
The night-shift order
Extraction is extended to run continuously, day and night, for the first time — the mountain given no season of rest at all.
23 an t-Sultain 1895 DE Cnoc chaol
The night crews at Cnoc chaol
The order is felt first at Cnoc chaol, where the Company's newest galleries are opened to crews working by ore-lamp in two shifts. The custodians' roll records that the hill was given no silence at all, and then leaves the rest of the page blank.
3 an Lùnastal 1896 DE Cnoc chaol
The night-shift strike
The crews at Cnoc chaol refuse the night shift and are replaced within a week by crews brought from the coast under the Company's new contracts. The Lamp-Watch pays the strikers' families for a season and runs out of money.
5 an Dùbhlachd 1896 DE Muileann dhomhain
The strikebreakers of Muileann dhomhain
The crews that replace the strikers at Cnoc chaol are brought through Muileann dhomhain, where the townsfolk turn them away from every door. They sleep in the Company's barns, and several go home the next season.
17 an t-Ògmhios 1897 DE Ros dhomhain
Matthew Dunne's sermon
The Mission's minister at Ros dhomhain, Matthew Dunne, preaches against the night-shift order from the chapel pulpit, saying the Ròdaich are right that even the ground must rest. The Company complains to the Mission. Dunne is recalled to an Tìr Thall, and the sermon is copied by the Lamp-Watch and read in the camps.
12 an t-Sultain 1898 DE Cnoc chaol
The lung-rot at Cnoc chaol
A wasting sickness of the lungs spreads among the night crews at Cnoc chaol and Baile thais. Unlike the Green Death, it kills slowly. The Company pays a pension to widows for a year, then stops.
22 am Màrt 1899 DE Muileann chrom
Iain Maor and the night shift
Iain Maor, overseer at Muileann chrom, writes to the Company that the night shift is killing his crews faster than it is paying for them. The letter survives because the Company filed it with his dismissal, which was reversed a month later for want of anyone else.
14 an Lùnastal 1899 DE Baile ghorm
Ore-lamps from Baile ghorm
The potteries of Baile ghorm take a contract for clay lamp-bodies for the night crews, thousands in a year. The potters' own record notes that they are the first lamps ever made on the island for work in the dark by order.
21 an Gearran 1900 DE
Fionnan born
A second child manifests the same unprecedented bonding Aisling did half a century earlier. The exposure is not a one-time accident. It is an ongoing industrial condition.
19 an Cèitean 1901 DE Ros dhomhain
The Administration's census
The Administration counts the people of Rodos by district for the first time. Its figures for the humans are precise to the household; its figures for the Ròdaich are round to the hundred, and in the hill districts to the thousand.
20 an Giblean 1902 DE Dùn thais
Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, last of the Deer masters
The last master of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh to teach openly in the colonial age, Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, dies at Dùn thais. No successor is named, and the school's register ends with her death. It will be taken up again only long after the humans are gone.
5 am Màrt 1903 DE Muileann chaol
The custodians' records at Muileann chaol
The custodians of the east begin sending copies of their rolls to the town of Muileann chaol, which still kept Beathag nic Thòmais's loft of papers, for safekeeping, away from the Residency's reach. The copying is done in the houses of three families and kept in a cellar.
5 am Faoilleach 1904 DE Muileann chaol
The second Muileann chaol
Some of the copies bound for Muileann chaol go by error to the smaller town of the same name further north, and are kept there for years before the mistake is found. The custodians' record of them notes that they were kept just as well.
23 am Faoilleach 1905 DE
The word finally coined
Facing two confirmed cases, Rodian custodians settle on a term for what's happening: fuil-ghuail, "coal-blood" — rendered in the humans' tongue as obsidian-touched. It is meant clinically. It will outlive that intention.
21 an Gearran 1905 DE Cill ghlas
The custodians who named it
The word was agreed by a meeting of custodians held at the shrine of Cill ghlas, where the oldest cutting still stood open. They chose a plain word for a medical register. The roll records the vote and does not record who proposed it.
26 an t-Samhain 1906 DE Ros dhomhain
The Administration's register
The Residency, hearing of the word, orders that any Ròdaich child showing the condition be reported to the Commissioner's office. The custodians comply by reporting none.
7 an Giblean 1908 DE
The third currency reform
Traditional Rodian barter is formally abolished as legal tender entirely. Every transaction on the island now runs through human coinage.
17 an t-Sultain 1908 DE Ros dhomhain
The barter houses closed
The barter houses at Ros dhomhain and Cathair dhearg, where cloth and fish had changed hands without coin since before the Crossing, are closed by order. A clerk of the Residency notes that the ledgers are now "complete for the first time."
22 am Màrt 1909 DE Inis mhòr
The fishwives of Inis mhòr
The fishwives of Inis mhòr, who had sold by barter at the harbour steps since before the Crossing, refuse to take coin for a week in protest at the barter houses' closing. They give their fish away instead. The Company's clerks record it as a glut.
17 an t-Ògmhios 1909 DE Cathair dhearg
Marks borrowed at interest
With barter abolished, the hill villages borrow marks from the Company's stores to buy seed, at interest. Within a few years most of the villages of Muileann chrom owe the Company more than a year's crops.
20 an Giblean 1910 DE Muileann òg
The old market at Muileann òg
The old barter market at Muileann òg, where hill and coast had met to trade since the Holy Age, closes after its last season. The ground stands empty until it is used, long after, for a fair.
12 an t-Sultain 1910 DE Muileann chrom
Mòrag nic Iain Maor
Iain Maor dies, and his daughter Mòrag takes the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, the first woman to hold it. The Company approves her appointment in a letter that calls her "a safe pair of hands."
11 an Dàmhair 1910 DE Ros dhomhain
Charles Merriman Commissioner
Edward Vane dies at the Residency. His successor, Charles Merriman, arrives with a small company of armed constables, the first standing force the Administration has kept on Rodos.
26 an t-Iuchar 1911 DE Muileann shean
The constable post at Muileann shean
Merriman's first constable post is built at Muileann shean on the northern ore road, a stone house with a yard for horses. The townsfolk call it the humans' second Residency, and do not mean it kindly.
24 an Lùnastal 1911 DE Tobar ghorm
A barracks at Tobar ghorm
A second post is raised at Tobar ghorm, near the northern workings. The village's custodian is paid a rent for the ground and uses it, the record notes, to buy the village out of its debts to the Company store.
25 an Giblean 1912 DE Baile chrom
A grey-night gathering at Baile chrom
The Mission at Cathair gheal reports that human labourers near Baile chrom have been meeting at night in the fields to pray to a grey goose. The Mission cannot find the source of the practice and describes it as a superstition learned from the Ròdaich. The Ròdaich of Baile chrom disown it.
3 an Cèitean 1912 DE Ros dhomhain
The dockers' strike at Ros dhomhain
The dockers at Ros dhomhain, Ròdaich and human alike, refuse to load ore for nine days over the new berth charges. It is the only strike of the age in which human workers join Ròdaich ones. Merriman's constables end it, and the human dockers are shipped west.
29 an Dàmhair 1912 DE Seann Vell
Seann Vell's dockers stay out
The dockers of Seann Vell, the harbour next to Ros dhomhain, refuse to load the ore diverted to them during the strike. When it ends they are not shipped west, having no humans among them, but they are not hired again either.
1 an Giblean 1913 DE
Lorccan born
A third case, born into a mining town rather than a mining camp — proof the phenomenon has outgrown any single site.
3 am Màrt 1914 DE
Cian born
A fourth, within a year of the third — the closest the immortal generation comes to being born in a cluster rather than a scatter.
4 am Faoilleach 1915 DE Cill ghlas
Blasting-powder at Cill ghlas
The Company begins driving galleries under the hills around Cill ghlas with blasting-powder shipped from an Tìr Thall. The custodians of the shrine ask that no charge be set within sight of the old cutting. The Company's engineer marks their request on his plan and sets the charges below it.
2 an Gearran 1915 DE Caol ìseal
Powder landed at Caol ìseal
The blasting-powder for the new galleries is landed at Caol ìseal on the northern coast, away from the crowded southern harbours, and carted inland under guard. The town's custodians ask what is in the barrels and are told it is lamp-oil.
9 an t-Ògmhios 1916 DE
Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The Rending — a fault line tears open in the hills east of the capital, around Cill ghlas during a routine excavation, killing dozens and closing an entire mining district for a generation.
17 an t-Ògmhios 1916 DE
The first open confrontation
A mining accident, blamed by Rodian workers on human indifference to safety, becomes the first recorded violent clash between the two populations.
3 an t-Iuchar 1916 DE Cill ghlas
The shrine at Cill ghlas lost
The old cutting at Cill ghlas, where the custodians had kept the rites through the whole age, is swallowed by the Rending with its shrine. The custodians' roll records the loss of the shrine before the loss of the dead, and a later copyist has corrected the order.
22 an t-Samhain 1916 DE Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The district closed
The Company closes the whole district of the Rending and fences it, leaving Cill ghlas and its hamlets without work. The villages empty toward Baile thais and Muileann dhearg, and the closed district is left to thorn.
5 an Dùbhlachd 1916 DE Achadh chaol
Achadh chaol raised by the displaced
People of the closed district build a new village at Achadh chaol, on the edge of the fenced ground, on land lent by the custodians of Muileann dhomhain. It is the only settlement founded in the age by Ròdaich for Ròdaich without a Company surveyor's hand in it.
13 an Dùbhlachd 1916 DE Muileann chrom
The clash at Muileann chrom
The accident that began the clash was a flooded gallery at Muileann chrom, in which seven died after the pumps were stopped to save fuel. When the Company's agent came to the pithead the crews stoned him and his constables, and the constables fired. Four Ròdaich and one constable were killed.
4 am Faoilleach 1917 DE Muileann chrom
Mòrag Maor at the inquiry
At the Administration's inquiry into the clash, the overseer Mòrag nic Iain Maor testifies that the pumps were stopped on the agent's order. Her evidence is struck from the record. The Lamp-Watch obtains a copy of it anyway.
2 an Gearran 1917 DE Baile thais
The grey fever
A fever of the chest comes in on the ships and runs across the whole island, from the capital to the eastern farms. It kills the young and strong more than the old, the Mission notes with alarm. The camps, already hungry, bury more than the towns.
14 an t-Iuchar 1917 DE Cathair mhòr
The grey fever at Cathair mhòr
At Cathair mhòr the grey fever closes the market for the first time in the town's memory. The custodians' roll records the dead by street, and the longest list is the street where the carters lived.
6 an Dùbhlachd 1917 DE Dùn thais
The grey fever at Dùn thais
At Dùn thais the fever takes the physician who had been sent by the Administration to treat it, and two of the Mission's nurses. The Deer masters' old houses are opened as sick-rooms.
27 am Faoilleach 1918 DE
The second organized petition
This one includes an implicit threat rather than a plea. It is the first Rodian document the human administration bothers to respond to — with increased security, not concessions.
12 an Lùnastal 1918 DE Cnoc dhìreach
The signatories of Cnoc dhìreach
The custodian of Cnoc dhìreach, Coinneach Ruadh, signs the second petition and is dismissed from his post as clerk to the Company store the same week. He is one of eleven signatories who lose Company work over it.
29 an Dùbhlachd 1918 DE Baile thais
Eilidh nic Raghnaill
The second petition was drafted by Eilidh nic Raghnaill, a crew-leader of Baile thais and a member of the Lamp-Watch, and signed by custodians and crew-leaders from thirty-one settlements. It ends with a sentence the Residency underlined: that the hill would not be worked by people who were not asked.
25 an Gearran 1919 DE Ros dhomhain
The constabulary enlarged
Merriman's answer is to triple the constabulary and post companies at Muileann chrom, Baile thais, Ceann fhada and Cnoc chaol, with a fortified store at each. The constables are paid from the tithe.
26 am Màrt 1919 DE Dùn chrom
Barracks at Dùn chrom
A constabulary barracks is built at Dùn chrom, on the capital side of the hills, with room for two hundred men. It stands empty for most of its first year for want of constables to fill it.
24 an Giblean 1919 DE Seann Skell
Ìomhar Seabhag
At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Ìomhar Seabhag preaches that Mòd's hunger has turned toward those who have eaten the hill. The hawk-shrines of the west begin to serve as meeting houses for the Lamp-Watch, and the constables do not yet know it.
23 an Cèitean 1919 DE Ros gheal
The hawk-faithful of Ros gheal
At Ros gheal the hawk-faithful fishing families, who had chased out the Company's customs officers a century before, raise a shrine to Mòd on the harbour wall. The constables order it down. It is rebuilt three times in a single season.
21 an t-Ògmhios 1919 DE Inis bhàn
The hawk and the Deer at Inis bhàn
At Inis bhàn the priests of the hawk and a few who still keep the Deer school's questions in private meet for a disputation, the first between the two in living memory. The record calls it inconclusive, and notes that both sides afterward signed the petition.
20 an t-Iuchar 1919 DE Baile chrom
The grey fever in the north-west
The grey fever returns and settles in the north-west, around Baile chrom and the concession towns, where it kills humans as readily as Ròdaich. The Mission's hospital at Cathair gheal overflows, and Ròdaich and human patients lie in the same wards for the first time.
6 am Màrt 1920 DE Muileann fhionn
Muileann fhionn shut in
Muileann fhionn, a Ròdaich mill town in the north-west, closes its roads against the fever and keeps them closed for a season. Human carters of the concession are turned back with their loads at the town's edge.
18 an Giblean 1920 DE Tobar fhiadhaich
The fever at Tobar fhiadhaich
At Tobar fhiadhaich in the north the fever takes one household in three. The custodians of the village burn no huts, having heard of Àth ghlas in their grandparents' time but judging it too late.
9 an t-Sultain 1920 DE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The taverns fortify
Roadside houses along the old mining routes begin doubling as informal militia waypoints — infrastructure quietly repurposing itself for a conflict not yet declared.
17 an t-Sultain 1920 DE An Taigh-seinnse Òir
An Taigh-seinnse Òir
An Taigh-seinnse Òir, the great house on the eastern road beyond Dùn dhearg, digs a well in its yard and builds a wall round the well. The keeper tells the Company's carters it is against thieves.
14 an Dàmhair 1920 DE An Leòmhann Buidhe
An Leòmhann Buidhe
An Leòmhann Buidhe, the roadside house on the northern road through the Deer country, takes on six new ostlers in a single season, none of whom know anything about horses.
22 am Faoilleach 1921 DE An Taigh-òsta Grianach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach walled
An Taigh-òsta Grianach, known since the songs of Fearchar Bàrd as the singing house, raises a wall around its yard and puts a watch on its gate.
3 an t-Iuchar 1921 DE Am Buabhall Fortanach
Am Buabhall Fortanach barred
Am Buabhall Fortanach, the great roadside tavern on the south-western road, takes to barring its gates at dusk and keeping a watch on the roof. Its keeper, Tormod Buabhall, keeps a list of travellers that he sends up the road each week, to whom the record does not say.
30 an Lùnastal 1921 DE Doire shean
The harbour of Doire shean
The little harbour of Doire shean, below Am Buabhall Fortanach, becomes the landing place for the goods the house cannot take by road. The fishermen of Doire shean are paid in silver from the east.
28 an t-Sultain 1921 DE An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
At An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, on the northern road, the stables are rebuilt with a loft for sleeping men. The Company's carters notice that the loft is never empty and never has the same men in it.
27 an Dàmhair 1921 DE An Sligeanach Fad' às
An Sligeanach Fad' às
An Sligeanach Fad' às, on the eastern road near the silver country, becomes the post-house through which the Lamp-Watch sends word from the camps to Muileann chiar. The silver guild pays its keeper's rent.
25 an t-Samhain 1921 DE Àth fhiadhaich
The runners of Àth fhiadhaich
Runners from Àth fhiadhaich carry the Lamp-Watch's letters from An Sligeanach Fad' às to the silver town. They are boys of twelve and thirteen, too young to be stopped by constables.
28 am Faoilleach 1922 DE Achadh mhòr
Achadh mhòr keeps the ledgers
The Lamp-Watch's ledgers of money received from the silver guild are kept at Achadh mhòr, a village near the house on the eastern road, in the roof of the village's shrine.
26 an Gearran 1922 DE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
Seònaid's house
An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the carters' house on the ore road reopened by Seònaid Bhàn in the early years of the extraction, is kept now by her great-grandson Aonghas. It is the busiest of the fortified houses, and the one the constables search most often and find least in.
27 am Màrt 1922 DE
The first coordinated work stoppage
Multiple mining regions halt extraction on the same day for the first time — proof that Rodian resistance, for all its scattering, could act as one when it chose to.
27 am Màrt 1922 DE Muileann bheag
Muileann bheag in the north-east
The workings at Muileann bheag in the north-east, among the Deer villages, stop with the rest. The town's custodian writes that it was the first thing the town had done in concert with the hills in a hundred years.
27 am Màrt 1922 DE Àth dhomhain
The northern pits at Àth dhomhain
The pits north of the hills at Àth dhomhain stop with the rest on the day of the stoppage, having received the signal by a runner rather than the beacon. Their crew-leaders are among those shipped west.
27 am Màrt 1922 DE Ceann bheag
Ceann bheag stops
The ore stage at Ceann bheag on the northern coast stops loading the same day. Its dockers had not been told of the stoppage in advance; they stop because the ore stops arriving.
27 am Màrt 1922 DE Cnoc gheal
The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal
The quarrymen of Cnoc gheal in the north-east, who cut stone for the Company's buildings, put down their tools on the day of the stoppage without being asked. Nobody in the record says why.
27 am Màrt 1922 DE Muileann chrom
The day the pits stopped
On the day of the stoppage every working in the Muileann chrom district halted at once, together with Baile thais, Cnoc chaol, the silver town and the eastern pits at Ros fhionn. The signal was a beacon fire lit on the hills above Doire mhòr, which the Company took for a heath fire.
27 am Màrt 1922 DE Ros dhomhain
The ore ships wait
The Company's steamships wait at Ros dhomhain for six days with empty holds. The agents at the quay write that they have never before seen the harbour so quiet, and that it frightened them more than the crowds.
30 an Dùbhlachd 1922 DE Ros dhomhain
The stoppage broken
The stoppage ends when the constables close the Company stores in every district at once. Forty crew-leaders are arrested; thirty-two are released without charge, eight are shipped west to an Tìr Thall for trial and are not heard of again.
28 am Faoilleach 1923 DE Doire mhòr
Beacon hill at Doire mhòr
Doire mhòr, which had refused the first contract and then lost its water, has by now only a few households. The beacon of the stoppage was lit on its hill by the descendants of Beathag Dhubh's people, and the constables burn the hill's heather to deny it to them.
25 an Giblean 1923 DE An Cuan Siar
Fewer ships from the west
The keepers' daybooks at the five beacons record fewer ships arriving from an Tìr Thall each year, and the ships that come are older. The Company's letters speak of troubles at home that they do not describe.
13 an Giblean 1924 DE Caol leathan
Caol leathan's idle harbour
At Caol leathan the wool-ships for the humans' market wait for cargo space that does not come. The merchants of the town begin selling their wool inland again, by barter, which is illegal.
9 an Dàmhair 1924 DE Caol bheag
Caol bheag's empty quay
The Company's quay at Caol bheag on the northern coast, built for the eastern trade, handles one ship in a season. The Company's agent there writes that he has been forgotten.
24 an Cèitean 1925 DE
Imperial overreach begins openly
Human administrators begin issuing directives with no Rodian counsel sought at all — the polite fiction of permission finally dropped.
2 an t-Samhain 1925 DE Ros dhomhain
Lionel Strake Commissioner
Charles Merriman leaves Rodos in ill health. Lionel Strake, a soldier, replaces him. His commission, read aloud at the Residency, makes no mention of the Council of Custodians, and he does not call on it.
26 an Gearran 1926 DE Cathair dhearg
The council locked out
Strake has the council hall at Cathair dhearg locked and its keys lodged at the Residency. The custodians meet instead in the Dark Unicorn's temple, whose priests, who had blessed the humans' coin, now shelter those who had petitioned against it.
27 am Màrt 1926 DE
The confiscation edict
Human authorities formally claim the right to seize any Rodian dwelling deemed necessary for extraction expansion. It is the single most-cited grievance in every surviving account of what came next.
25 an Giblean 1926 DE Doire mhòr
The seizure of Doire mhòr
The first dwellings taken under the edict are those of Doire mhòr, for a new shaft beneath the hill. The last households are carried out by constables. The village that refused the first contract is the first to be emptied by the last.
17 an t-Sultain 1926 DE Baile dhomhain
Evictions at Baile dhomhain
At Baile dhomhain, the first camp laid out on paper, two streets are pulled down for a spoil-tip. The families are offered huts at Àth ìseal and marks for their timber; most go to kin in the hill villages instead.
24 an Cèitean 1927 DE Muileann chrom
Mòrag Maor lays down the staff
Mòrag nic Iain Maor, fourth of her line to hold the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, refuses to carry out evictions in her district and breaks the staff at the Company's door. Three other overseers resign in the same month. The Company appoints humans to their places.
21 an t-Iuchar 1927 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver guild arms
The silver guild of Muileann chiar, still holding its seam under the compact made a century before, begins buying rifles through the eastern pirates. Its ledger enters them as refining tools.
19 an Lùnastal 1927 DE Spùinneadairean-mara
Rifles by way of the pirates
The rifles for the silver guild come ashore from the raiders' boats in the eastern waters, where no Company gunboat has patrolled for years. The raiders take payment in silver bar, by weight.
20 an Lùnastal 1927 DE Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
The council at Cnoc bheag forest
Custodians, crew-leaders of the Lamp-Watch and the dissenting priests of the Dark Unicorn meet in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag and form a single council for the mining regions. Eilidh nic Raghnaill is chosen to speak for it. The meeting is not recorded by any human source.
3 am Faoilleach 1928 DE Ros dhomhain
The arrest order
Strake orders the arrest of Eilidh nic Raghnaill and the members of the forest council. The constables go to Baile thais and find the house empty and the town silent.
6 am Faoilleach 1928 DE
War declared
Rodian resistance, coordinated for the first time across multiple mining regions, moves from grievance to open conflict.
20 an Gearran 1928 DE Muileann chrom
The stores taken at Muileann chrom
The war opens in the hills. At Muileann chrom the fortified store is rushed at first light by crews under Mòrag nic Iain, and its eleven constables surrender without a shot fired. The store's rifles and its grain are carried off before noon.
28 an Gearran 1928 DE Ceann fhada
The quay at Ceann fhada seized
Crews from the camps take the Company's ore quay at Ceann fhada and sink two barges across its mouth. No ore leaves the hills by water again in the age.
16 an Cèitean 1928 DE Baile thais
The siege of the store at Baile thais
At Baile thais the constables hold their walled pithead against the town for eleven days, the same span as the first strike a lifetime before. They surrender on the twelfth, when their water runs out. Eilidh nic Raghnaill sends them under guard to the coast unharmed, an order the Residency did not expect and did not reciprocate.
24 an Cèitean 1928 DE Baile gharbh
The northern pits rise
The crews at Baile gharbh and the northern pits rise in the same week, take the constable posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and send the constables south on foot.
1 an t-Ògmhios 1928 DE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The ore road cut
Aonghas, keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, closes the gates of the house across the ore road, and the men in its loft come down armed. The road between the capital and the hills is cut at its halfway stage and stays cut.
9 an t-Ògmhios 1928 DE Muileann dhearg
Uilleam Gobha's forge
At Muileann dhearg the smith Uilleam Gobha turns the Company's own blasting-powder into grenades cased in ore-tin, and forges pike-heads from rails torn up in the galleries. The rebels' council records that it could not have fought its first season without him.
30 an t-Ògmhios 1928 DE Cathair dhearg
The capital rises
At Cathair dhearg the custodians break the Residency's locks on their council hall and sit in it again. The townsfolk hold Drochaid Cathair dhearg against the constables sent up from the harbour, and the bridge built for ore-carts is barricaded with them.
11 an t-Iuchar 1928 DE Cathair dhomhain
Cathair dhomhain joins
At Cathair dhomhain the townsfolk break open the Company's warehouse, the first building on Rodos the Company ever owned, and carry off its tools for the council's companies.
9 an Lùnastal 1928 DE Muileann mhin
Muileann mhin takes sides
At Muileann mhin, a small port just east of the capital, the townsfolk argue for three days and then send boats to the council. The boats carry food up the coast to the capital through the winter.
17 an Lùnastal 1928 DE Ros dhomhain
The Residency fortified
Lionel Strake withdraws the Administration into the Residency above Ros dhomhain and fortifies the Company's quarter of the harbour. The city below it, overwhelmingly Ròdaich, neither joins the rising nor opposes it, and the constables do not trust it enough to leave the walls.
25 an Lùnastal 1928 DE Àth chiar
The fight at the ford of Àth chiar
A column of constables and Company guards under Major Peter Ashdown marches up the ore road to relieve the hills and is met at the ford of Àth chiar. The rebels hold the far bank. Ashdown loses forty men and his baggage and turns back; the rebels lose nineteen, whose names the council's roll gives in full.
11 an t-Samhain 1928 DE Dùn chrom
Ashdown's retreat through Dùn chrom
Ashdown's column falls back through Dùn chrom and stops at the barracks there for a night. In the morning the town has closed its gates behind them, and the column continues to the coast without its wounded, whom the townsfolk keep and nurse.
19 an t-Samhain 1928 DE Muileann chiar
The silver town rises
The silver guild of Muileann chiar declares for the council and opens its armoury. The Company agents in the town are escorted to the coast with their papers. It is the only place on the island where the rising took nothing, the guild's ledger notes, because the humans had never held anything there to take.
27 an t-Samhain 1928 DE Dùn ìseal
The surrender at Dùn ìseal
The small constabulary post at Dùn ìseal, cut off by the rising at the silver town, surrenders to the silver guild's riflemen after a single exchange of fire. The east of the island is clear of human arms.
5 an Dùbhlachd 1928 DE Dùn dhearg
Dùn dhearg declares
The custodians of Dùn dhearg declare for the council and send it grain. It is the town whose custodian had written the only surviving defence of the Small-Burning Law, and the declaration quotes it.
3 am Faoilleach 1929 DE Cnoc leathan
Cnoc leathan's riflemen
Riflemen raised at Cnoc leathan in the east join the silver guild's companies and garrison the eastern road. The Company's carters on the road are allowed to go home with their carts.
15 am Faoilleach 1929 DE Ros fhionn
The eastern pits at Ros fhionn
The crews of the eastern workings around Ros fhionn stop the pumps and walk out, letting the lower galleries flood. The Company's engineers there take ship for Ros dhomhain. The bridge on the eastern ore road falls silent.
17 am Faoilleach 1929 DE Seann Toll
Seann Toll shelled
A Company steamship shells the ore stage at Seann Toll to deny it to the rebels, and sets the fishing town behind it burning. Twenty-three townsfolk die. It is the first time the humans turn the island's own ore, burning in their boilers, against a Ròdaich town.
27 am Faoilleach 1929 DE Inis mhòr
Coaling at Inis mhòr
The Company steamships coal at Inis mhòr, the harbour just east of the capital's bay, from the ore stacked on its quay. Townsfolk set the stacks alight. The ships put in at Ros dhomhain instead, and burn their own stores.
1 an Gearran 1929 DE Seann Chwen
The fishermen of Seann Chwen
Fishing boats from Seann Chwen and Ros ruadh, sailing by night along the south coast, board a Company coaster at anchor and burn her. The Company withdraws its coastal shipping to the harbours of Ros dhomhain and Ros bheag.
13 an Gearran 1929 DE Seann Chwen
The other Seann Chwen
The fishermen of the other Seann Chwen, on the south coast further west, join the raids along the shore. The record keeps the two towns apart by naming their boats.
15 an Gearran 1929 DE Cathair gheal
Cathair gheal behind its walls
The human town of Cathair gheal, on the northern concession, closes its gates and raises a militia, but sends none of it south to the Residency. Its magistrate writes to both sides asking to be left alone. The council grants it; Strake does not reply.
25 an Gearran 1929 DE Muileann àrsaidh
Muileann àrsaidh closes its road
The concession town of Muileann àrsaidh closes its road with carts and keeps a watch on it, against both sides. No one attacks it. The watch is kept for the rest of the war.
2 am Màrt 1929 DE Seann Skell
The hawk-shrines open
Ìomhar Seabhag declares from the shrine at Seann Skell that the war is Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who fed it. Hawk-shrines across the west become recruiting houses, and a company of the hawk-faithful marches south to join the council.
16 am Màrt 1929 DE Seann Skell
The hawk company at Seann Skell
The company of the hawk-faithful is mustered at Seann Skell, the western city, from which the human port of Ros bheag lies a short march to the south-west. It holds the road between Ros bheag and the north-west for the rest of the war.
31 am Màrt 1929 DE Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The southern beacon dark
The keepers at Tobar dhearg put out the beacon, and the keepers at Àth dhearg and Baile ìseal follow. Company ships feeling their way along the coast by night run on the reefs the beacons were built to light, and two are lost.
29 an Giblean 1929 DE An Cuan Siar
No relief from the west
The Administration's letter-books record repeated requests for troops and ships from an Tìr Thall. One ship arrives in the whole first year of the war, carrying dispatches and a few crates of cartridges, and sails again within the week.
11 an Cèitean 1929 DE Ros dhomhain
The winter lines
Through the first winter of the war the council holds the hills, the east and the capital; Strake holds the Residency, the quarter of the harbour below it, and the western ports. Neither side has the strength to attack the other.
28 an Cèitean 1929 DE Seann Warr
Grain from Seann Warr
The farming town of Seann Warr in the south-east, not the salt port of the same name in the west, sends grain to the hills through the winter by the eastern roads. The council's roll lists the carts.
9 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE Cathair dhearg
Hunger in the capital
Cathair dhearg goes short through the winter, its harbour held by the Residency. The custodians share out the grain by household. The roll records that the custodians took the same share as everyone else.
10 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE
The burning of the third currency's records
Rebels destroy the human administration's tithe ledgers in three separate raids — an act later chroniclers treat as symbolically decisive even though its practical effect was small.
26 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE Ros dhomhain
The counting-house at Ros dhomhain
The first raid was on the Company's counting-house at the Ros dhomhain quay, inside the lines. Men of the harbour quarter led by Dùghall Dubh came in over the roofs, carried the tithe books into the yard and burned them.
8 an t-Iuchar 1929 DE Ceann àrsaidh
The tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh
The second raid burned the Administration's tithe-house at Ceann àrsaidh, where the portion owed by every settlement in the hills had been entered since the first schedule. The clerks were let go. The custodians of Ceann àrsaidh asked that one ledger be spared for the record, and were refused by their own people.
9 an t-Iuchar 1929 DE Muileann chrom
The weigh-house at Muileann chrom
The third raid burned the Company's weigh-house at Muileann chrom with its steelyard ledgers. The ore of the hills since the first contract had been entered there by the ton. The rebels' own chronicler writes that the fire burned green.
6 an Lùnastal 1929 DE Cnoc ghorm
The fight at Cnoc ghorm
Company guards and constables sallying from the capital's harbour to recover the eastern road are driven back at Cnoc ghorm, in the hills beyond the capital. It is the last attempt of the war by the Administration to reach the mining district.
7 an Lùnastal 1929 DE Ros dhomhain
The harbour quarter changes sides
The Ròdaich of the Ros dhomhain harbour quarter, after the counting-house raid, open the lower gates to the council's companies. Strake is left holding the Residency and the Company's quays alone.
25 an Lùnastal 1929 DE Cuan uaine
Cuan uaine opens its harbour
The harbour of Cuan uaine, east of the capital, opens to the council's boats. With it and the Ros dhomhain harbour quarter both lost, the Residency can be supplied only by sea.
4 an t-Sultain 1929 DE Ros dhomhain
Strake abandons the Residency
Lionel Strake evacuates the Residency by sea with his officials, the Mission's clergy and the Company's agents, and removes the Administration to Ros bheag. The council's companies enter the Residency the next morning and find it stripped of everything but its furniture.
5 an t-Sultain 1929 DE Ros bheag
Ros bheag the last seat
At Ros bheag, the western port the humans had used since the early years, Strake sets up what remains of the Administration. The human families of the west and the south, a few thousand in all, gather behind its walls.
21 an t-Sultain 1929 DE Ros àrsaidh
Outposts at Ros àrsaidh
Strake posts constables at Ros àrsaidh, north of Ros bheag, to hold the coast road. The townsfolk bring them food and news, and the news is always a day old.
23 an t-Sultain 1929 DE Ros bheag
Hunger in Ros bheag
With the roads cut and no ships from the west, Ros bheag runs short of food within months. The Company's stores are opened to the human families and to the Ròdaich townsfolk alike, on Strake's order, the one act of his that the Ròdaich record credits.
3 an Dàmhair 1929 DE Cuan shean
Cuan shean refuses the humans
The custodians of Cuan shean, the town where the first humans came ashore, close its harbour to Company ships. The council's roll notes the irony without comment.
4 an Dàmhair 1929 DE Baile dhìreach
The families of Baile dhìreach
At Baile dhìreach the descendants of the old joint council, many of them of both peoples, are asked by each side which they are. The record says most of them refused to answer, and that neither side forced them.
20 an Dàmhair 1929 DE An Cuan Siar
The last ship from the west
The last ship recorded arriving from an Tìr Thall anchors at Ros bheag. She brings no troops and no grain, only a sealed letter for the Commissioner, and she sails again on the next tide with as many passengers as she can hold.
1 an t-Samhain 1929 DE Àth àrsaidh
The truce of Àth àrsaidh
Envoys of the council and of the Administration meet at Àth àrsaidh, on the edge of the northern concession. They agree a truce: the humans remaining on Rodos to withdraw into the north-west under the council's safe-conduct, the council to leave the concession towns standing.
2 an t-Samhain 1929 DE Baile Mòr ruadh
Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns
Baile Mòr ruadh, the largest town of the north-west, is named in the truce as the place where the columns will be received. Its Ròdaich people are given the choice of staying or going south. The record gives the numbers of each and they are close.
20 an t-Samhain 1929 DE Cuan shean
The columns go north
The human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west march north along the western roads under guard of the council's companies. Few of them had ever lived in the north. The roll records that no column was attacked, and that none was helped.
30 an t-Samhain 1929 DE Àth chrom
The columns at Àth chrom
The columns cross the ford at Àth chrom on the way north. The custodians of the town stand at the ford and count them over, and the count is the last the Ròdaich make of the humans on Rodos in this age.
1 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE Àth leathan
Àth leathan
At Àth leathan, on the last stage before the northern territory, the columns camp for a night. The custodians of the town record that the humans asked the name of the place, and that the name was written down by several of them.
5 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE Cuan shean
The ship that sailed west
Lionel Strake, the last Commissioner, sails west from Cuan shean with his officials in the last ship on the island that could make the crossing. The keeper at Taigh-solais Baile chrom records her passing in his daybook. Nothing on Rodos records her arriving anywhere.
19 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The beacons relit
The council orders the five beacons lit again, from Baile chrom round to Tobar dhearg. The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, continue to be kept, with nothing in them.
29 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE Muileann chaol
The rolls sent to Muileann chaol
The custodians send what survives of the age's rolls, their copies of the petitions, the book of Baile thais and the letter-books left in the Residency, to the cellars at Muileann chaol. What the Administration's own clerks carried west with Strake is not known.
1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE
The Severance
The war ends with the crossing itself closed. Whatever let humans reach Rodos shuts. The humans still on the island are shepherded to the northern territory their descendants hold today. Cian and Lorccan, not yet twenty, grow up in its immediate wake.

Age V · An Aois Ùr the New Age

22 am Màrt 1930 DE
The Tuathaich homeland fixed
Human descendants stranded by the Severance are formally settled in the island's north — a confinement, not a homecoming, though later generations will simply call it home.
3 an t-Ògmhios 1930 DE Cathair dhearg
The Severance companies stood down
The war-companies that fought the last campaign against the human administration are disbanded at Cathair dhearg. Their rolls are handed to the council rather than burned, and the companies are never formally abolished; they survive as names on a list.
31 an t-Iuchar 1930 DE Caol mhòr
The boundary stones set
Stones are set on the roads running north to mark where the Tuathaich territory begins. No wall follows them. Many still stand at the roadside, and nobody has been paid to move them.
9 an Dùbhlachd 1930 DE Doire ghlas
The hungry year at Doire ghlas
Cut off from the stores that used to come over the water from an Tìr Thall, the northern settlements go short of grain in their first year alone. Tuathaich memory, taken down long afterwards, puts the dead at Doire ghlas above two hundred. No Ròdaich count was made.
11 an t-Ògmhios 1931 DE Ros dhomhain
The human counting-houses emptied
Council clerks enter the human administration's counting-houses at Cathair dhearg, Ros dhomhain and Seann Skell and carry off everything written. What the raids of the war left of the tithe ledgers is boxed with the rest, unread, because few of the clerks can read the humans' hand.
10 an t-Iuchar 1931 DE Inis àrsaidh
The north-west ports without a master
At Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh, the humans' harbour officers leave with the last ships before the crossing closes, taking their keys. The Tuathaich fishermen break the locks on the harbour stores and share out what they find by household.
27 an t-Iuchar 1931 DE Cathair dhearg
Rìoghachd Ròdais declared
The state formally restyles itself a kingdom in form, whatever it remains in function — the same contradiction its own records still carry today.
25 an Lùnastal 1931 DE Caol mhòr
The Moot at Caol mhòr
Tuathaich householders from the northern towns meet at Caol mhòr and choose a speaker, Walter Hale, a former harbour clerk. The Moot has no standing in Ròdaich law. It meets anyway and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from this meeting to the present.
23 an t-Sultain 1931 DE Cathair dhearg
The council of the kingdom seated
A royal council of twelve is seated at Cathair dhearg, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the Severance war. Its minute-books are the oldest continuous record of the state in this age.
11 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE Ros dhomhain
The harbour-houses of Ros dhomhain taken over
The customs sheds the humans built at Ros dhomhain, the kingdom's largest port, pass to Ròdaich harbour-masters. The first of them, Dùghall mac Iain, keeps the humans' tariff in force for want of another and translates it line by line over the following years.
19 an t-Ògmhios 1932 DE An Cuan Siar
The ship sent west
The council sends a ship out past the western capes to look for the crossing the humans used. It comes back after a month of open water and reports nothing: no land, no ship, no sign of the passage. No second ship is sent.
7 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE Cathair dhearg
Niall crowned
The first ruler of the restored kingdom takes the throne at Cathair dhearg — the opening name in the line the state's own chronicles keep unbroken from here forward.
15 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE Cathair dhearg
A saying enters speech
The crowning passes with so little dispute that 'mar a thàinig Niall', the way Niall came, becomes a saying for any smooth handing-over of power. Its first written use is in a Cathair dhearg tavern ledger, set against a debt settled without argument.
23 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE Cathair dhearg
The shires drawn
The council divides the kingdom into siorrachdan, each named for its seat, and keeps most of the human administration's district lines under the new names. The humans' surveys are the only complete ones on the island; the kingdom uses them and does not say so.
4 am Faoilleach 1933 DE Ceann mhòr
The maoir appointed
A maor is appointed to each shire to collect the Crown's dues and keep its peace. In the Tuathaich shires the maoir are Ròdaich, lodged in the seat towns; at Ceann mhòr the maor's house is the old human magistrate's, and the townspeople call it by the old name.
21 am Faoilleach 1933 DE Baile Mòr mhòr
The maor of Baile Mòr mhòr
The first maor of Siorrachd Baile Mòr mhòr, Coinneach mac Ailein, holds his court under the market roof of the town, since the humans' courthouse has burned. He keeps the court there after the new courthouse is built, and so do his successors.
2 an Gearran 1933 DE
Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
The Great Wave strikes the southern coast without warning, devastating Cnoc chaol, Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin in a single night — the first disaster the new state responds to on its own terms.
24 an t-Samhain 1933 DE Cuan dhearg
The dead of the Great Wave counted
Relief parties from Cathair dhearg reach Cuan dhearg on the southern coast and count the dead of the three settlements at a little over nine hundred. The harbour at Cuan dhearg is gone. Its boats are found in the fields behind the town.
6 an Dùbhlachd 1933 DE Achadh mhin
Achadh mhin under salt
The fields of Achadh mhin lie under salt and will not bear. The council moves the survivors to higher ground and pays for their seed from the treasury, the first relief the restored kingdom ever grants.
23 an Dùbhlachd 1933 DE Cnoc chaol
Cnoc chaol rebuilt on the hill
Cnoc chaol is rebuilt on the slope behind the old town, out of the wave's reach. The old site is left as the water left it. The townspeople call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there.
4 am Faoilleach 1934 DE Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol
Tonn
The accounts gathered from survivors by the relief parties use 'tonn', wave, for anything sudden and overwhelming. Within a generation the sense is heard across the south: 'tha e san tonn', he is in the wave of it.
1 an Giblean 1934 DE Eilean mhin
The wave's reach on Eilean mhin
The Great Wave also crosses the low island of Eilean mhin off the southern coast, where no one then lived year-round. The shepherds who summered there do not go back.
30 an Giblean 1934 DE
The old human coinage withdrawn
Every remaining piece of human currency is formally demonetized. A new Rìoghachd coinage, minted with obsidian-dust ink in its seal, replaces it within a year.
9 an Dàmhair 1934 DE Cathair dhearg
The mint at Cathair dhearg
A mint is set up in the old human counting-house at Cathair dhearg under Fearchar mac Dhòmhnaill, called Fearchar Bonn. The seal of each coin is pressed with an ink ground from obsidian dust, so that a clipped coin shows the colour at its edge.
7 an t-Samhain 1934 DE Caol mhòr
The northern savings voided
Tuathaich households kept what savings they had in the humans' coin. With its withdrawal those savings are worth their metal by weight and no more. The Moot at Caol mhòr petitions the council for an exchange. The petition is received and filed.
2 an Gearran 1935 DE Doire mhin
Joseph Marlow's ploughshares
At Doire mhin in the north a smith named Joseph Marlow melts down his neighbours' withdrawn coin and casts it into ploughshares, which he sells back to them at the cost of the charcoal. Tuathaich songs still name him.
3 am Màrt 1935 DE Inis thais
The coin at Inis thais
At Inis thais on the south-west coast the new coin is short for most of the year and the town's merchants trade in chits written on the Wolf house's paper. The chits are redeemed at the Wolf house door when the coin arrives, and the house keeps a tenth.
18 an Giblean 1935 DE
Creideamh nan Ròdach formalized
The Obsidian Rite becomes organized doctrine rather than diffuse folk reverence, built around the leyline and the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched.
30 an Giblean 1935 DE Seann Skell
The first high custodian of the Rite
Dòmhnall mac Thormoid is named Àrd-choimheadaiche of Creideamh nan Ròdach and seated at Seann Skell on the southern coast, where the Rite's largest house stands. His first charge is a written order of worship. There had never been one.
17 an Cèitean 1935 DE Cnoc bheag
The Hawk houses refuse
The houses of Creideamh an t-Seabhaig around Cnoc bheag decline the new order of worship, holding that the Rite's older form needs no custodian above the local altar. They are not compelled. The long quarrel between the two forms of the Rite begins here.
29 an Cèitean 1935 DE Baile Mòr fhionn
The Wolf houses stand aside
The houses of Creideamh a' Mhadaidh-allaidh in the south-west, whose god Clach is not the Rite's, are asked to send witnesses to the formalizing of the Rite at Seann Skell. They send none, and a letter saying they wish it well.
2 an Gearran 1936 DE Caol mhòr
The Moot's schoolhouse petition
Walter Hale asks the council for leave to open schools in the north that teach in the humans' tongue. The council answers that the kingdom's schools teach in Ròdais and that it has no others. The Moot's minute calls the answer 'clear, at least'.
26 an Gearran 1936 DE Cathair dhearg
The capital's faith and the court
The house of Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh at Cathair dhearg, the capital's own faith, is given the keeping of the coronation regalia, as it had been before the humans came. The Rite's high custodian asks for a share of the keeping and is refused.
30 an t-Iuchar 1936 DE
The first post-Severance census
The state counts its own population for the first time since reclaiming the island — and quietly notes, without further comment, exactly how few obsidian-touched individuals actually exist.
15 an Lùnastal 1936 DE Doire ghlas
The count taken from the road
Ròdaich census clerks count the Tuathaich towns of Siorrachd Doire ghlas from the road, without entering most houses. The Moot keeps its own tally the same year. The two totals differ by nearly a fifth, and each side keeps its own.
23 an Lùnastal 1936 DE Cathair dhomhain
The circuit justices
Justices are appointed to ride circuit among the shires, the first of them Eilidh nic Leòid of Cathair dhomhain. Her circuit covers eleven shires of the south-west and takes most of a year to ride once.
3 am Màrt 1937 DE Muileann bhàn
Muileann bhàn's waterworks
Muileann bhàn, on the southern plain, builds the first public waterworks of the restored kingdom: a stone tank on the hill fed by the mill-race, with lead pipes to four street wells. The Guild of Hewers sends its surveyors to learn how it was done.
10 an t-Sultain 1937 DE Seann Bhral
The Leòid ruling
Sitting at Seann Bhral, Eilidh nic Leòid rules that land held by Tuathaich under human title passes to the Crown, while the right to work it stays with the holders and their heirs. The ruling is cited in nearly every land case of the age that follows.
9 an Dàmhair 1937 DE Muileann chrom
The ore line repaired
The railway the humans built from the central mountains to the sea, broken in three places during the Severance war, is repaired as far as Muileann chrom. A Rail Board is formed at Cathair dhearg to run it, with a clerk, two engineers and the humans' timetable.
17 an Dùbhlachd 1937 DE Drochaid Cathair dhearg
The bridge at Cathair dhearg re-dedicated
The stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain below the capital, rebuilt under the humans, is re-dedicated with a Ròdais name-stone. The humans' stone is not removed. It is turned to face the river.
15 am Faoilleach 1938 DE Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
The necropolis at Cnoc dhìreach
The shire of Ceann mhin closes the old burial ground at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach to new graves, since the vines have broken too many stones to find room. Families of the town still tend the old graves, and some say the place is not empty after dark.
13 an Gearran 1938 DE
Creideamh nan Tuathach persists
