Tuathaich communities keep their own folk-shamanic tradition alive in the north — including, quietly, the First Canoe fragment the Ròdaich priesthood still calls superstition.
14 am Màrt 1938 DE Baile chrom
The Grey Night kept openly
At Baile chrom in the far north-west, the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane holds the rites of Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise in the open for the first time since the Severance. The cult keeps one night of silence in the year for Sìne, the Peaceful Goose. Outsiders are not told which night it is.
12 an Giblean 1938 DE Cnoc ghorm
The Scorpion houses of the north
Most Tuathaich towns keep the worship of Cnut, the Yellow Scorpion, as the Ròdaich of the west coast do; how the settlers came to it the record does not say. A house of Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe is built at Cnoc ghorm, the largest in the north.
29 an Giblean 1939 DE Cnoc ghorm
The school of the Scorpion at Cnoc ghorm
The Scorpion house at Cnoc ghorm opens a school for its priests, teaching in the humans' tongue and reading the Scorpion's scripture in the Ròdais text the west-coast houses use. It is the only place in the north where both are taught.
11 an Cèitean 1939 DE
The border wall proposed
A formal boundary between Ròdaich and Tuathaich territory is proposed for the first time. It is rejected — not out of principle, records suggest, but because it's considered unnecessary. The two populations are already staying apart on their own.
9 an t-Ògmhios 1939 DE Cathair dhearg
The minute on the wall
The council minute that rejects the boundary wall runs to four lines. The fourth reads: 'They do not come south.' It is initialled by five of the twelve councillors, and the other seven did not sign against it.
8 an t-Iuchar 1939 DE Allt an Àigh
The Allt an Àigh walk
Followers of Seann Spioradan nan Ròdach keep up their yearly walk to the holy well called Allt an Àigh in the east, whose water the old tales say brings fortune. The custodians of the Rite discourage the walk and do not forbid it.
11 an Gearran 1940 DE Achadh gharbh
The walkers at Achadh gharbh
The walkers to Allt an Àigh lodge at Achadh gharbh on the way, and the village builds a long hall for them. The hall's keeper writes each walker's shire in a book, which by the end of the decade holds names from fifty shires.
15 an Cèitean 1940 DE
Extraction resumes at full scale
The mine's post-Severance yield matches, then exceeds, its colonial-era output. Nothing about the method changed. Only who profits did.
23 an Cèitean 1940 DE Achadh dhomhain
The Sloc Mòr concession
The Crown grants the working of the Sloc Mòr, the great shaft at Achadh dhomhain, to Uisdean mac Ùisdein of Cathair mhòr, whose house held an overseer's post under the humans. The terms give the Crown a fifth of the yield. They are the humans' terms with the names changed.
18 an t-Samhain 1940 DE Cnoc fhiadhaich
The night-shift kept
The council declines to end the continuous working of the vein, day and night, that the humans ordered two generations before. The mountain is still given no season of rest. The custodians of the Rite enter a protest and then bless the shafts.
14 am Màrt 1941 DE Muileann dhearg
The pit towns fill
Ròdaich families from the hungry east move to the vein-towns for wages. Muileann dhearg doubles in size within three years, and its hall of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, shut since the humans' time, is taken for a hewers' lodging and enlarged twice in the same span.
6 an Lùnastal 1941 DE Baile thais
Baile thais grows on the ore road
Baile thais, where the ore road from the central mountains meets the east coast, takes on carters, inns and a ropewalk. Its population doubles in a decade, and the town is given a shire court.
4 an t-Sultain 1941 DE Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders off Cathair gheal
Ships that no longer fly any flag, some crewed by men who once served the human administration, begin raiding the coast off Cathair gheal in the north-west. The Tuathaich towns suffer first and are not defended.
3 an Dàmhair 1941 DE Achadh dhomhain
The ore line reaches the Sloc Mòr
The repaired railway is carried up the valley to the pithead at Achadh dhomhain. The first ore train from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg runs under the kingdom's name and on the humans' rails.
25 an Cèitean 1942 DE Achadh dhomhain
The quarry at Achadh dhomhain
The spoil of the Sloc Mòr, a black-veined grey stone, is cut and sold as building stone under the house of Mac Ùisdein's quarry-mark. It is used for public buildings across the south for the next forty years.
8 an t-Iuchar 1942 DE Muileann chrom
The shunting yards at Muileann chrom
The Rail Board lays new sidings at Muileann chrom, where ore trains from the Sloc Mòr are broken up and made up again for the ports. The yard's families, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted separately by the Board and live apart in rows by the lines.
21 an t-Sultain 1942 DE
The guild system restored
The old apprentice-binding custom from the Holy Age is revived in modified form, now explicitly reserved for Ròdaich applicants only.
20 an Dàmhair 1942 DE Achadh dhomhain
The Guild of Hewers chartered
The first guild under the restored custom, the Guild of Hewers, is chartered at Achadh dhomhain. Its oath is taken with a hand on a piece of ore. Its rolls are open to Ròdaich only, as the charter requires.
29 am Faoilleach 1943 DE Ros dhomhain
The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain
The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain take a guild charter of their own and bind their first thirty apprentices in a single day on the slipway.
28 am Màrt 1943 DE Cuan shean
The indentures broken
At Cuan shean and Seann Bhral, Tuathaich boys already bound to Ròdaich masters are released from their indentures under the charter rule. Some go north. Most stay on as day-labour, outside the guilds and their wages.
26 an Giblean 1943 DE Ceann àrsaidh
The chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh
The ship-chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh, on the southern coast east of the capital, take a guild charter and a monopoly of supplying the Crown's patrol boats. The monopoly outlasts the patrol boats.
23 an t-Ògmhios 1943 DE Muileann mhin
The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin
The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, who make the ore lamps used in every shaft on the island, are chartered as a guild. Their mark, a flame over a hammer, is stamped on every lamp and is the only guild mark the humans' traders had ever copied.
6 am Faoilleach 1944 DE Baile chiar
The weavers of Baile chiar
The weavers of Baile chiar are chartered as a guild. Their cloth, woven from southern wool, undersells the northern cloth at the fair until the mills of Doire ghlas are built.
14 am Faoilleach 1944 DE Doire ghlas
Agnes Pike's school
Agnes Pike, a Tuathaich teacher, opens a school at Doire ghlas that teaches in the humans' tongue, with Moot money and without the council's leave. Within a decade there are nine such schools in the north. The council never licenses them and never closes them.
19 an t-Iuchar 1944 DE Scàineadh Cill ghlas
The Cill ghlas district reopened
The mining district closed since the Rending is surveyed and declared safe to work. The first new shafts are cut well back from the old fault line, on the surveyors' word.
27 an t-Iuchar 1944 DE Ceann mhòr
The Leòid circuit in the north
Eilidh nic Leòid rides the northern circuit for the first time and holds court at Ceann mhòr. Of the nineteen cases brought before her, seventeen are Tuathaich suits over land. She finds for the Crown in fifteen, citing her own ruling.
2 an Giblean 1945 DE Cathair dhomhain
Eilidh nic Leòid dies
Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain. Her rulings are bound as a single book, the first law-book of the restored kingdom, and every circuit justice after her carries a copy.
1 an Cèitean 1945 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Leabharlann Muileann chaol founded
A great library is established at Muileann chaol — the institution that will eventually keep the most complete surviving record of everything in this chronicle.
28 an t-Ògmhios 1945 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Ailean Leabhar, first keeper
Ailean mac Iain, called Ailean Leabhar, is appointed the first keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol. He brings with him the council's minute-books and what survived of the humans' tithe ledgers, takes in the custodians' rolls kept in the town's cellars since the Severance war, and spends his first years having them read.
3 an t-Samhain 1945 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
A chur san Leabharlann
Within a few years, 'a chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything made settled and beyond dispute. Ailean Leabhar is recorded as disliking the phrase, on the ground that the library settles nothing and only keeps it.
30 an Cèitean 1946 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The first readers
The library's first reading room opens to anyone who can show a letter from a shire maor. The first reader entered in its book is a shipwright of Ros dhomhain, asking for the humans' plans of their hulls.
27 an t-Iuchar 1946 DE Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The bath-house at the hot springs
A new bath-house is built over the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, paid for by the Guild of Hewers for miners sick with the dust. The guild's sick-roll for its first year lists four hundred men by name and shift.
25 an Lùnastal 1946 DE Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The keepers of the five lights
The five lighthouses built under the humans are given Ròdaich keepers by royal warrant. At Taigh-solais Baile chrom, on the Tuathaich coast, the keeper is a Ròdaich man lodged in a Tuathaich town, and his warrant tells him to report what he sees on land as well as at sea.
22 an Dàmhair 1946 DE Muileann chaol
The Muileann chaol town grows
Copyists, binders and paper-makers settle in Muileann chaol around the library. The town takes a market charter, and its first market day is held in the library's yard.
23 an t-Sultain 1947 DE Tobar dhìreach
The paper-mill at Tobar dhìreach
A paper-mill is built at Tobar dhìreach, a few miles from the library, on the stream below the village. For the next half-century nearly every page of the royal chronicle is written on its paper.
20 an t-Samhain 1947 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The first royal chronicler appointed
A formal office is created specifically to maintain the kingdom's records — the direct ancestor of the archive this very document draws from.
19 an Dùbhlachd 1947 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill
The first royal chronicler is Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a clerk of the council. She keeps her record at Muileann chaol, not at the capital, and writes in her first entry that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne.
25 am Màrt 1948 DE Àth àrsaidh
The first chronicle circuit
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sends clerks to every shire to copy parish books, grave-lists and harbour rolls. The returns from the south fill forty chests. The returns from Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh and the other northern shires fill one; few Tuathaich will speak to the clerks.
2 an Giblean 1948 DE Inis bheag
The chest from Inis bheag
The chronicle clerks at Inis bheag on the north-east coast are shown a parish book going back before the humans' coming, kept in the Seann Spioradan house there. The keeper lets it be copied and not taken.
20 an t-Sultain 1948 DE Cuan bheag
Boats lost off Cuan bheag
A storm out of the west drowns eleven Tuathaich fishermen off Cuan bheag in the north. The village has no lifeboat. The Moot buys one by subscription and asks the council to pay half; the council pays a third.
28 an t-Sultain 1948 DE Uilebheist na Mara
The thing off the north-west cape
Fishermen out of Achadh àrsaidh report a creature longer than their boats in the waters off the north-west cape. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill records the report and adds that the same waters are where the raiders shelter.
9 an Gearran 1949 DE Eilean dhubh
The Eilean dhubh sheep-count
A royal clerk is sent to count the flocks on Eilean dhubh, the largest of the outer isles, to set the island's dues. The islanders count them for him, and the dues are set on their count.
10 am Màrt 1949 DE Cathair gheal
Cathair gheal arms its boats
The Tuathaich fishermen of Cathair gheal arm their own boats and drive the raiders out of the bay. The council, asked for help twice, had sent none. It later fines the town for bearing arms without licence, and the fine is paid.
8 an Giblean 1949 DE Cathair mhòr
The market cross at Cathair mhòr
A market cross is raised at Cathair mhòr, paid for by the house of Mac Ùisdein, with the house's name cut on all four faces. The town's wool and ore markets are moved to its foot.
7 an Cèitean 1950 DE Caol leathan
The Wolf house at Caol leathan
The Wolf house at Caol leathan, the largest of the faith, is rebuilt with a tower from which a bell rings at the hours. The town sets its market and its courts by the bell.
16 an Dàmhair 1950 DE Fèill Muileann òg
Fèill Muileann òg established
An annual fair becomes the island's largest recurring gathering, drawing trade from every province the state controls.
14 an t-Samhain 1950 DE Fèill Muileann òg
Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules
The first toll-mistress of the fair at Muileann òg, Oighrig nic Mhathain, sets its rules: a stall-fee in coin, a court of the fair for disputes, and Tuathaich goods sold only through Ròdaich factors. The rules are read aloud at each fair's opening to this day.
26 an t-Samhain 1950 DE Dùn chrom
The fair's road
The road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is widened and metalled for the fair's carts, passing Dùn chrom, which takes a toll at its gate and grows on it.
2 an Lùnastal 1951 DE Dùn chrom
Dùn chrom's gate-toll
The toll taken at Dùn chrom's gate on the fair road pays for a new wall on the town's southern side. The townspeople call it the fair's wall, and the fair's carters call it something else.
31 an Lùnastal 1951 DE Cathair dhearg
Niall dies; Brìghde crowned
His daughter succeeds him without contest — mortal succession within an immortal-adjacent aristocracy, unremarkable at the time, unusual in hindsight.
29 an t-Sultain 1951 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The chronicler's use of the saying
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes that the succession came 'mar a thàinig Niall', the first time the saying appears in the royal record. It is the only idiom she allows into the chronicle in her whole tenure.
28 an Dàmhair 1951 DE Seann Dunn
The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn
The Seann Spioradan houses of the east coast build a common hall at Seann Dunn, where the ancestors of forty families are named aloud each year by their living heads. The list is copied to the library the next year and grows by a few names every year after.
25 an Gearran 1952 DE Cuan ruadh
Cuan ruadh's harbour light
Cuan ruadh on the east coast, which has no lighthouse of the five, raises a harbour light of its own on the mole, lit with ore bought by the town. The Lighthouse Board declines to take it on.
4 am Màrt 1952 DE Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Còmhrag Ceann leathan established
A brutal annual melee tournament begins at Ceann leathan, ostensibly a martial tradition, increasingly a release valve for a population with fewer and fewer other outlets.
22 an Lùnastal 1952 DE Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Calum Ruadh
The first champion of the Còmhrag the record remembers is Calum mac Aonghais, called Calum Ruadh, a hewer from Muileann chrom. Two men die in the melee he wins. The prize is a year's wages and the right to carry arms in any shire.
30 an Lùnastal 1952 DE Ceann leathan
Ceann leathan's inns
Ceann leathan builds four new inns for the Còmhrag crowds. The fair-wardens of the town, who take a share of every room, become the Còmhrag's keepers in all but name.
10 am Màrt 1953 DE Ros gheal
The ore-ships of Ros gheal
Ros gheal on the north-central coast builds a dock for the grain-ships of the Hawk country. The Hawk houses bless the dock and ask a tithe of the dues. The shire gives them a twentieth.
7 an t-Ògmhios 1953 DE
Splatter and Dodge's generation born
A cluster of births in the Class-08-adjacent shunting families — the generation that will grow up to become Dubhan's closest allies, Seachran and Brean among them.
6 an t-Iuchar 1953 DE Seann Bhral
Seann Bhral in the south
Seann Bhral on the south coast, not to be confused with its namesake in the west, becomes the kingdom's largest fishing port, landing more fish than Ros dhomhain. Its curing-sheds run the length of the harbour.
4 an Lùnastal 1954 DE An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn
The circus at Seann Chwen
The travelling show that calls itself An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is first recorded, pitched near Seann Chwen on the southern coast. The chronicler's clerk could not say what the acts were meant to show. Neither, the clerk adds, could the crowd, which came back the next night.
2 an t-Sultain 1954 DE Seann Bhral
The Scorpion at Seann Bhral
The house of Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe at Seann Bhral, one of the oldest on the west coast, refuses to admit Tuathaich worshippers from the north who come for its feast. Its keeper says the god is the same and the house is not.
11 an Gearran 1955 DE Cnoc ghorm
The northern Scorpion feast
Turned away at Seann Bhral, the Tuathaich worshippers of the Scorpion hold the feast at Cnoc ghorm instead. It is kept there every year after, and the northern feast is larger than the western within a generation.
12 am Màrt 1955 DE
The Depletion first acknowledged
Survey reports begin quietly noting the vein's declining yield. The state does not act on them for years.
9 an Cèitean 1955 DE Achadh dhomhain
Iain Mapa's survey
The survey behind the report is the work of Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, of the Mine Board. His measurements of the faces of the Sloc Mòr show the vein thinning to the east and south. The Board files the survey without circulating it, and Iain Mapa is moved to the silver works at Muileann chiar.
4 am Faoilleach 1956 DE Cathair mhòr
The Mine Board at Cathair mhòr
The Mine Board, which had sat at Cathair dhearg since the Sloc Mòr concession, moves its clerks to Cathair mhòr to be nearer the mountain. Its surveys are kept there, not sent to the library, by the Board's own rule.
15 an t-Ògmhios 1956 DE Baile chrom
The Grey Night forbidden
A Ròdaich magistrate at Baile chrom forbids the gatherings of the Grey Night cult as disorderly. Hannah Crane is fined. The vigil moves indoors and goes on.
9 an t-Iuchar 1956 DE Cuan dhearg
The harbour at Cuan dhearg reopened
The harbour at Cuan dhearg, lost to the Great Wave, is reopened with a new mole of dressed stone. The first boat in is one of those found in the fields behind the old town, refloated and kept by the harbour-master as a relic.
13 am Faoilleach 1957 DE Achadh mhin
Achadh mhin resettled
The fields of Achadh mhin bear again, and a few of the families moved away after the Great Wave come back to them. The shire gives them their old boundaries from the humans' survey.
11 an Gearran 1957 DE Cathair dhearg
Eòghan crowned
Brìghde's reign ends young — no cause is recorded publicly. Her cousin Eòghan takes the throne amid the first real succession tension the restored kingdom has faced.
16 an t-Samhain 1957 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The succession entry
The royal chronicler's entry for the succession gives the fact and nothing more. The chroniclers who followed Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill have added nothing to it.
15 an Dùbhlachd 1957 DE Cathair dhearg
Dissent recorded in council
For the first time the council's minutes record votes against a succession. They name the councillors who voted and not their reasons. Two of them do not sit again.
12 am Màrt 1958 DE Inis bhàn
Inis bhàn's fire
Fire takes the warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn on the north-central coast and burns for two days. The town's Hawk house takes in the homeless. The fire-bell the town buys afterwards is the loudest in the kingdom.
9 an Cèitean 1958 DE
Dubhan born
Born mortal, into the exact confinement the Severance created, decades after the war that closed the island to the people his line descends from.
7 an t-Ògmhios 1958 DE Doire ghlas
The Tuathaich schools counted
The Moot counts eleven schools in the north teaching in the humans' tongue, and three that have begun to teach Ròdais as well, at the parents' asking. Agnes Pike's school at Doire ghlas is among the three.
10 an Giblean 1959 DE Cathair mhòr
The stone house of Mac Ùisdein
Uisdean mac Ùisdein's house at Cathair mhòr is rebuilt in stone quarried from the spoil of the Sloc Mòr, the largest private house in the kingdom. The Guild of Hewers holds its feast in the new hall.
26 an Cèitean 1959 DE Caol mhòr
The northern fishing grounds
Licences to fish the waters south and east of Caol mhòr are reserved to Ròdaich boats. The Tuathaich boats are left the northern grounds, which the raiders also work.
24 an t-Ògmhios 1959 DE Doire shean
Doire shean's harbour
Doire shean in the south-west builds a stone harbour for the fishing boats of the Wolf country, the first new harbour since the Severance not paid for by the Crown. The Wolf house lends the money and takes the harbour dues.
3 an Giblean 1960 DE Làrach an Dùin
Trenches at Làrach an Dùin
Diggers sent by the library open trenches at Làrach an Dùin on the south-east coast. They find walls older than any Ròdaich building and no writing at all. Ailean Leabhar orders the finds catalogued as of the Old Ones, purpose unknown.
7 an Dàmhair 1960 DE Làrach an Teampaill
Làrach an Teampaill measured
The library's diggers measure the ruin called Làrach an Teampaill in the east but do not dig it, at the asking of the Seann Spioradan houses of the district. The keeper enters it as measured and let be.
29 am Màrt 1961 DE Carragh Cnoc bheag
The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
A scribe of the library copies the inscription on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag, stroke by stroke. It matches no script known on the island. The copy is filed and the obelisk is fenced.
27 an Giblean 1961 DE Taigh-solais Baile chrom
A lighthouse on the Tuathaich coast
The Ròdaich keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom reports to the council that the Grey Night cult keeps its vigil in the dark of the lighthouse's own shadow. The council takes no action.
26 an Cèitean 1961 DE Àth bheag
Salt-pans of Àth bheag
Salt-pans are dug on the flats below Àth bheag on the east coast, and within a few years the town supplies the whole eastern seaboard. The salt is carried inland by the old drove road past Baile ìseal.
1 am Faoilleach 1962 DE Cathair fhada
Cathair fhada's grain-store
Cathair fhada on the southern plain builds a Crown grain-store large enough to feed the south for a season. It is filled from the south's own harvests, and first opened in the dry years at Achadh shean.
30 am Faoilleach 1962 DE
The second post-Severance census
The gap between Ròdaich and Tuathaich living standards is, for the first time, measured rather than simply observed. The report is not made public.
28 an Gearran 1962 DE Caol mhòr
Walter Hale dies
Walter Hale, first speaker of the Moot, dies at Caol mhòr. The Moot chooses Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow, to follow him. She is the first woman to hold the chair.
30 am Faoilleach 1963 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The census clerks' private note
One of the census clerks, Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire, leaves among her papers a note that she had asked to see the gap report and been refused. The note reached the library with her papers after her death and is the only mention of the report outside the council.
11 an Gearran 1963 DE Àth àrsaidh
The Tuathaich doctors
The Moot pays for two Tuathaich women to be taught medicine by a Ròdaich physician at Àth àrsaidh, who takes them in defiance of his guild. He is struck from the guild's rolls. They practise in the north for forty years.
12 am Màrt 1963 DE Abhainn ìseal
The Abhainn ìseal floods
The Abhainn ìseal, the longest river on the island, breaks its banks along its lower reach, carrying away three bridges and a stretch of the ore line's embankment. The line is closed for most of a year and the ports live on stored ore.
26 an Cèitean 1964 DE Inis ìseal
The Hawk houses' own custodian
The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag name a custodian of their own, Raonaid nic Iain, and seat her at Inis ìseal. The high custodian at Seann Skell refuses to recognise her. The houses carry on as if he had.
29 an t-Samhain 1964 DE Inis ìseal
Raonaid nic Iain at Inis ìseal
Raonaid nic Iain, custodian of the Hawk houses, writes out the Hawk's order of worship, which had been said and never written. The Hawk houses read it aloud once a year and keep the written copy locked away.
27 an Giblean 1965 DE Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Six dead at the Còmhrag
Six fighters die at the Còmhrag, the most in any year yet. The custodians of the Rite petition for it to end. The fair-wardens of Ceann leathan, whose town lives off the crowds, refuse.
6 an Dàmhair 1965 DE Ceann leathan
The circus at Ceann leathan
An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitches at Ceann leathan in the year of the Còmhrag's six dead and plays to the crowds who stay on after the melee. The fair-wardens are said to have paid it to come.
4 an t-Samhain 1965 DE Ceann leathan
The ore line reaches Ceann leathan
The railway is carried through to the port of Ceann leathan, so that ore can be shipped from a second harbour. Ceann leathan's quays are rebuilt for ore ships, and the town outgrows its walls.
1 am Faoilleach 1966 DE Ros bheag
Ros bheag's shipyard
Ros bheag on the west coast opens a shipyard for ore-ships, so that the western ports need no longer send to Ros dhomhain for hulls. The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain protest to the guild court and lose.
19 an t-Sultain 1966 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
The silver at depth
The silver seam at Muileann chiar, which the Ròdaich kept from the humans, is found richer at depth than anyone expected. The town's old silver guild takes a charter under the restored custom. Iain Mapa, working there since the Board moved him, measures the new faces.
3 an Dùbhlachd 1966 DE Dùn thais
Dùn thais in the west
Dùn thais on the west coast is granted the right to hold its own court of the sea, deciding salvage and wreck along its shore. Its first session awards a raider's hulk to the fishermen who drove it aground.
8 an t-Ògmhios 1967 DE Dùn thais
Dùn thais in the east
Its namesake Dùn thais in the east, seat of its own shire, builds a covered market for the hill farms. The two towns' courts are confused in the royal record for a decade until Tormod Pinn marks them west and east.
18 an Dàmhair 1967 DE Marbh-bheò Doire uaine
The dead and not dead of Doire uaine
Herders near Doire uaine refuse to graze the hills above the town, where old inscriptions tell of a thing that is dead and does not rest. A shepherd goes missing there. The magistrate records wolves.
23 an t-Ògmhios 1968 DE Muileann dhearg
The fall at Muileann dhearg
A gallery of the reopened Cill ghlas district gives way under Muileann dhearg, along a line the surveyors had marked as sound. Thirty-one hewers die. It is small beside the Rending. It is the same fault.
1 an t-Iuchar 1968 DE
The mine-safety reforms
New excavation rules are introduced after a smaller echo of the old Scàineadh Cill ghlas collapse. They apply to Ròdaich workers. Enforcement in Tuathaich-adjacent sites is inconsistent, records suggest deliberately so.
19 an Dùbhlachd 1968 DE Àth leathan
The timber at Àth leathan
At the pits around Àth leathan, where Ròdaich overseers work Tuathaich hands, the new timbering rules are posted and not paid for. The overseers' books, which reached the library later, show the timber ordered and never delivered.
3 an t-Sultain 1969 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Mòrag nic Coinnich, keeper
Ailean Leabhar dies at Muileann chaol, and Mòrag nic Coinnich becomes keeper of the library. She begins the practice, kept ever since, of writing each item's source beside the item itself.
2 an Dàmhair 1969 DE Achadh dhomhain
The pit families of Achadh dhomhain
After the fall at Muileann dhearg, forty hewers' families leave Achadh dhomhain for the fishing ports of the south. The Guild of Hewers binds sixty apprentices to fill the rolls. None of them are Tuathaich.
31 an Dàmhair 1969 DE Fèill Muileann òg
Fire at the fair
Fire runs through the stalls of the fair at Muileann òg. The fair's court sits in a field the next day and the fair goes on. Oighrig nic Mhathain, toll-mistress since the first fair, dies of her burns.
29 an t-Samhain 1969 DE Muileann leathan
The Tuathaich wool carts
The Rail Board refuses to carry goods consigned by the Moot, citing the fair's rule on factors. The wool of the north goes south to Muileann òg by cart, a week on the road, and is sold by factors when it arrives.
26 am Faoilleach 1970 DE Àth fhada
The Tuathaich carters' road
The carters taking northern wool to the fair go by Cnoc ghorm, Àth fhada and the old road down to Inis àrsaidh, and the Tuathaich villages on the way open inns for them. The road is called the Carters' Road in the north and nothing in the south.
2 an t-Iuchar 1970 DE
Dubhan's childhood
He grows up watching an eternally young caste hold every real advantage on an island his own ancestors were pushed to the edge of. The obsidian was never his to inherit.
28 an Dùbhlachd 1970 DE Caol mhòr
The Moot's pit register
The Moot at Caol mhòr begins a register of Tuathaich hewers killed or maimed in the western pits, since no Ròdaich book counts them. Mary Coyle's clerks enter the first year's names from the families' own word. The register is kept to the present and has never been sent south.
5 an Cèitean 1971 DE Ros mhòr
Ros mhòr's boatyard
A boatyard is opened at Ros mhòr in the north by Tuathaich boatbuilders turned out of the guild yards. Its boats are built to the humans' old lines and are faster than anything in the south.
31 an t-Iuchar 1971 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Tormod Pinn
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill lays down the office of royal chronicler. Her successor, Tormod mac Sheumais, called Tormod Pinn for the speed of his hand, keeps the record for more than twenty years and writes more of it than anyone before or since.
25 an Giblean 1972 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's last entry
Her last entry as chronicler is a list of what the record does not hold: the northern towns' own accounts, the humans' treaties in their own tongue, the Board's surveys. Tormod Pinn copies the list into the front of his first book and does not add to it.
3 an Cèitean 1972 DE Tiormachd Achadh shean
Dry years at Achadh shean
Dry years return to the country around Achadh shean, where the Long Drought settled in the humans' time. This time the council sends grain up the ore line and pays for it out of the Sloc Mòr's share. Nobody dies of hunger in the shire, and the chronicler records the fact.
6 an t-Samhain 1972 DE Achadh shean
The wells of Siorrachd Achadh shean
The maor of Siorrachd Achadh shean has twelve wells dug to the rock along the drove road, each marked with the shire's name and the council's. Four of them are still drawn from.
9 am Faoilleach 1973 DE Achadh shean
Grain by the ore line
The grain for Achadh shean comes from the store at Cathair fhada and goes by the ore line for the first time. The Rail Board charges the council for the carriage.
7 an Gearran 1973 DE Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders at Baile ìseal
Raiders land near Baile ìseal on the far east coast and burn the salt-sheds that serve Àth bheag. The kingdom's patrol boats arrive two days later and find the sheds cold.
12 an t-Samhain 1973 DE Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
Murchadh mac Coinnich's log
Murchadh mac Coinnich, keeper of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, begins entering every unlit ship he sees in the lighthouse log with its heading and the hour. His logs, kept for most of his life, are the fullest record of the eastern raiders the library holds.
9 am Faoilleach 1974 DE Àth bheag
The pirates' names
Murchadh mac Coinnich's log names the eastern raiders' ships as the fishermen of Àth bheag name them, since the raiders fly no flag. The names pass into the royal record from his log.
11 an Dùbhlachd 1974 DE Còmhrag Ceann leathan
The Còmhrag at its height
The Còmhrag draws its largest crowd yet to Ceann leathan, and the fair-wardens build timber stands along the three sides of the field. The champion is Ealasaid nic Coinnich of Àth ghlas, the first woman to win it. She does not fight again.
14 an Dàmhair 1975 DE Cnoc bheag
The Hawk port of Cnoc bheag
Cnoc bheag, the largest town of the Hawk country, passes Cathair mhòr in population. Its harbour takes the grain of the north-central coast and its Hawk house is the richest of any faith outside the capital.
12 an t-Samhain 1975 DE
The Feallsanachd an Fhèidh revival
The old philosophical school, dormant since the colonial period, reopens — its founding question, why the vein answers some and not others, suddenly urgent again as the vein itself starts running short.
11 an Dùbhlachd 1975 DE Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's lectures
The revived school's first teacher is Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain, who lectures in the sacred wood near Muileann chiar in the east, where the Fèidh had last met under the humans. Her opening question is the school's oldest, put plainly: why the vein answers some hands and not others.
9 an t-Ògmhios 1976 DE Baile gharbh
The Fèidh in Siorrachd Baile gharbh
Houses of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh in Siorrachd Baile gharbh in the north-east, dormant since the humans' time, reopen at Baile gharbh and Àth fhada. Their teachers walk to the sacred wood to hear Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain and walk back.
5 an Dùbhlachd 1976 DE Caol shean
The school at Caol shean
The Fèidh school takes a house at Caol shean, the largest town of its faith on the east coast, and begins to teach in the wet months, when the wood is too sodden for lectures. Its students copy the census note on the obsidian-touched and debate it openly.
13 an Dùbhlachd 1976 DE Cnoc bheag
The Hawk given a place
A council of the Rite at Seann Skell offers the Hawk houses of Cnoc bheag a place under the high custodian with their own order of worship. The Hawk houses accept the place and keep their order. The quarrel is quieter after this. It is not over.
7 an Gearran 1977 DE Caol chrom
The north-eastern harbours
Caol chrom and Caol gharbh on the north-east coast combine their harbour dues to pay for a breakwater across the strait between them. It takes eight years to build and is still the longest on the island.
23 an Giblean 1977 DE Muileann leathan
Daniel Frayne's copying school
At Muileann leathan in the north, a clerk of the Moot named Daniel Frayne teaches young Tuathaich to copy and bind books, since the guilds that do it in the south will not take them. The bindings of Muileann leathan are later found in Ròdaich libraries without their makers' names.
22 an Cèitean 1977 DE Cidhe Beag
The Abhainn uaine ferries
The boat-landing at Cidhe Beag on the Abhainn uaine is licensed as a ferry, carrying passengers and small freight down the river toward the coast. Its first licensee is an old boatman who had worked the landing without a licence for forty years.
24 am Faoilleach 1978 DE Loch chrom
Loch chrom
Fishermen on Loch chrom, the island's only lake of any size, are given a licence to net its trout, which had been kept for the Crown's table. The Crown's table is supplied first each year.
22 an Gearran 1978 DE Colbh Cnoc chiar
The pillar at Cnoc chiar
Students of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh try to read the pillar near Cnoc chiar by setting it against the obelisk at Cnoc bheag and the column at Cnoc ghorm. They find signs in common and no meaning. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes that the Old Ones were here and said so, and that nobody living can hear it.
23 am Màrt 1979 DE Inis chrom
Flood at Inis chrom
A storm tide floods the lower town at Inis chrom on the south-west coast, drowning the net-lofts and the rope-walk. The town rebuilds both on piles, which is how they stand now.
21 an Giblean 1979 DE Cnoc leathan
Cnoc leathan's schools
Cnoc leathan in the east opens a school in every one of its six parishes, paid from the shire's dues, the first shire to do so. The council asks how it paid for them and is shown the accounts.
20 an Cèitean 1979 DE Cathair mhòr
Alasdair mac Ùisdein's loan
Alasdair mac Ùisdein, grandson of the first holder of the Sloc Mòr concession, borrows against the house's share to pay for a search for a second vein. The Mine Board lends its surveyors. The Crown lends its name.
13 an Giblean 1980 DE Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
The Feallsanachd on the search
Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes to the Mine Board that the search for a second vein asks the wrong question: that the school has always asked why the vein answers some hands, and nobody has asked why there is one vein. The Board files the letter.
21 an Giblean 1980 DE
The failed vein expansion
A costly attempt to locate a second obsidian deposit elsewhere on the island turns up nothing — the same result the Holy Age's failed attempt found centuries earlier, forgotten and rediscovered the hard way.
17 an Dàmhair 1980 DE Dùn dhearg
Forty-one dry shafts
The search's borings run from the hills above Dùn dhearg to the moors south of Baile ruadh. Forty-one shafts are sunk and none strikes the vein. Mòrag nic Coinnich later finds, in a Holy Age list at the library, the same hills named as searched and barren.
6 an t-Ògmhios 1981 DE Dùn dhearg
Dùn dhearg's claim
The town of Dùn dhearg, whose hills held a dozen of the dry shafts, claims damages from the house of Mac Ùisdein for spoiled grazing. The circuit court awards them. The house pays a third before it sells.
5 an t-Iuchar 1981 DE Cathair mhòr
The house of Mac Ùisdein sells half
To meet its debts, the house of Mac Ùisdein sells half its share in the Sloc Mòr back to the Crown. Its stone house at Cathair mhòr is let to the Mine Board, which moves its offices there.
3 an Lùnastal 1981 DE Baile ruadh
The shafts at Baile ruadh left open
The dry shafts of the search are left open on the moors near Baile ruadh. Sheep and one child fall into them before the shire fences them at its own cost. The shire's claim on the house of Mac Ùisdein for the fencing is never paid.
9 an Giblean 1982 DE Muileann dhomhain
The Muileann dhomhain mills
The mills of Muileann dhomhain in the south-east, which ground grain for the vein-towns, turn to grinding bark for the tanners when the vein-towns' orders fall. The town's miller-families keep their mark and change their trade.
5 an t-Iuchar 1982 DE Seann Tarr
The rope-makers of Seann Tarr
The rope-makers of Seann Tarr on the north-east coast are chartered as a guild, the last guild the restored custom creates for a trade that the humans had not touched. Their hemp comes from the fields around Doire uaine and Achadh naomh.
1 an t-Sultain 1982 DE Seann Tarr
Seann Tarr's chest remembered
The rope-makers' charter at Seann Tarr is kept in the shire's own chest, not sent to Cathair dhearg, by the shire's rule. The shire keeper of Seann Tarr keeps a list of what the chest holds and sends the list alone.
30 an t-Sultain 1982 DE An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn
The Circus at Inis àrsaidh
An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is recorded again, this time pitched on the common near Inis àrsaidh on the west coast. The magistrate who licenses it enters the acts as 'various' and the fee as paid.
11 am Màrt 1983 DE Ceann mhin
Ceann mhin's fish-market
Ceann mhin, the great port south-east of the capital, opens a covered fish-market over the old strand. Fish from Seann Bhral and the eastern grounds is sold there for the capital.
8 an Cèitean 1983 DE Còmhrag Ceann leathan
Edged tools banned from the Còmhrag
After a fighter is killed with a hewer's pick, the fair-wardens of Ceann leathan ban edged tools from the Còmhrag. Staves and fists remain allowed, and so the deaths go on, fewer.
6 an t-Ògmhios 1983 DE Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The drowned lighthouse keeper
The keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg on the south coast drowns going out to a boat aground on the reef below the light. The boat's crew are saved by the keeper's daughter, Ciorstaidh nic Artair, who is given the keeper's warrant in his place.
11 am Màrt 1984 DE Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef mark
Ciorstaidh nic Artair has an iron post set on the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, painted and hung with a bell. No boat goes aground there while she keeps the light.
13 an t-Ògmhios 1984 DE Caol mhòr
Mary Coyle lays down the chair
Mary Coyle lays down the Moot's chair at Caol mhòr. Her successor, Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan, is the first speaker born after the Severance.
9 an Dùbhlachd 1984 DE Fèill Muileann òg
The Fèill's northern day
The court of the fair at Muileann òg sets aside one day of the fair for goods from the northern shires, still sold through Ròdaich factors but under the northern makers' own marks. It is the first time a Tuathaich name is written on anything sold there.
12 am Faoilleach 1985 DE Baile chiar
The Tuathaich marks at the fair
The first northern mark sold under its own name at the fair is the cloth of the Doire ghlas weavers, a grey twill with a white thread at the selvedge. The southern weavers of Baile chiar begin weaving a white thread into their own.
11 am Màrt 1985 DE
The Depletion becomes undeniable
What was a quiet survey note in 1955 is now an open crisis. The last untouched sections of the vein are identified — and are smaller than anyone wants to admit.
14 an Dùbhlachd 1985 DE Achadh dhomhain
Catrìona nic Neacail's map
The Mine Board's surveyor-general, Catrìona nic Neacail, publishes the map of the vein's last untouched sections. It fits on one sheet. She resigns within the year and goes to teach at the Fèidh school at Caol shean.
9 an Giblean 1986 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Iain Mapa's survey found
Among the Board's files, Catrìona nic Neacail finds Iain Mapa's survey of thirty years before, which shows the same thinning she had just measured. She sends a copy to the library with a note of when the Board received it.
8 an Cèitean 1986 DE Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid
Iain Mapa dies
Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, dies at Muileann chiar, where the Board had sent him. His own copy of his survey is found among his papers, with the Board's receipt pinned to it.
6 an t-Ògmhios 1986 DE Muileann dhearg
Muileann dhearg empties
Muileann dhearg loses a third of its households to the ports in a few years. Its hall of the Fèidh is closed, and its bell is sold to the school at Caol shean, where it still rings for lectures.
5 an t-Iuchar 1986 DE Ceann leathan
Ceann leathan's ore quays idle
Ore ships wait at Ceann leathan for cargoes that come in half-loads. The harbour dues fall by half, and the fair-wardens of the town raise the Còmhrag's gate-price to make it up.
30 an t-Sultain 1987 DE Baile Mòr dhomhain
Baile Mòr dhomhain's market
Baile Mòr dhomhain in the northern hills becomes the market for the hill country's wool and hides as the ore-towns' trade falls away. Its market day draws more carts than the fair at Muileann òg for two years running.
29 an Dàmhair 1987 DE Cathair dhearg
Mairead crowned
Eòghan's reign ends in the same decade the Depletion becomes public knowledge — his successor inherits a kingdom whose founding resource is visibly failing for the first time in the restored era.
23 an t-Samhain 1987 DE Achadh dhomhain
The Hewers bind no apprentices
The Guild of Hewers binds no new apprentices for the first time since its charter. Its masters vote to keep the rolls open to the sons and daughters of members only.
19 an Giblean 1988 DE Muileann shean
Muileann shean's school of hewers
Muileann shean in the north opens a school for hewers' sons and daughters who will not be bound, teaching them to read, reckon and survey. Most of its first pupils go to the ports.
27 an Giblean 1988 DE Doire ghlas
The Doire ghlas mills
Wool mills are built at Doire ghlas with Moot money, the north's first works tied to nothing in the vein. The Rail Board refuses their cloth until a ruling of the circuit court at Seann Bhral compels it to carry any goods that pay the rate.
31 an Dàmhair 1988 DE Seann Bhral
The Seann Bhral ruling
The circuit justice at Seann Bhral, Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, rules that the Rail Board is a carrier of the Crown and must carry for any payer. It is the first ruling the Moot ever wins in a Ròdaich court. The Board appeals and the council lets the appeal lapse.
30 an t-Iuchar 1989 DE Achadh dhomhain
The Crown's share of the Sloc Mòr
The Crown buys the last of the house of Mac Ùisdein's working shafts at the Sloc Mòr and leaves the house its share in the spoil and the quarry. From this point the vein is worked by the Board in the Crown's name alone.
28 an Lùnastal 1989 DE Àth fhiadhaich
The copper at Àth fhiadhaich
Copper is found in the hills behind Àth fhiadhaich on the east coast. The Board opens a working with men laid off from the Sloc Mòr. It pays wages. It is not the vein, and the town's Seann Spioradan house holds no blessing for it.
2 an t-Ògmhios 1990 DE Àth fhiadhaich
Àth fhiadhaich's copper-town
The copper workings at Àth fhiadhaich draw miners from the failing vein-towns. The town builds a new street for them and names it for the Sloc Mòr, and the Seann Spioradan house there objects to the name.
1 an t-Iuchar 1990 DE
Dubhan begins his experiments
Early, unsuccessful attempts to synthesize a substitute fuel from mining byproducts — failures the historical record barely bothers to name.
13 an t-Iuchar 1990 DE Achadh dhomhain
The Sloc Mòr's pumps
The lowest galleries of the Sloc Mòr are allowed to flood. The pumps cost more to run than the ore beneath them is worth. The Board's minute calls it a pause.
17 an Giblean 1991 DE Seann Bhral
The pumps sold
The Board sells the Sloc Mòr's great pumps to the harbour at Seann Bhral in the south, where they drain the new dry dock. They are the only machines of the vein still at work in the next generation.
16 an Cèitean 1991 DE Imrich nam Pantar
The panthers cross the south-west
A great movement of panthers crosses the south-west near Baile dhomhain. Herders lose stock for a month. Tormod Pinn records it as a thing named in the Holy Age lists and not seen in living memory.
13 an t-Iuchar 1991 DE Baile ghorm
The hides of Baile ghorm
Tanners at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast buy the hides of the panthers killed by herders, and their trade outlasts the migration by a decade. Panther-skin saddles from Baile ghorm are sold at the fair at Muileann òg under the town's mark.
11 an Lùnastal 1991 DE Imrich nam Pantar
Imrich nam Pantar in the record
Tormod Pinn's entry on the panthers is the longest in his book for the year. He sets it beside the Holy Age list and notes that the old list also names the year after the panthers as a hungry one.
10 an Gearran 1992 DE Muileann mhin
The ore-lamp shortage
The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin cut their output by half for want of ore to burn in the lamps they make. Shaft-lamps are lent between pits, and the guild's minute-book records who lent to whom.
18 an Gearran 1992 DE Muileann chrom
Unrest at Muileann chrom
The yard families at Muileann chrom stop the ore trains for three days over cut wages. The Rail Board settles on the fourth and dismisses eleven men on the fifth.
7 an Lùnastal 1992 DE Cathair fhada
The hungry year that was not
The harvest after the panthers' crossing is a good one across the south. Tormod Pinn records it and draws a line through his own note of the year before.
8 an Dàmhair 1993 DE
The third post-Severance census
Population figures are published openly for the first time in Rìoghachd history — a small, symbolic transparency reform that changes nothing structurally.
6 an t-Samhain 1993 DE Caol mhòr
The figures read at the Moot
The published figures are read aloud at the Moot at Caol mhòr. They show the northern towns at about half the Ròdaich measure in every column the clerks chose to take. The Moot's minute says only: 'Now written.'
8 am Faoilleach 1994 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The count of the touched
The published census, like the first, carries a line for the obsidian-touched. It gives a number and nothing else. Tormod Pinn copies it into the chronicle without comment, as Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill had done for the first.
28 an Lùnastal 1994 DE Inis thais
The census in the Wolf country
In the Wolf shires of the south-west, the Wolf houses publish their own count of their people beside the kingdom's, for the first time. The two agree to within a hundred.
26 an t-Sultain 1994 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh
Tormod Pinn dies at his desk at Muileann chaol. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh becomes royal chronicler. She is the first to add, at the foot of each year, a note of what the record could not learn.
10 an Dùbhlachd 1994 DE Ros gheal
The Hawk houses' registers
The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Ros gheal send their birth-rolls to the library for the first time, on condition that the rolls be filed under Creideamh an t-Seabhaig and not under the Rite. Mòrag nic Coinnich agrees.
6 an Gearran 1995 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first foot-note
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first note of what the record could not learn is of the northern shires: that the census clerks were told the figures and did not count them, and that the figures they were told were the Moot's.
7 am Màrt 1995 DE Seann Tarr
The record-chests called in
Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks travel to thirty shire towns to bring their record-chests to Muileann chaol. At Seann Tarr the shire's keeper burns the chest rather than send it, saying the shire's record belongs in the shire. He is fined; the chest is not recovered.
5 an Giblean 1995 DE Cathair naomh
Cathair naomh sends its rolls
The keeper of Cathair naomh in the north sends her shire's rolls to the library in two carts, with the town's own chronicle, kept by a single family for four generations. Mòrag nic Coinnich enters it as the best-kept shire record received.
29 am Faoilleach 1996 DE Seann Toll
The Seann Toll chest
Seann Toll in the north sends its chest willingly and asks for a copy of everything in it. Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks make the copy, and the shire's copy is the model for every copy the library has made since.
26 an t-Iuchar 1996 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The library expansion
Leabharlann Muileann chaol doubles its holdings, absorbing several smaller provincial archives into one central record — the moment Rodian history starts being kept in one place instead of many.
3 an Lùnastal 1996 DE Caol mhòr
No northern chest
No Tuathaich record is called in. The Moot's minute-books, the schools' registers and the vigil-books of Baile chrom stay in the north, in private keeping, as they always had.
2 an t-Ògmhios 1997 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The library's new wing
The expanded library is housed in a new wing at Muileann chaol built of the grey stone from the Sloc Mòr's spoil. The provincial chests fill three floors. The fourth is left empty for what was not sent.
30 an t-Iuchar 1997 DE Àth leathan
The branch line to Àth leathan closed
The Rail Board closes the branch line to Àth leathan, citing falling yield from the western pits. The Tuathaich pits go on working, and their coal goes by cart to the western ports and by boat from there.
28 an Lùnastal 1997 DE Àth leathan
The Moot's hewers take the pits
With the Board's overseers withdrawn from Àth leathan, the Tuathaich hewers there go on working the pits under their own pit captains, paying the Crown's fifth by the Leòid ruling. The Board accepts the payments and records them as arrears.
7 am Màrt 1998 DE Cnoc thais
Cnoc thais in the western hills
At Cnoc thais in the western hills the Tuathaich pits pass to their hewers when the Board's overseers leave, and the pit captain Tom Varley's father is chosen to keep the accounts. The town's own register of the pits begins.
5 an Giblean 1998 DE An Sligeanach Fad' às
The Sligeanach's great year
An Sligeanach Fad' às, the roadside tavern by Ceann bhàn on the southern road, is sold to a family of Achadh mhòr drovers, who build a second hall for the drove trade. It becomes the largest house on the old mining roads.
4 an Cèitean 1998 DE Seann Dunn
The eastern fishing grounds fail
The herring do not come to the grounds off Seann Dunn for the second year together. Boats from the east coast go north to fish the grounds off Caol mhòr, which the licence law reserves to them, and the Tuathaich boats are pushed farther out.
30 an t-Iuchar 1999 DE Inis mhin
Inis mhin's boats
The Tuathaich boats of Inis mhin, pushed out from their grounds by the eastern boats, fish the deep water past the northern isles. Two are lost in the first year and none after, and Inis mhin's catch passes Caol mhòr's.
28 an Lùnastal 1999 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper
Mòrag nic Coinnich retires after some thirty years as keeper. Raghnall mac Mhuirich, her deputy, becomes keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol.
26 an t-Sultain 1999 DE Fèill Muileann òg
The ore price at the fair
The price of ore-fuel at the fair at Muileann òg doubles as the Board cuts its sales. The fair's court fixes a ceiling price and cannot hold it.
26 an Cèitean 2000 DE Cnoc fhiadhaich
Ore thieves at Cnoc fhiadhaich
The Board posts watchmen at the spoil-heaps of Cnoc fhiadhaich after households of the town are found picking ore from the waste to burn. The watchmen are from the town and see nothing.
19 an t-Ògmhios 2000 DE
The first working dubhan
A crude but functional synthetic fuel is produced. It is not yet an economy. It is, for now, one man's answer to a crisis the caste in power still hasn't fully faced.
21 an t-Samhain 2000 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel
At the foot of the year the royal chronicler writes that a fuel made without the vein is reported from the north, and that she has not seen it. Hers is the first mention of dubhan in the royal record, and she spells the word three ways in two lines.
28 an t-Sultain 2001 DE Caol mhòr
The Board's inquiry
The Mine Board sends two surveyors north to learn whether the new fuel burns as it is said to. Their report, which reached the library, says that it burns, that it smells, and that it is not ore.
27 an Dàmhair 2001 DE Cathair dhearg
The lamp-houses of the capital
Cathair dhearg's street-lamps, which burned ore since the humans set them up, are left dark in the poorer streets to save fuel. The dark streets are the first to be lit again when dubhan comes.
22 am Faoilleach 2002 DE Fèill Muileann òg
The last ore sale at the fair
The court of the fair at Muileann òg records its last sale of ore-fuel by the cartload. Ore is sold at the fair after this only by the sack, and at last only by the lump, for altars.
1 an Lùnastal 2002 DE Cathair dhearg
Cathal crowned
Mairead's reign ends as Dubhan's early experiments are still failing more than succeeding — Cathal inherits a kingdom that doesn't yet know how close its own solution already is.
30 an Lùnastal 2002 DE Cathair dhearg
The mint's new dies
The mint at Cathair dhearg cuts new dies for the coinage of the reign. They are the first dies not cut by a pupil of Fearchar Bonn's workshop, and the obsidian ink is still pressed into the seal.
20 an Gearran 2003 DE Seann Skell
The shipmasters' works at Seann Skell
A works for making dubhan is set up at Seann Skell on the southern coast by a company of shipmasters, the first on the island outside the north. The record does not say on what terms they had the process.
25 an t-Samhain 2003 DE Seann Skell
The high custodian's letter
The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell writes to every house of the Rite that the new fuel is not forbidden, since it is not ore, and not blessed, since it is not ore. The letter is read in the houses and argued about in the Fèidh schools for years.
24 an Dùbhlachd 2003 DE Seann Skell
The Seann Skell works' first year
The dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast sell their first year's output to the fishing boats of the south coast and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg. The works' chimney is the tallest thing on the coast.
4 am Màrt 2004 DE Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
Peigi nic Ascaill's trial lamp
Peigi nic Ascaill, engineer to the Lighthouse Board, fits a dubhan burner to a spare lamp in the yard below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and runs it for a hundred nights. Murchadh mac Coinnich, retired from the light, keeps the trial's log for her.
7 an t-Sultain 2004 DE Caol fhiadhaich
The fishing boats of Caol fhiadhaich
The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast fit dubhan engines to the first fishing boats. The Shipwrights' Guild calls the work unlawful for its members. The boatwrights leave the guild and keep the work.
23 an Giblean 2005 DE Ros dhomhain
The shipwrights' guild court
The Shipwrights' Guild court at Ros dhomhain rules that fitting an engine is not shipwrighting and so not within its charter. The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich are readmitted to the guild. They decline.
22 an Cèitean 2005 DE Taigh-solais Baile chrom
The lighthouses converted
The five coastal beacons, still running on obsidian-lit flame for over a century, are the first infrastructure formally converted to dubhan power.
19 an t-Iuchar 2005 DE Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
The last obsidian flame
The obsidian flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg is carried in a closed lantern to the Rite's house at Seann Skell and allowed to burn out on the altar. Custodians from four shires attend, and Ciorstaidh nic Artair, keeper of the light, carries the lantern.
26 am Faoilleach 2006 DE Taigh-solais Muileann bheag
Taigh-solais Muileann bheag converted
The beacon at Muileann bheag on the Tuathaich north coast is converted with the others. Its dubhan is carried by cart from the north, the only one of the five lights whose fuel does not come by sea from Seann Skell.
25 am Màrt 2006 DE Taigh-solais Àth dhearg
Taigh-solais Àth dhearg converted
At Taigh-solais Àth dhearg on the north-east cape the conversion takes a month longer than at the others, because the stair is too narrow for the new tank. The tank is lifted to the lamp-room from outside by a crane borrowed from the rope-walk at Seann Tarr.
20 an t-Ògmhios 2006 DE Taigh-solais Baile chrom
Taigh-solais Baile chrom converted
At Taigh-solais Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast, the conversion is done by Tuathaich fitters from Caol mhòr, the Lighthouse Board having none of its own to send that far. The keeper's report names none of them.
28 an Dùbhlachd 2006 DE Muileann mhin
The lamp-makers turn
The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin begin making dubhan lamps and ask for their guild mark to be allowed on them. The guild court allows it after a year's argument. The flame over the hammer is kept.
9 am Faoilleach 2007 DE Muileann leathan
Daniel Frayne dies
Daniel Frayne, speaker of the Moot, dies at Muileann leathan. The Moot chooses Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas, a mill manager, to follow him.
24 an Gearran 2007 DE Muileann leathan
The binders of Muileann leathan
The Moot sends Daniel Frayne's pupils, the binders of Muileann leathan, to rebind the Moot's minute-books from the first meeting. The rebound set is kept at Caol mhòr, and a second set is made and hidden, the Moot's minute says, elsewhere.
1 an Cèitean 2007 DE Muileann chrom
The ore line's first dubhan engine
The Rail Board runs its first dubhan engine on the ore line, from the yards at Muileann chrom to Cathair dhearg. It carries no ore. It carries dubhan to the capital's lamp-houses and comes back empty.
11 an Dùbhlachd 2007 DE Àth bheag
The eastern salt-road
Salt from Àth bheag goes to the inland towns by dubhan lorry for the first time, on the drove road past Baile ìseal. The drovers of the east coast sell their oxen within a few years.
22 am Màrt 2008 DE Achadh mhòr
Achadh mhòr's drovers
The drovers of Achadh mhòr in the south, with no oxen to drive, buy lorries. The drove-inn at An Sligeanach Fad' às keeps its trade by selling them dubhan.
30 am Màrt 2008 DE An Taigh-seinnse Òir
The tavern circuit modernizes
Roadside houses along the old mining routes install dubhan lamps, ending centuries of oil-and-wick lighting in a single decade.
25 an t-Sultain 2008 DE An Leòmhann Buidhe
An Leòmhann Buidhe keeps a wick
At An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north-east road, the landlord keeps one wick lamp burning over the door beside the new dubhan lamps. The custom spreads along the circuit, and a wick lamp over an inn door is still called a Leòmhann.
19 an Dàmhair 2008 DE Am Buabhall Fortanach
Am Buabhall Fortanach
Am Buabhall Fortanach, the tavern on the south-west road near Doire shean, installs its dubhan lamps last of the great inns. Its landlady's account-book gives the cost as a year's takings.
3 an Gearran 2009 DE An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
The Taigh-seinnse Mòr's hall
An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on the old ore road above Cuan chrom, opens a second hall lit entirely by dubhan. The hall is let for weddings, wakes and the meetings of the Guild of Hewers, whose own hall at Achadh dhomhain has been sold.
4 am Màrt 2009 DE An Taigh-òsta Grianach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach
An Taigh-òsta Grianach, on the south-east road near Cnoc dhìreach, is rebuilt with dubhan lamps in every room and a dubhan pump at the door. It is the first inn on the island to sell fuel as well as beds.
2 an Giblean 2009 DE Muileann chrom
The ore engines laid up
The Rail Board's ore-fired engines are laid up in a siding at Muileann chrom and never run again. The yard families who drove them are retrained on the dubhan engines, those who will be.
11 an t-Sultain 2009 DE An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the north road above Muileann fhada is the last of the great inns to keep a wick lamp in every room. Its landlord writes to the Board that the dubhan smell drives away his guests. It does not, and he puts in the lamps the following year.
10 an Dàmhair 2009 DE Muileann dhearg
Muileann dhearg closed
The last working face under Muileann dhearg is closed. The town's remaining families are moved by the Board to Seann Toll on the coast, and Muileann dhearg is left with its chapel, its graves and a caretaker.
27 an t-Iuchar 2010 DE Seann Toll
The Muileann dhearg families at Seann Toll
The families from Muileann dhearg are settled in a new row at the edge of Seann Toll, which the town calls the Hewers' Row. Few of them find work at sea. Most work on the dubhan tanks at the harbour.
25 an Lùnastal 2010 DE Muileann dhearg
Muileann dhearg's chapel
The Fèidh chapel at Muileann dhearg is given to the town's caretaker to keep, with the graves. The Fèidh school at Caol shean sends a teacher once a year to hold the town's one remaining lecture, which few come to.
23 an t-Sultain 2010 DE
The word spreads before the fuel does
"Dubhan" begins appearing in common speech to mean the fuel itself, not the man, years before the economy built on it is complete.
22 an Dàmhair 2010 DE Caol shean
Dubhan-tùsail
The word 'dubhan-tùsail' is first recorded, in a letter of the Fèidh school at Caol shean, for an early attempt at anything that looked like a dead end before it wasn't. The letter uses it of the school's own revival.
1 an Cèitean 2011 DE Muileann chrom
The Rail Board's new name
The Rail Board drops 'ore' from the name of its main line in its own timetables, calling it only the line. Everyone else goes on calling it the ore line.
30 an Cèitean 2011 DE Achadh dhomhain
The Guild of Hewers dissolved
The Guild of Hewers, chartered at Achadh dhomhain in the first years of the restored custom, dissolves itself. Its rolls, its oath-stone of ore and its sick-roll go to the library. Its last master, Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, writes that the guild had outlived the mountain's patience.
28 an t-Ògmhios 2011 DE Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
The bath-house given to the Rite
The bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, built by the Hewers for their sick, passes to the Rite's custodians with the guild's other goods. It is opened to anyone who pays, the first time it has been open to Tuathaich.
1 am Màrt 2012 DE Achadh dhomhain
The Achadh dhomhain hall
The Hewers' hall at Achadh dhomhain, sold before the guild dissolved, becomes a dubhan depot. Its carved lintel, with the guild's oath cut into it, is left in place over the pumps.
9 am Màrt 2012 DE
The dubhan economy takes shape
Markets, military logistics, and shipping begin shifting wholesale to the new fuel. The obsidian caste, watching its own power source fail, does not object.
4 an t-Sultain 2012 DE Ros dhomhain
The house of Mac Ùisdein moves
The house of Mac Ùisdein sells what remains of its share in the Sloc Mòr's spoil and quarry and puts its money into dubhan shipping at Ros dhomhain. Of the families that held the vein, it is the only one that moved before the vein failed it.
15 an t-Sultain 2012 DE Ros dhomhain
The fleet's first dubhan hulls
The kingdom's patrol boats at Ros dhomhain are refitted for dubhan, and for the first time they can outrun the raiders. The next two raider hulks taken are brought into Ros dhomhain under tow.
2 an t-Iuchar 2013 DE Ros dhomhain
Raiders taken to Ros dhomhain
The crews of the raider hulks brought into Ros dhomhain are tried at the court of the sea there. Several of them are Tuathaich. The court hangs none, sends the Ròdaich among them to the quarries at Achadh dhomhain and the Tuathaich home to the north.
29 an Lùnastal 2013 DE Seann Skell
The Fuel-Fitters chartered
The fitters of dubhan engines, who had worked outside every guild, are chartered as the Guild of Fuel-Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast. Its rolls, like those of every guild before it, are open to Ròdaich only. The Tuathaich fitters already in the trade are let go.
27 an t-Sultain 2013 DE Caol mhòr
Tuathaich fitters go north
The fitters let go by the charter rule go back to the northern towns and fit engines there without a guild. Caol mhòr's harbour has more dubhan boats than any port of its size in the south within a few years.
24 an t-Samhain 2013 DE Caol mhòr
The Moot on the new economy
The Moot at Caol mhòr, under Martha Greaves, debates whether the north should take up the new fuel or keep to its own seams. The Moot votes to take it up. The delegates from the western pit towns walk out.
8 am Màrt 2014 DE Ceann mhòr
The Tuathaich depots
Dubhan depots open at Caol mhòr, Doire ghlas and Ceann mhòr, supplied by sea. Martha Greaves writes in the Moot's minute that the north now buys its fire from the south, and does not say whether this is good.
5 an Cèitean 2014 DE
The fourth currency reform
Rìoghachd coinage is re-pegged to dubhan output rather than obsidian reserves for the first time — an economic admission, quietly made, of which resource actually runs the kingdom now.
3 an t-Ògmhios 2014 DE Cathair dhearg
The plain seal
The mint at Cathair dhearg stops pressing obsidian ink into the coinage seal. The new seal is plain. Fearchar Bonn's first dies are given to the library, where they are kept in the case beside the Guild of Hewers' oath-stone.
31 an t-Iuchar 2014 DE Seann Skell
The Rite's protest on the seal
The high custodian at Seann Skell protests the plain seal to the council as a sign that the kingdom no longer holds the vein sacred. The council's answer is that the kingdom never said it did. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh copies both letters into the chronicle.
27 am Màrt 2015 DE Muileann àrsaidh
The western pit towns meet
Delegates of the western pit towns meet at Muileann àrsaidh, apart from the Moot. They agree to go on working their seams and to sell their coal to any household in the north that will buy it.
6 an Giblean 2015 DE Àth naomh
Àth naomh joins the pit towns
Àth naomh, a Tuathaich town of the western hills with only a few old shafts, joins the pit towns' agreement, its delegates saying that the town would rather be cold with its neighbours than warm alone.
25 an Giblean 2015 DE
Tuathaich resistance organizes
A cluster of northern communities refuse to fold into the new economy, continuing to work the last workable coal seams rather than trade independence for dependence on one man's fuel.
24 an Cèitean 2015 DE Àth leathan
The holdout towns
The towns that refuse are Àth leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg in the western hills. Their spokeswoman is Ruth Calder, a pit captain's daughter from Àth leathan. The Moot at Caol mhòr does not join them and does not condemn them.
4 an t-Samhain 2015 DE Cnoc thais
Tom Varley's pits
At Cnoc thais the pit captain Tom Varley reopens two shafts that had lain abandoned since the humans' time. The coal from them is poor. It is theirs, and it heats the town.
30 am Faoilleach 2016 DE Tobar dhearg
Tobar dhearg of the hills
Tobar dhearg in the western hills, the smallest of the holdout towns, has one pit and forty hewers. It sends its coal to Cathair gheal on the coast and receives fish in exchange.
7 an Gearran 2016 DE Doire ghlas
Ellen Marsh's books
Ellen Marsh, a schoolteacher of Doire ghlas, finishes a collection of Tuathaich accounts of the Severance and the settlement, taken down from the old in the north over many years. It fills eleven books. It is her request that goes to the library.
15 an Gearran 2016 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The library's Tuathaich wing proposed
A formal request to archive Tuathaich oral history alongside the official Ròdaich record is submitted to Leabharlann Muileann chaol. It is tabled, not rejected — and remains tabled to this day.
12 an Lùnastal 2016 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The keeper's answer
Raghnall mac Mhuirich's answer to Ellen Marsh says that the request awaits the council's view on the standing of oral testimony. The council has not given one.
20 an Lùnastal 2016 DE Doire ghlas
Ellen Marsh's reply
Ellen Marsh writes back to the keeper that oral testimony was good enough for the census clerks when they took the Moot's figures. Her letter is filed with the request.
21 an Gearran 2017 DE Doire ghlas
The coal price in the north
The holdout pits sell their coal to Tuathaich households across the north at less than the price of dubhan. The Moot's own wool mills at Doire ghlas buy it. The Board's revenue from the north falls for the first time since the Severance.
22 am Màrt 2017 DE Cathair mhòr
The Board's northern revenue
The Mine Board's accounts show its northern revenue down by a quarter. The Board's report to the council names the western pits as the cause and the Leòid ruling as the remedy.
20 an Giblean 2017 DE Seann Bhral
The seams declared Crown property
The Mine Board declares the western seams Crown property under the Leòid ruling, holding that the right to work them lapsed when the holders stopped paying the fifth. The holders say they stopped paying when the Board stopped carrying the coal. The pits are ordered closed.
16 an Dàmhair 2017 DE Seann Skell
Enforcers posted to the west
A company of the Board's enforcers is posted at Seann Skell on the western coast to close the pits. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh notes that it is the first armed company the kingdom has sent toward the north since the Severance.
23 am Faoilleach 2018 DE Seann Skell
The enforcers' depot
The enforcers at Seann Skell on the west coast build a dubhan depot for their lorries at the town's edge. The town's Scorpion house refuses to bless it, and the high custodian of the Rite sends a priest to do so instead.
31 an Lùnastal 2018 DE Caol mhòr
The Moot's warning
Martha Greaves writes to the council from Caol mhòr that the western towns will not close their pits for a letter, and asks for a year's delay while the Moot talks with them. The letter is received and filed.
29 an t-Sultain 2018 DE
First skirmishes
Minor, unrecorded clashes between state enforcers and Tuathaich coal-holdouts begin — too small individually to name, together the clear runway into open war.
28 an Dàmhair 2018 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The chronicler asks
At the foot of the year Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh writes that clashes are reported in the west, that the Board's reports of them are not given to the chronicler, and that she has asked for them. They were not given.
26 an t-Samhain 2018 DE Muileann àrsaidh
The pit-heads walled
The pit-heads at Muileann àrsaidh are walled with spoil and timber, and the road into the town from the south is dug across. The Board's enforcers at Seann Skell report the town closed to them.
25 an Dùbhlachd 2018 DE Àth leathan
Ruth Calder's letter
Ruth Calder writes to the council for the western towns, offering to pay the Crown's fifth in coal if the Board will carry it and let the pits work until the seams are spent. The letter reached the library. No answer to it did.
23 am Faoilleach 2019 DE Caol mhòr
The Moot stands apart
The Moot at Caol mhòr resolves that it is not a party to the quarrel between the Board and the western towns, and will feed anyone who comes to its towns hungry. The resolution is carried by nine votes.
4 an t-Iuchar 2019 DE Doire ghlas
The Moot's granaries
The Moot orders its granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas filled beyond the usual, paying from the wool-mill revenue. The minute gives no reason.
2 an Lùnastal 2019 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Sìleas nic Rath
Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh lays down the office, and Sìleas nic Rath, her clerk, becomes royal chronicler. Her record of the war is the one the library would later seal.
28 an Dàmhair 2019 DE
The mobilization order
Regiments not called to active service since the Severance itself are reformed and re-equipped, openly, months before anyone in power admits a war is coming.
26 an t-Samhain 2019 DE Cathair dhearg
Somhairle mac Lachlainn
Command of the reformed regiments is given to Somhairle mac Lachlainn, who had risen among the Board's enforcers. The rolls of the Severance companies are brought out of the council's chests at Cathair dhearg to name the reformed regiments, and the old names are read aloud before new men.
25 an Dùbhlachd 2019 DE Cathair dhearg
The Moot's last petition
Martha Greaves carries a petition from the Moot to the council at Cathair dhearg in person, asking that the western pits be left to work out their seams, which the Moot says will be spent within a few years in any case. It is received and filed. She is the first speaker of the Moot to enter the council chamber.
12 am Faoilleach 2020 DE Seann Bhral
Arms by the ore line
The Rail Board carries arms and dubhan from Cathair dhearg to Seann Bhral on the ore line and its western branch. The yard at Muileann chrom works day and night on the trains.
20 am Faoilleach 2020 DE Àth leathan
The hewers gather at Àth leathan
Hewers from the five western towns gather at Àth leathan, where the road from the south enters the hills. The Board's lists name Ruth Calder and Tom Varley among them.
28 am Faoilleach 2020 DE Seann Skell
The regiments go west
The reformed regiments set out from Cathair dhearg by the western road, their carts and lorries running on dubhan, to join the enforcers at Seann Skell on the west coast.
11 an Giblean 2020 DE Àraich Àth leathan
Battle of Àth leathan
The first major engagement of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War. The state, already leaning on Dubhan's fuel to prop up its fading power, moves against the holdouts directly.
11 an Giblean 2020 DE Àraich Àth leathan
The dead of Àth leathan
The open record counts the kingdom's dead at Àth leathan and does not count the holdouts'. Tuathaich telling puts theirs in the hundreds. Ruth Calder's name does not appear in the open record after this battle.
11 an Giblean 2020 DE Muileann àrsaidh
Into the hills
After Àth leathan the holdouts give up the southern pits and fall back into the hills around Muileann àrsaidh and Cnoc thais. The pits at Àth leathan are taken without a fight and flooded on the Board's order.
13 an Giblean 2020 DE Seann Skell
An seachdamh rèisimeid raised
The seventh regiment is raised from the levies of the west coast and stationed at Seann Skell, the port nearest the western hills. It holds the road behind the army and the field of Àth leathan.
21 an Giblean 2020 DE Àraich Àth leathan
The field of Àth leathan after
The field of Àth leathan is left unploughed. The seventh regiment's patrols pass it on the road to the western hills and report it empty.
29 an Giblean 2020 DE
The wartime tithe
A temporary tax increase, justified by the war, on every dubhan transaction in the kingdom. It is never repealed once the war ends.
7 an Cèitean 2020 DE Fèill Muileann òg
The tithe at the pumps
The wartime tithe is collected at the dubhan depots, where a clerk of the Treasury sits beside every pump. The fair-court at Muileann òg records the first complaint against it within a month.
13 an Cèitean 2020 DE Inis mhòr
A' chiad rèisimeid raised
The first regiment is raised at Inis mhòr, the port beside the capital, from the capital's own companies. It guards the council, the mint and the bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain.
20 an Cèitean 2020 DE Àth gharbh
A' chiad chabhlach raised
The first fleet is raised from the south-west harbours and stationed at Àth gharbh. It is sent round the western cape to stop coal going out by sea from the Tuathaich ports.
21 an Cèitean 2020 DE Cuan shean
An ceathramh cabhlach raised
The fourth fleet is raised at Cuan shean on the west coast and joins the first off the Tuathaich shore. Between them they close Seann Skell and Cnoc bhàn in the north-west to every boat but fishing boats, and search those.
5 an t-Ògmhios 2020 DE Muileann àrsaidh
The siege of Muileann àrsaidh
The regiments invest Muileann àrsaidh. The town holds for weeks on stored coal and potatoes, and its pit-heads are taken one at a time. Sìleas nic Rath's open record gives the day it fell and nothing else.
13 an t-Ògmhios 2020 DE Cathair mhòr
An treas rèisimeid raised
The third regiment is raised at Cathair mhòr, where the Mine Board keeps its offices in the old stone house of Mac Ùisdein. Its first muster is held under the market cross the house had raised.
21 an t-Ògmhios 2020 DE Seann Warr
An còigeamh rèisimeid raised
The fifth regiment is raised at Seann Warr on the west coast below the capital. It is sent north to relieve the regiments before Muileann àrsaidh.
29 an t-Ògmhios 2020 DE Cathair dhearg
The capital's lamp-houses rationed
Dubhan for the army is taken ahead of every other use. The capital's poorer streets go dark again, as they had before the fuel came, and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg ration by street.
17 an t-Iuchar 2020 DE Caol mhòr
Families at Caol mhòr
Families from the western pits come into Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas with what they can carry. The Moot feeds them from its own stores, as it had resolved. The council sends nothing and forbids nothing.
25 an t-Iuchar 2020 DE Caol mhòr
The Moot's granaries opened
The Moot opens its granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas to the families from the west. Its minute records the amount given and the names of the families, which are among the few Tuathaich records of the war the library does not hold.
2 an Lùnastal 2020 DE Doire ghlas
Agnes Pike's school as a shelter
The school at Doire ghlas that Agnes Pike founded is given over to the families from the west, its benches used for beds. Ellen Marsh, who teaches there, takes down the families' accounts.
10 an Lùnastal 2020 DE Cnoc thais
Cnoc thais taken
Cnoc thais is taken after the regiments cut the road to its pits. Tom Varley's two shafts are fired and sealed. The open record gives the number of holdouts taken and not the number who went on into the hills.
23 an t-Sultain 2020 DE Seann Skell
An dàrna cabhlach raised
The second fleet is raised at Seann Skell on the southern coast to keep the eastern and southern waters while the first and fourth are in the north-west.
2 an Dàmhair 2020 DE Spùinneadairean-mara
Raiders take the salt-boats
