With the fleets drawn north-west, raiders from the eastern waters take two salt-boats off Àth bheag and burn a third. The second fleet runs one of the raiders down off Baile ìseal.
17 an Dàmhair 2020 DE Cnoc bheag
An siathamh rèisimeid raised
The sixth regiment is raised at Cnoc bheag, the great port of the Hawk houses on the north-central coast. It holds the northern road between the Tuathaich shires and the middle of the island, and the Hawk houses bless its colours in their own order.
25 an Dàmhair 2020 DE Àth dhìreach
An dàrna rèisimeid raised
The second regiment is raised at Àth dhìreach in the east and set to guard the ore line and the library road. Its camp is the first soldiery the town of Muileann chaol has seen.
2 an t-Samhain 2020 DE Caol bheag
An ceathramh rèisimeid raised
The fourth regiment is raised at Caol bheag on the north-east coast. It is shipped west round the north coast in hired dubhan hulls and landed at Ceann mhòr in the Tuathaich north.
10 an t-Samhain 2020 DE Ceann mhòr
The regiments at Ceann mhòr
The fourth regiment is quartered at Ceann mhòr, in the old human magistrate's house that the maor had kept since the shires were drawn. The Moot protests the quartering. The protest is received.
15 an t-Samhain 2020 DE Cathair gheal
The fishermen of Cathair gheal
The fleets off the north-west search the fishing boats of Cathair gheal every day they go out. The fishermen petition the Moot, which petitions the council. The searching goes on.
16 an t-Samhain 2020 DE Inis uaine
An t-ochdamh rèisimeid raised
The eighth regiment is raised at Inis uaine on the east coast to guard the dubhan depots and tanks of the eastern ports, which the council fears the holdouts might fire.
1 an Dùbhlachd 2020 DE Baile ghorm
An treas cabhlach raised
The third fleet is raised at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast and carries the army's dubhan up the west coast in tank-hulls to the regiments in the hills.
9 an Dùbhlachd 2020 DE Baile chrom
The Baile chrom vigil
The Grey Night cult at Baile chrom keeps its vigil as always. The regiments quartered along the coast report a night when the whole town was dark and silent, and search it, and find nothing.
17 an Dùbhlachd 2020 DE Àth naomh
Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg
The last two western towns, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg, open their roads to the regiments without a siege. Their pits are flooded. The open record names no holdouts taken at either.
25 an Dùbhlachd 2020 DE Seann Skell
An naoidheamh rèisimeid raised
The ninth regiment is raised at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the second of that name in the regimental list, to guard the dubhan works the shipmasters built there. The regimental clerks tell the two apart by their coasts.
29 an Dàmhair 2021 DE Muileann mhin
The column goes south
A column of holdouts, several hundred strong, leaves the western hills and moves south-east through the middle of the island toward the capital. Why it did so is in the sealed archive. The name Tuathaich telling gives its leader is Owen Barrow. The open record gives no name.
24 an t-Samhain 2021 DE Àth bheag
The column's road
The column's road south-east runs by Àth bheag in the west, Muileann mhin and the edge of the capital's country. The towns it passes report it, and the open record copies their reports and not the regiments'.
6 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE Muileann ghlas
The camp by Muileann ghlas
The column passes Muileann òg and makes camp on the fields by Muileann ghlas, within a day's walk of Cathair dhearg. The first and third regiments are brought down the fair road to meet it.
9 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE Fèill Muileann òg
The fair-ground emptied
The fair-ground at Muileann òg is cleared of its standing booths to give the first and third regiments room to camp. Its court's books for the year end without a closing entry.
10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE Àraich Muileann ghlas
Battle of Muileann ghlas
The war's second and final major battle. The Tuathaich holdouts are broken within a single year's campaign — descendants of the humans once pushed to the island's edge, pushed back again, this time by a fuel one of their own invented.
10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE Àraich Muileann ghlas
The field at Muileann ghlas
The open record lists the first and third regiments on the field at Muileann ghlas and gives no count of the column's dead. The regiments' own dead are named on a stone at Cathair mhòr, set up the following year.
10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE Àraich Àth leathan
The last pits give up
Word of Muileann ghlas reaches the hills, and the holdouts still in them come down to the seventh regiment's posts on the Àth leathan road. They are disarmed and sent home. The open record counts their weapons.
10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE
An Cogadh Fada ends
Nine regiments and four fleets, still active today, were raised in this campaign; each is named for the town it is stationed in.
10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE Caol mhòr
Fadachadh
Among Tuathaich speakers, 'chaidh am fadachadh', they got long-warred, begins to be said of the defeat in the west, and then of any defeat after holding out too long. It is said as a joke, and the people who say it do not laugh.
13 am Faoilleach 2022 DE Cathair dhearg
The regiments stay on their stations
The nine regiments and four fleets are not stood down. The council keeps each at the town it was raised in and pays them from the wartime tithe.
26 am Faoilleach 2022 DE
The dubhan monopoly completes
With the last organized resistance gone, Dubhan's fuel becomes functionally mandatory across the entire island economy.
11 an Gearran 2022 DE Àth leathan
The western seams flooded
By the Board's order the last western seams are flooded and their shafts capped with concrete. The seventh regiment stands by at each capping. No coal is dug on the island outside the Board's own works after this.
24 an Gearran 2022 DE Caol mhòr
The prisoners sent home
The holdouts held since Muileann ghlas are released from the capital's gaol and sent north under the first regiment's escort as far as the boundary stones. The Moot's register adds their names to the dead and maimed it has kept since the Severance, in a column of its own.
4 an t-Iuchar 2022 DE Cathair dhearg
Somhairle mac Lachlainn seated
Somhairle mac Lachlainn is given a seat on the council. He is the first soldier to sit there since the captains of the Severance war.
31 an Lùnastal 2022 DE Àth leathan
The seventh regiment at Àth leathan
The seventh regiment builds a post on the road below Àth leathan and keeps a company there. The post is called the Àth leathan post in the regimental lists and something else in the town.
15 an Dùbhlachd 2022 DE Cathair mhòr
The stone at Cathair mhòr
A stone is set up at Cathair mhòr with the names of the regiments' dead from Àth leathan and Muileann ghlas. It stands beside the market cross of the house of Mac Ùisdein.
28 an Dùbhlachd 2022 DE Àraich Muileann ghlas
The Muileann ghlas field
The field at Muileann ghlas where the column camped is sown again. The farmer who holds it finds weapons in the furrows for years and hands them to the first regiment, which keeps a list.
27 an Giblean 2023 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The library's war archive sealed
Leabharlann Muileann chaol's complete Long War record is formally sealed from public access for a term of fifty years — the only sealed archive in the kingdom's history.
22 an Cèitean 2023 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
Sìleas nic Rath's open chronicle
What remains open of the royal chronicle for the war years is Sìleas nic Rath's list of places, the regiments present and the counts she was allowed. Her full record went into the sealed archive with the rest.
26 an Cèitean 2023 DE Àraich Àth leathan
The cairn at Àth leathan
Tuathaich families build a cairn on the field of Àth leathan without leave. The seventh regiment's patrols leave it standing, and it grows by a stone or two every time the patrols pass.
2 an Lùnastal 2023 DE Cathair dhearg
The tithe carried forward
The Treasury's accounts carry the wartime tithe forward as a standing line under the regiments' pay. No minute of the council records a decision to keep it.
29 an t-Sultain 2023 DE Seann Skell
The Fuel-Fitters and the regiments
The Guild of Fuel-Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast is given the contract for the regiments' engines and the fleets' hulls, and doubles its rolls. The rule of the charter holds, and all its new fitters are Ròdaich.
28 an Dàmhair 2023 DE Taigh-solais Baile ìseal
The second fleet off Baile ìseal
The second fleet runs down the raiders off Baile ìseal who had taken the salt-boats during the war, and brings their hulls into Seann Skell. The lighthouse log at Baile ìseal records the chase from the lamp-room.
23 an Giblean 2024 DE Spùinneadairean-mara
The fourth fleet in the north-west
The fourth fleet, kept on the Tuathaich coast after the war, searches the raiders' bays off Cathair gheal and finds them empty. The fishermen of Cathair gheal say the raiders left when the fleets came and will be back when they go.
25 an Cèitean 2024 DE Baile ghorm
The third fleet's tank-hulls
The third fleet at Baile ghorm keeps its tank-hulls after the war and runs dubhan up the west coast to the Tuathaich depots on the council's contract. The Moot pays the freight.
2 an t-Ògmhios 2024 DE Uilebheist na Mara
The creature off the cape again
The fourth fleet's log for the year records a thing longer than a patrol boat off the north-west cape, where the Tuathaich fishermen had reported one in Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's time. The log records it as a whale.
10 an t-Ògmhios 2024 DE Cathair dhomhain
Anna nic Phàil's motion
The proposal to compensate the Tuathaich communities is carried into the council by Anna nic Phàil, councillor for Cathair dhomhain, on a petition from the Moot under Martha Greaves. She speaks for it once.
18 an t-Ògmhios 2024 DE Cathair dhearg
The reparations debate
A proposal to formally compensate Tuathaich communities for wartime losses is raised in the capital and quietly allowed to die without a vote.
27 an Dàmhair 2024 DE Caol mhòr
The Moot's minute on the reparations
The Moot's minute on the reparations motion runs to one line: 'Allowed to die.' Martha Greaves lays down the chair the same year. The Moot chooses Peter Hale, a great-grandson of its first speaker, to follow her.
6 an Dùbhlachd 2024 DE Seann Warr
The fifth regiment's barracks
The fifth regiment builds stone barracks at Seann Warr, the first permanent quarters any of the nine regiments has had. The town gives the land and takes the regiment's custom.
14 an Dùbhlachd 2024 DE Inis uaine
The eighth regiment at Inis uaine
The eighth regiment's guard on the eastern dubhan tanks at Inis uaine is made permanent. The regiment's officers take houses in the town, and Inis uaine's Seann Spioradan house adds the regiment to its prayers.
22 an Dùbhlachd 2024 DE Caol bheag
The fourth regiment leaves Ceann mhòr
The fourth regiment leaves the old magistrate's house at Ceann mhòr and goes home to Caol bheag. The Moot asks for the house to be given to the town. It is given to the maor.
18 an Giblean 2025 DE Caol mhòr
Seann-chunntas
Tuathaich speakers begin to name the tabled archive request and the dead reparations motion together as 'seann-chunntas', an old reckoning that nobody in power will act on and nobody has cancelled. Official Ròdaich usage does not take the word up.
17 an Cèitean 2025 DE Achadh dhomhain
The Sloc Mòr closed
The Mine Board closes the upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr at Achadh dhomhain. One face is kept open under the custody of the Rite, to cut ore for the altars, a few baskets a year.
29 an Cèitean 2025 DE Achadh dhomhain
The last hewers
Twelve hewers are kept at the Sloc Mòr to cut the altar-ore under the Rite's custody. They are the last of their trade working the vein on the island, and the Rite gives them its own oath, not the dissolved guild's.
15 an t-Ògmhios 2025 DE Còmhrag Ceann leathan
The regiments at the Còmhrag
Fighters from the regiments are entered in the Còmhrag at Ceann leathan for the first time. The ninth regiment's man wins it. The fair-wardens raise the gate-price again.
27 an t-Ògmhios 2025 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The second regiment's library guard
The second regiment at Àth dhìreach keeps a guard at Leabharlann Muileann chaol on the sealed war archive. The keeper, Raghnall mac Mhuirich, writes to the council that the library had not asked for one.
14 an t-Iuchar 2025 DE Achadh dhomhain
The ore line carries no ore
The last ore train runs from Achadh dhomhain to Cathair dhearg. The ore line keeps its name and carries dubhan, wool and soldiers.
12 an Lùnastal 2025 DE Caol mhòr
The sixth regiment on the northern road
The sixth regiment at Cnoc bheag keeps posts on the northern road where the boundary stones stand. Tuathaich going south show a pass for the first time since the Severance. The council's minute calls the passes temporary.
10 an t-Sultain 2025 DE Fèill Muileann òg
The fair of the present year
The fair at Muileann òg draws traders from every shire the state controls. Tuathaich wool is sold there on its northern day, through Ròdaich factors, as it has been since the first fair.
9 an Dàmhair 2025 DE Còmhrag Ceann leathan
The Còmhrag of the present year
The Còmhrag at Ceann leathan is fought with staves and fists, as it has been since edged tools were banned. Two regiments and nine shires send fighters. One man dies.
7 an t-Samhain 2025 DE Doire ghlas
The eleven books
Ellen Marsh's eleven books are copied by hand in the Tuathaich schools and kept in the north. The library's catalogue lists the tabled request and not the books.
19 am Faoilleach 2026 DE Caol mhòr
The Moot of the present year
The Moot at Caol mhòr meets under Peter Hale. Its minute-books run unbroken from Walter Hale's first meeting. It has no standing in Ròdaich law and has never asked for any.
17 an Gearran 2026 DE Seann Skell
The dubhan works of the present
Dubhan is made at Seann Skell on the southern coast and at works in the east and north. Every lamp, engine, ship and lorry on the island runs on it. The coinage is pegged to it, and the tithe is taken on every sale.
29 an t-Iuchar 2026 DE Seann Skell
The altar-ore
The Rite's twelve hewers at the Sloc Mòr cut the year's altar-ore. It fills four baskets. The high custodian at Seann Skell divides it among the houses of the Rite by lot.
22 an t-Samhain 2026 DE Leabharlann Muileann chaol
The chronicler's note on the present
Sìleas nic Rath writes at the foot of the year that the kingdom's record is complete in every part but two: the war, which is sealed, and the north, which was not asked.
21 an Dùbhlachd 2026 DE Cathair dhearg
The present
The coal is all but gone. The dubhan economy runs on a name that used to belong to one man. The Ròdaich hold the capital and the sea. The Tuathaich hold the north, a grievance five years old, and a First-Canoe memory the people who twice defeated them still call folklore.

Appendix A — The Rulers and Houses of Rodos

This appendix sets out the lines of those who ruled on Rodos, age by age, as the surviving lists give them: the two oral lists of the Ancient Age; the Keepers' roll and the king-list of the Holy Age; the crown of the Age of Sundering as the custody-book and the king-list record it; the council, the Commissioners and the overseers of the Age of Strangers; and the rulers of the restored kingdom. After the tables come short accounts of each line, an account of the seven houses of custody, and an account of how the keeping of the vein and the keeping of the realm were joined and parted.

The tables give only rulers whom the lists and chronicles name. Where a list says that names are missing, the table says so, and gives none. A reign is dated by the rolls that record its beginning and its end. Where no roll marks one or the other, the table gives "—". Where the rolls fix it only roughly, the year is marked c. Many rulers are known only from a single mention in the middle of their reign. For these the table gives "in office" and the year of that mention.

I. The Tables

The Stone Kings of Dùn ìseal (Rìghrean na Cloiche), Age I. The oldest oral list, held on the hill of Dùn ìseal. It "gives no lengths of reign" (9 an Lùnastal 7600 BDE). The year shown is the year of the deed each king's telling remembers. It is not a year of accession.

NameBynameHouseCame to the flameKeepingThe keeping

II. The Ancient Age: the Two Lists

Before the Binding, Rodos kept its rulers only in recitation. The Stone Kings' list belonged to the hill of Dùn ìseal and is older than the name Ròdaich (9 an Lùnastal 7600 BDE). The Red Hill list belonged to the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. Each list remembers a holder for one deed and gives no length of reign. For a long time neither mentions the other. They first meet at the ford where the fair of Muileann òg is now held, when Raghnall Ceannfhionn traded salt for wool with the Red Hill (10 an Cèitean 6426 BDE). The peace of the ford held through a fosterage: Eilidh Ghlas's son went west to Lachlann an Altraim and came home grown under Peigi Dhubh (31 am Màrt 5174 BDE). Neither list keeps the foster-son's name.

A third office ran beside the two lines and answered to neither. From 26 an t-Samhain 5198 BDE the keeper of the slab over the crack was chosen by lot. When Calum Ciar asked for the lot to be drawn in his sight, the households refused him, and from then on the Stone Kings ruled the grazing and not the vein (7 an Cèitean 5185 BDE).

Catrìona Mhòr is the hardest name in either list. The tellings set three things "in her time": the first coming of Dùn dhearg to the ford, the first recital of both lists together, and the keepers' request that their charge be declared (9 an t-Iuchar 3225 BDE). The three fall across more than half a century: a long reign, but not a longer one than a life can hold. The Library does not know whether one holder saw all three or the tellings drew a neighbour's deeds to one famous name. Both lists end in her generation. The Holy Age says the Binding came "centuries before anything like a king" (23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE). The Hall that kept that saying did not count the holders of the hills as kings, and the name Rìghrean na Cloiche is the later scribes'.

III. The Holy Age: the Keepers and the Kings

The Keepers came first. The nine hearths chose each one, and for many generations they chose from the house of Muireach. Under Eilidh nic Ìomhair, the first Keeper from outside that house, the office was bound to four houses of custody: Sliochd Mhuirich, Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Thormoid and Sliochd Raghnaill (29 an Giblean 2607 BDE). The Keeper held the flame, the galleries and the Small-Burning Law, and raised no spears. When Seumas Bàn found that more than half the Keepers on the roll were of his own house, he had the fact struck from its preface (16 an t-Samhain 164 BDE). The unstruck copy survived him.

Kingship began in the granaries of Dùn dhearg. The households who ate Sliochd Ìomhair's grain called Goraidh mac Ìomhair their rìgh (28 an Cèitean 2325 BDE), and he took care to claim nothing over the vein. By the division of keeping, the rìgh held the roads, the granaries and the lowland peace, and the Keeper held the rest (9 an t-Sultain 2305 BDE). The early rulers were rulers of roads, and the first war between Ròdaich, Iain Garbh's War of the Roads, was fought over tolls.

The king-list says plainly where it fails. It gives eleven bare names after Catrìona Ghlic (1 an t-Sultain 1779 BDE) and nine after Tormod Òg (29 am Màrt 439 BDE), and Tormod Scrìobhaiche marked which of his names came from reciters (18 an t-Sultain 1668 BDE). The list's years give Goraidh Mòr, his daughter, her son and his niece some eighty years of rule apiece before the niece's son, Iain Garbh, takes the hall: more years than four lives in one line can hold one after another. There, as wherever the list's years outrun the lives of the named, the Library takes it that the reciters' names stand for more reigns than they name, and does not correct them.

Beathag Mhòr, the first banrìgh, moved the seat to Cathair dhearg (12 am Faoilleach 1280 BDE). When Oighrig nic Lachlainn died without an heir, the Four Houses met at Dùn ìseal, and the Keeper set the stone cup in the hands of Gilleasbuig Mòr of Sliochd Thormoid (12 am Màrt 483 BDE). The house of Tormod held the red hall from then to the close of the age. Mòr nic Coinnich took the cup from the Keeper in the same way, and her name closes the king-list.

IV. The Age of Sundering: the Crown and the Houses

Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill would neither send anyone across the water nor keep anyone back (11 an Dàmhair 38 BDE). Her sister Mòrag went, as a leader of the departed, and six years after the Setting-Out the queen struck Mòrag's line from the succession "as persons no longer on Rodos" (1 an Lùnastal 7 DE). Beathag's own line ended with her grandson Ìomhar.

From then on the seven houses made the kings whenever blood failed. They chose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Clann Fhearchair (19 an Gearran 143 DE), and the crown passed through Sìleas nic Fhearchair to her son's line. That line ended with Tormod Bàn, who died without naming an heir. In the War of the Three Claimants that followed, Raghnall Ruadh, master of the vein-house, used the ore itself as a weapon (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE). Catrìona Bhuadhach won the crown and bound it, and the custodians with it, never to withhold the handful from a lawful hearth (12 an Gearran 526 DE).

The house of Catrìona ended with Eilidh Bhàn. The record calls her its fifth ruler, and the annals name four of the five. The houses, meeting at the vein-house, named Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill (23 am Màrt 807 DE). His house held the crown and the vein-house together for the rest of the age, through a brothers' war and some of the longest reigns in the list. The last crowning the annals record is Gormshuil nic Thormoid's (9 an Dùbhlachd 1727 DE). No annal records her death, an heir, or how the crown fell vacant. The next age finds the Council of Custodians sitting in its place (11 am Faoilleach 1781 DE).

V. The Age of Strangers: the Council, the Commissioners and the Maoir

The Council of Custodians gave the humans leave to stay, and its high custodian signed the first treaty in a tongue he could not read (7 an Cèitean 1787 DE). After that the council's power only shrank. It asked for its tally and was sent the Company's accounts. From 22 an t-Sultain 1884 DE it could not agree on a high custodian. The last Commissioner locked it out of its hall (26 an Gearran 1926 DE). What authority the custodians still had went with them into the forest council of the mining regions (20 an Lùnastal 1927 DE), which chose Eilidh nic Raghnaill to speak for it and fought the war that ended the age.

The Commissioners governed from the Residency at Ros dhomhain. Over the age the office and the Company drew together: Walter Crane went from chief agent at the pits to Commissioner, and a Company agent held the seal after his death. The last Commissioner sailed west, and nothing on Rodos records where he arrived (5 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE).

The overseers were the Company's rulers at the pithead, all of them Ròdaich (21 an Lùnastal 1816 DE). At Muileann chrom the staff went from father to son, against the custodians' hope, and the byname Maor went with it, until Mòrag nic Iain Maor broke the staff rather than carry out evictions (24 an Cèitean 1927 DE).

VI. The New Age: the Restored Kingdom

The kingdom was restored in order. The war-companies were stood down (3 an t-Ògmhios 1930 DE), the state was styled Rìoghachd Ròdais (27 an t-Iuchar 1931 DE), and a royal council of twelve, drawn from the custodian families and the captains of the war, took its seat (23 an t-Sultain 1931 DE). Only then was a king crowned. The Crown's officer in each shire took the word maor (4 am Faoilleach 1933 DE), and the house of the Dark Unicorn at Cathair dhearg was given back the keeping of the regalia (26 an Gearran 1936 DE).

The chronicle of the restored kingdom names five rulers and records their successions and nothing more, and this appendix follows it. The table above gives all that is recorded of them.

VII. Of the Seven Houses

The seven houses of custody were made from what the Sundering left. With nearly one household in five gone onto the roll of the willing, the remaining custodian households were regrouped into seven houses. Each house answered to the vein-house for its share of the ore and of the measured burning (4 an t-Iuchar 16 DE). The houses were:

HouseSeat or country, where the record gives oneHoly Age house of the same nameNotable in the record
Clann MhuirichDùn ìseal (as Sliochd Mhuirich)Sliochd Mhuirich, the Keepers' houseGave most of the Holy Age's Keepers; in this age the record names it rarely
Clann FhearchairBaile Mòr dhomhainSliochd Fhearchair, the silversmiths of Muileann chiarThe first king chosen by the houses; the double court
Clann ÌomhairDùn dheargSliochd Ìomhair, the first kings' houseWalled Dùn dhearg in stone, the first walls raised by a house rather than the crown (12 an t-Sultain 222 DE)
Clann Raghnaill—Sliochd Raghnaill of Seann TarrRaghnall Ruadh the claimant; from Dòmhnall Ruadh, the crown and the vein-house together
Clann Thormoid—Sliochd Thormoid of Seann DunnThe last kings of the Holy Age were of the house of Tormod; in this age it has no entry of its own
Clann Choinnich—noneRebuilt the bath-house at the hot springs; brought the silver petitions; swore last to Catrìona Bheag
Clann Lachlainn—noneNamed among the seven; the record keeps no deed of its own

The regrouping was the first act in the record to treat the right to the ore as inherited by house instead of earned by apprenticeship. Everything that followed came from it. The houses drew lots at the vein-house for the galleries each would keep (30 an Giblean 70 DE). Their heads wore silver neck-rings from Muileann chiar, and on feast days they wore the blue of Baile ghorm until that blue was lost. When blood failed they made kings, once at the capital (19 an Gearran 143 DE) and once at the vein-house (21 an Giblean 802 DE). They split among the three claimants, and later divided four to three between the brothers (8 an t-Ògmhios 1231 DE). From Dòmhnall Ruadh's reign the heads of the seven sat as the king's council (6 an t-Ògmhios 820 DE), and the custodian class and the court became one body.

The houses also forbade things. They forbade Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn's question at their own tables (1 an Giblean 285 DE), the first question in the record forbidden instead of an act. The king's council closed the house at Dùn thais for a generation after Raghnall mac Chaluim tabled the lengths of lives (29 an Giblean 1180 DE). His table found that the heads of the houses lived a few years longer than their tenants. Clann Choinnich twice asked leave to burn the ore beyond the measure for the silver smelt. The council refused the first petition (31 an Lùnastal 1520 DE) and the second by one voice (5 an Gearran 1737 DE). The house did not bring it again, and the petition lies in the vein-house unanswered (28 an Dùbhlachd 1767 DE). The census of hands shows the houses narrowing. At the last count of the age, three of the seven held more than half the right between them (27 an Gearran 1752 DE).

Two of the seven names have no house of the same name in the Holy Age record, and for the other five the record gives the name and not the descent. The Library notes that Clann Choinnich shares its name with Coinneach Bàn, grandfather of Mòr nic Coinnich, and Clann Lachlainn with Lachlann Bàn, father of the last queen of Goraidh Mòr's line. The record does not say that either house descends from either man, and the Library does not claim it. After the Sundering age the seven are not named again as a body. The custodian families go on sitting in the Council of Custodians in the Age of Strangers, and the royal council of twelve of the New Age is drawn partly from them (23 an t-Sultain 1931 DE).

VIII. Of the Vein-House and the Crown

Through every age the island's rulers had to answer one question: who keeps the vein, and who keeps everyone else. The answer changed four times.

In the Ancient Age the answer was separation. The keepers of the slab were chosen by lot, and the kings of the hills were refused a hand in the lot (4 an t-Iuchar 5189 BDE). In the Holy Age the separation became law. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal held the flame and the galleries, and the rìgh held the roads and the granaries. Neither could do the other's work (9 an t-Sultain 2305 BDE). The Hall lent its authority to the crown twice. The first time was the stone cup set in Gilleasbuig Mòr's hands, when the line of kings failed (12 am Màrt 483 BDE), and the second was the same act for Mòr nic Coinnich.

In the Age of Sundering the Hall's heir was the vein-house above Muileann dhearg (14 an Lùnastal 37 BDE), and the separation failed. The first break was Raghnall Ruadh's. He was master of the vein-house and a claimant to the crown, and he used the ore as a weapon (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE). Catrìona Bhuadhach's ruling of the hearth was written to bind the custodians themselves. The second break came when the houses crowned the next master of the vein-house, and his reeves wrote into the custody-book that the ruler of Rodos is also master of the vein-house (6 an t-Ògmhios 820 DE). Dòmhnall Ruadh was buried at Muileann dhearg, by the vein-house. His successors took the ore-roads into the crown's keeping (12 an t-Samhain 900 DE). For nine centuries Rodos had one ruler over both the vein and the realm. Under that ruler the Small-Burning Law was never changed. Every petition to change it was refused or left unanswered.

In the Age of Strangers there was neither crown nor vein-house to hold the vein. The Council of Custodians sat in the crown's place and kept the vein in name only. The Law lapsed without repeal once enforcing it stopped paying (2 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE). The Company's overseers, not the custodians, ruled the pitheads.

The restored kingdom kept the separation in form and gave up its substance. The Crown granted the Sloc Mòr to a single house on the humans' terms with the names changed (23 an Cèitean 1940 DE), and in time bought every shaft back and worked the vein through its Board "in the Crown's name alone" (30 an t-Iuchar 1989 DE). The keeping of the rite passed to a high custodian of Creideamh nan Ròdach at Seann Skell (30 an Giblean 1935 DE). When that high custodian protested that the plain coinage seal showed the kingdom no longer held the vein sacred, the council answered that the kingdom had never said it did (31 an t-Iuchar 2014 DE). The last face of the Sloc Mòr is kept open under the custody of the Rite, to cut ore for the altars (17 an Cèitean 2025 DE). In the present year it filled four baskets, and the high custodian divided them among the houses of the Rite by lot (29 an t-Iuchar 2026 DE). This is the same method the keepers of the slab used to choose their keeper.

Appendix B — The Faiths of Rodos

This appendix sets down what the record holds about the faiths of Rodos: the nine the map names, the older reverence they grew out of, and the two matters every one of them has had to answer, the holiness of the vein and the question of why it answers some hands and not others. It draws on the annals, the Keepers' roll of Dùn ìseal, the custody-book of the vein-house, the registers that the schools and houses sent to Leabharlann Muileann chaol, and the map. Where a faith kept its own counsel, and several did, this appendix says so and leaves the gap open.

Each faith is entered under the Ròdais name the map gives it, with its god as the map gives the god. Where the record shows when a name first appears, that is noted. Where it does not, nothing more is claimed.

I. The Faiths in Brief

The map counts 505 burgs and sets each under one faith. The seat is the house the record treats as first among a faith's houses in the present age.

FaithIn the common tongueKind (as the map has it)GodBurgsSeat
Seann Spioradan nan Ròdachthe Old Spiritsfolk; shamanicCrom, an t-Àrd-Spiorad, the High Spirit126Dùn ìseal
Creideamh nan Ròdachthe Obsidian Riteorganised; pantheistDòrsair, Uilebheist nan Geataichean, the Monster of the Gates9Seann Skell (south coast)
Creideamh an t-Seabhaigthe Faith of the Hawkorganised; dualistMòd, an Seabhag Acrach, the Hungry Hawk14Cnoc bheag
Feallsanachd an Fhèidhthe Philosophy of the Deerorganised; philosophicalCamaran, am Fiadh Rìoghail, the Royal Stag133Dùn thais
Creideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibhthe Faith of the Dark Unicornorganised; dualistUallach, an t-Aon-adharcach Dubh, the Dark Unicorn103Cathair dhearg
