The day of the Setting-Out has never been kept as a feast. The chronicles stop describing the departed the moment the ships clear the harbour, and the island has kept its remembrance of them at the harbour, where the rolls stop, on the day the custody-book gives for the turn and not on the day they sailed. Since 23 am Màrt 700 DE the empty-harbour rite has fallen on that day, 25 an t-Samhain, though the harbour scribe, whose count the island follows, sets the turn on the day of the sailing. The Library is aware that the custody-book may have taken its day from the rite rather than the rite from the book. By the last entry of the Age of Sundering the rite was kept by eleven people (17 an t-Sultain 1764 DE). The chronicles of the later ages do not say how many keep it now.

The Severance, 1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE, is kept at Cathair dhearg by the council as the day the kingdom's modern history begins. The chronicle says the Mourning Custom of the Sundering, first made for a chosen parting, was reused uneasily for a very different departure in a later age, and the council's keeping of this day is the use most often meant. In the north the day is not kept. It is worked through like any other, and the Tuathaich say that this is their way of keeping it.

The Long War left two days. The Battle of Àth leathan, 11 an Giblean 2020 DE, opened An Cogadh Fada. Tuathaich families have raised a cairn without leave on the field at Àraich Àth leathan, and it grows by a stone or two whenever the patrols pass; whether they come on the day of the battle nobody has written down. The Battle of Muileann ghlas, 10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE, ended the war, and the regiments raised in the campaign keep that day at their stations. So the two days are kept by two peoples, and the library, whose war archive is sealed (27 an Giblean 2023 DE), holds what it can of both.

VIII. The Reckoning of the Humans, and Its Reconciling

The humans who came at the Crossing (5 am Faoilleach 1780 DE) brought a calendar of their own, and in most respects it was close to the island's. Their year had twelve months of the same lengths in the same order, with the same extra day in the second month every fourth year. Samuel Wren's word-lists (13 an Dùbhlachd 1781 DE), which survive in the Administration's letter-books, give the month-names in the two tongues side by side, and the clerks needed nothing more than that list to convert months. The chronicle notes that the humans crossed "the water the Rodians once crossed." Whether the likeness between the calendars has anything to do with that, nobody on Rodos knows, and the chronicles do not say.

The calendars differed in two things. The first was the beginning of the year. The humans began theirs at am Faoilleach, and the Ròdaich had begun theirs at Samhain since the Hall first filled the baskets. The second was the count of years. The humans numbered theirs from an epoch in their own land, which they named and did not explain, and their numbers were much larger than the island's. No Ròdaich scribe set down the name of that land (26 an Gearran 1781 DE), and the letter-books do not explain the epoch either.

The first written treaty (27 an Giblean 1787 DE) was drawn up in the humans' tongue only and dated by the humans' year only. The custodians entered it in their roll under its Diosal year and the month in which it was signed, and left the day to the Administration. The Harbour Articles, the Company's charter, and every contract for extraction were dated the same way. The same clerks who kept two sets of books for coin and barter (30 am Faoilleach 1797 DE) came to keep two dates at the head of every page, the humans' year above and the Diosal year beneath, and they complained about both.

By the third currency reform (7 an Giblean 1908 DE) every contract on the island ran from am Faoilleach, and the Ròdaich civil year had moved to the humans' beginning without any decree. The old Samhain year survived in the shrines, in the Hall's count of burnings until it lapsed, and among the custodians of Inis bhàn, who taught "the old reckoning" in their school (7 an t-Ògmhios 1831 DE). The Administration's census (19 an Cèitean 1901 DE) and its register (26 an t-Samhain 1906 DE) were dated by the humans' year alone.

The reconciling was finished after the Severance, when the humans no longer had any say in it. The council's clerks emptied the counting-houses (11 an t-Ògmhios 1931 DE) and boxed the ledgers unread, because few of them could read the humans' hand. Ailean Leabhar, the library's first keeper, spent his first years having them read (28 an t-Ògmhios 1945 DE). He had every date in them converted to the Diosal count, using the double-dated pages of the custodians' clerks as the key, and he kept the new year at am Faoilleach. His reason was that a century of contracts, ledgers and letters already stood on that footing. The kingdom has kept it since. Every year on Rodos, in every age, is therefore now counted from am Faoilleach to an Dùbhlachd. The people who lived before 1780 began their years at Samhain, and a reader of the old rolls should remember that.

The Tuathaich keep the Diosal count in their dealings with the kingdom. What count the northern parish books keep among themselves the library cannot say, since it receives few of them.

IX. The Five Ages

The five ages are the divisions of Clàr nan Aoisean as the library received and extended it. The table gives the first and the last thing remembered in each.

AgeRòdais nameEnglishSpanFirst eventLast event
IAn Aois Àrsaidhthe Ancient Age12,999 – 3,001 BDEThe crack in the stone, 20 am Faoilleach 12,918 BDEThe eve of the Binding, 7 an Lùnastal 3051 BDE
IIAn Aois Naomhthe Holy Age3,000 – 40 BDEThe Binding of the First Flame, 23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDEThe last age of even population, 1 an Cèitean 50 BDE
IIIAn Aois Scaraidhthe Age of Sundering39 BDE – 1779 DELand is found, 6 am Faoilleach 39 BDEThe silver petition laid aside, 28 an Dùbhlachd 1767 DE
IVAn Aois Choigreachthe Age of Strangers1780 – 1929 DEThe Crossing, 5 am Faoilleach 1780 DEThe Severance, 1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE
VAn Aois Ùrthe New Age1930 – 2026 DEThe Tuathaich homeland fixed, 22 am Màrt 1930 DEThe present, 21 an Dùbhlachd 2026 DE

Three things in the table need a word.

The span of the Ancient Age opens in 12,999 BDE, but its first event, the crack in the stone, falls some decades later. The span is the table's round beginning for an age that has none. The event is the oldest thing the island remembers.

The Age of Sundering is usually said to open with the Choosing, but the Choosing (8 an Dùbhlachd 39 BDE) is not the first thing in it. The age opens with the finding of the land (6 am Faoilleach 39 BDE), without which there would have been nothing to choose.

The Severance closes the Age of Strangers but falls in 1930, the first year of the New Age. The first events of the New Age follow it within that same year. The copyists of the cellar drew the boundary at the end of 1929, when the war had been decided and the columns had gone north, and they entered the Severance as the last act of the age it ended. The library has left the overlap as it found it.

X. Where the Dates Come From

Every event in this history carries a day, a month and a year, and they come from different places in different ages.

For the New Age and the Age of Strangers the days are remembered: they come from rolls, ledgers, letter-books and the chroniclers' own entries. For the Age of Sundering they are remembered more thinly, from the custody-book, the harbour rolls and the crown's king-list, and a good many were settled by agreement, as the day of the empty-harbour rite was. For the Holy Age the years come from the Keepers' roll, the king-lists and the Hall's count of burnings, which do not always agree, and the days mostly from the feasts and seasons the rolls name. For the Ancient Age everything rests on the tellings, the king-lists without lengths of reign, the tally walls and the tide-count. The tellings keep the order of things well and the distance between them poorly. Where they agree, the date is as sure as they are; where they disagree or fall silent, it is not, and such a date is safer for the order it keeps than for its year.

Appendix E — Words Born from History

This appendix gathers the words, names and sayings of Ròdais that the island's history made, or bent to a new sense. It is set out as a historical dictionary. Each entry gives the headword and its part of speech, what it says word for word, what it has come to mean, the event that gave it that meaning, and a line from the annals or the five books.

The chronicle's own list of Words Born from History is the core, and every word on it appears here with the meaning the chronicle gives it. The rest come from the annals and the books: titles and offices, laws and customs, the names of storms, places and quarrels, and the sayings the record quotes. A few are the words Ròdais built for the strangers' things. Ròdais took few loanwords from the humans, and most of those late (Appendix F); where the humans said train, engine or strike, it made a name from old roots, and some of those names are entered here under the years when the annals first needed them.

How to Read an Entry

The headword is given in full. An article (an, am, a') is written with it but not counted in the order, which is the Gaelic order of eighteen letters, a b c d e f g h i l m n o p r s t u, with the grave accent ignored. Dates are given in the Diosal count (Appendix D). Where no annal marks the first use of a word, the entry says so and gives only the event the word comes from. Citations are given as the sources give them: the annals in English, as this history renders their prose, the verses in Ròdais (Appendix F, Of Translation).

n. noun · m., f. masculine, feminine · pl. plural · v. verb · v.n. verbal noun · adj. adjective · phr. phrase or saying · lit. literally

The Glossary

A

a chur san Leabharlann phr. · lit. "to put it in the Library" To make a thing official and past dispute. From the founding of Leabharlann Muileann chaol (1 an Cèitean 1945 DE); within a few years it was said of anything settled (3 an t-Samhain 1945 DE).

"Ailean Leabhar is recorded as disliking the phrase, on the ground that the library settles nothing and only keeps it." — annals, 1945 DE

Aisling-aois n. f. · lit. "Aisling-age" An unnaturally long youth in anyone; said half in jest of ordinary people who look young for their years. From the first of the immortal generation, born in the mining camps (7 am Màrt 1848 DE). No annal marks its first use. It is the one word on the chronicle's list in which the joke and the myth are the same word.

"…and does not age the way the people around her do. Her name is Aisling." — annals, 1848 DE

Àrd-choimheadaiche n. m. · lit. "high watcher" The high custodian of Creideamh nan Ròdach, seated at Seann Skell. The office came with the formalizing of the Rite (18 an Giblean 1935 DE), and Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was the first to hold it (30 an Giblean 1935 DE). It is not the "high custodian" of the Age of Strangers, who headed the Council of Custodians; the two share an English name and nothing else.

"The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell writes to every house of the Rite that the new fuel is not forbidden, since it is not ore, and not blessed, since it is not ore." — annals, 2003 DE

B

bonn-rìoghachd n. m. · lit. "realm-coin" Currency. Under the humans the coin was the mark, and barter was pushed out in three reforms (13 an Gearran 1796 DE, 2 an Dàmhair 1865 DE, 7 an Giblean 1908 DE). The Ròdais word belongs to the coinage struck when the humans' coin was withdrawn (30 an Giblean 1934 DE). Its first mint-master was called Fearchar Bonn from his work (9 an Dàmhair 1934 DE). After the re-pegging to dubhan (5 an Cèitean 2014 DE) the realm-coin no longer rested on the vein.

"A new Rìoghachd coinage, minted with obsidian-dust ink in its seal, replaces it within a year." — annals, 1934 DE

C

carbad-iarainn n. m. · lit. "iron-chariot" A train; the first of the iarainn words Ròdais made for machines. The kingdom mended the humans' ore line (9 an Dàmhair 1937 DE) and ran its own first train on 3 an Dàmhair 1941 DE.

"The first ore train from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg runs under the kingdom's name and on the humans' rails." — annals, 1941 DE

Cha do chaill sinn blàr, ach chaill sinn an teine phr. · lit. "we did not lose a battle, but we lost the fire" A defeat without fighting. An unsigned verse of the cold shires, from the day Raghnall Ruadh refused the measured handful to every hearth that stood against him (24 am Faoilleach 519 DE).

"…the act turns more people against him than any battle." — annals, 519 DE

Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann phr. · lit. "we did not come; we were here" The doctrine of the Ancient Age, complete on Calbh Cnoc ghorm (6 an t-Samhain 8054 BDE). Who cut it is not known.

"If the doctrine has a birthplace, it may be here." — annals, 8054 BDE

Cha loisc clach na beinne do choigrich phr. · lit. "the mountain's stone will not burn for strangers" The Keepers' ruling that no ore might feed a beacon (30 an Cèitean 2851 BDE). It held until the humans' towers were lit with an ore flame (22 an t-Sultain 1870 DE).

"The Keepers rule that no ore may feed a beacon, since a beacon burns for strangers." — annals, 2851 BDE

Cha tàinig long phr. · lit. "no ship came" The entry in the beacon-keepers' daybooks from the Severance on, after the council had the five beacons relit (19 an Dùbhlachd 1929 DE).

"The keepers' daybooks, which had counted human ships since the ring was finished, continue to be kept, with nothing in them." — annals, 1929 DE

Chaidh a' mhèinn dhachaigh phr. · lit. "the ore went home" The tellings' words for the ore taken by Gilleasbuig Beag (2 an Lùnastal 5192 BDE), which was neither burned nor kept but laid back under the slab (4 an t-Iuchar 5191 BDE).

"The tellings make much of this: the ore went home." — annals, 5191 BDE

Cidhe an Diosail n. m. · lit. "the quay of the sunwise turn" The berth at Seann Skell from which the fleet of the Sundering sailed. Its old name, Cidhe an Iar, passed to a new fish-wharf so that trade could go on without the memory (13 am Màrt 28 DE, 15 an Lùnastal 28 DE).

"In the harbour rolls of Seann Skell the departure berth is entered as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn." — annals, 28 DE

Cogadh nam Bràithrean n. m. · lit. "the war of the brothers" The war between Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, named from its first battle (8 an t-Ògmhios 1231 DE).

"The houses divide, four to three, and Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, is named from this battle." — annals, 1231 DE

Comann nan Saor-luinge n. m. · lit. "the fellowship of the ship-wrights" The guild that built the fleet of the Sundering (24 an t-Sultain 35 BDE). It quietly dissolved when no one needed ocean-going hulls (27 an t-Ògmhios 45 DE).

"The custody-book calls it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights." — annals, 35 BDE

Còmhrag n. f. · lit. "combat" With the article, the yearly melee at Ceann leathan (4 am Màrt 1952 DE), fought on the field of the Holy Age road-guards' games (18 an t-Ògmhios 1325 BDE).

"Two men die in the melee he wins." — annals, of the first champion, 1952 DE

cridhe-iarainn n. m. · lit. "iron-heart" An engine. The annals first need it for the shunting engines at Muileann chrom (8 an t-Iuchar 1942 DE), and again when the Shipwrights' Guild court ruled that fitting one to a boat was not shipwrighting (23 an Giblean 2005 DE).

"The yard's families, who work the small engines that move the wagons, are counted separately by the Board." — annals, 1942 DE

cuimhne-coinneimh n. f. · lit. "meeting-memory" Minutes. Above all, those of the Moot at Caol mhòr, which has no standing in Ròdach law and has kept its minutes since its first sitting (25 an Lùnastal 1931 DE). See Tha e scrìobhte a-nis.

"It meets anyway and keeps its own minutes, which run unbroken from this meeting to the present." — annals, 1931 DE

D

diosal adv., n. m. · lit. "sunwise" The sunwise turn; the Rodos form of deiseal. The fleet went once round the harbour of Seann Skell sunwise (19 an Giblean 1 DE), and the years were counted from that turn (22 am Faoilleach 5 DE).

"Before making for open water the fleet went once round the harbour of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck." — the Third Book

dòrlach n. m. · lit. "a handful" The sealed measure of ore. The vein-house allowed one to each departing ship (17 an t-Ògmhios 15 BDE). See Làn na glaice.

Dòrlach airson an teallaich ùir, / is an seann teallach fhathast blàth. "A handful for the new hearth, and the old hearth still warm." — the Third Book

Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan phr. · lit. "black the coal, and black the dubhan" A rhyme of the north, heard in both tongues, from the years when the coinage was pegged to the new fuel (5 an Cèitean 2014 DE).

Dubh an gual, 's dubh an dubhan, / ach cò leis an teine? "Black the coal, and black the dubhan; but whose is the fire?" — the Fifth Book

dubhan n. m. · lit. "the black one" (dubh + -an) The synthetic fuel, written with a small letter. From the name of Dubhan, born 1958 DE, whose first working fuel came on 19 an t-Ògmhios 2000 DE. The man's name wore down into a common noun, as a title may wear down into the name of a dish.

"'Dubhan' begins appearing in common speech to mean the fuel itself, not the man." — annals, 2010 DE

dubhan-tùsail n. m. · lit. "dubhan of the beginning" A rough first attempt that looked like a dead end and later mattered; used in any field. From Dubhan's failed experiments (1 an t-Iuchar 1990 DE). First recorded in a letter of the Fèidh school at Caol shean, of the school's own revival (22 an Dàmhair 2010 DE).

"…for an early attempt at anything that looked like a dead end before it wasn't." — annals, 2010 DE

F

fadachadh v.n. m. · lit. "lengthening", from fadaich, fada To be crushed after holding out too long; am fadachadh, a total and final defeat. Narrowed by An Cogadh Fada, from Àth leathan (11 an Giblean 2020 DE) to Muileann ghlas (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE), and first heard among Tuathaich speakers of their own defeat (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE).

"…'chaidh am fadachadh', they got long-warred… It is said as a joke, and the people who say it do not laugh." — annals, 2021 DE

faire-obrach n. f. · lit. "work-watch" A shift. The annals first need it for the humans' night-shift order (25 an Lùnastal 1895 DE), which the kingdom kept (18 an t-Samhain 1940 DE).

Cha d' fhuair a' bheinn fois a-riamh, / is cha d' fhuair sinne. "The mountain never got its rest, and neither did we." — the hewers' saying, the Fifth Book

Fèill n. f. · lit. "feast-day, fair" With a town's name, a fair; above all Fèill Muileann òg (16 an Dàmhair 1950 DE), heir to the harvest fair held there after the War of the Roads (5 an t-Iuchar 1325 BDE).

"An annual fair becomes the island's largest recurring gathering." — annals, 1950 DE

Fo mhullach an taighe, chan eil nàmh ann phr. · lit. "under the roof of the house there is no enemy" The road-peace, the oldest law on the island that no Keeper made (22 an Dàmhair 2824 BDE). The War of the Roads ended under such a roof (4 an Dàmhair 1993 BDE).

"…no feud may be pursued under an inn roof or within a spear's throw of its door." — annals, 2824 BDE

fuil-ghuail n. f. · lit. "coal-blood" The condition of those who bond with the vein and do not age as others do, and the people who have it. It had no word for half a century (13 am Faoilleach 1850 DE) until the custodians coined this one (23 am Faoilleach 1905 DE). The humans rendered it obsidian-touched.

"It is meant clinically. It will outlive that intention." — annals, 1905 DE

G

Gaoth Dhubh, A' n. f. · lit. "the black wind" The oldest storm whose name is kept (1 an Gearran 5184 BDE); the first named storm lost its name (30 am Faoilleach 7454 BDE). The harbour rolls went on naming storms: Am Fuath Mòr, "the great hate" (23 an t-Samhain 220 DE), and An Gàire Dubh, "the black laugh" (5 am Màrt 480 DE).

"It is the oldest storm whose name is kept." — annals, 5184 BDE

I

Ithidh Mòd an neach a dh'itheas an cnoc phr. · lit. "Mòd will eat whoever eats the hill" The saying of the feathered doors, from the years when the hawk-priests were barred and the crews carried the Hawk's sermons themselves (10 an Cèitean 1855 DE).

"The overseers' reports of these years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a disciplinary matter." — annals, 1855 DE

L

Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig n. m. · lit. "the law of the small burning" The Small-Burning Law: no household might burn more than a measured handful of ore in a season (13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE). The ruling of the hearth bound the custodians never to withhold that handful (12 an Gearran 526 DE). The Law was never repealed; it lapsed (2 an Dùbhlachd 1800 DE).

"No formal repeal is recorded — it simply stops being enforced once it stops being profitable to enforce." — annals, 1800 DE

Làn na glaice, 's gun tuilleadh phr. · lit. "the fill of the hollow hand, and no more" The measure of the Ancient Age (5 an Lùnastal 6590 BDE). When Fionnlagh Dall re-cut the stone cup to hold two palms (15 an t-Iuchar 2860 BDE), the saying became Làn an dà bhois, agus gun tuilleadh.

"It is nowhere written and everywhere kept." — annals, 6590 BDE

Loisc iad an leabhar, ach cha do loisc iad an cnoc phr. · lit. "they burned the book, but they did not burn the hill" Said of the raids on the tithe ledgers (10 an t-Ògmhios 1929 DE).

"…symbolically decisive even though its practical effect was small." — annals, 1929 DE

M

maor n. m., pl. maoir · lit. "steward" Under the humans, an overseer: a Ròdach set over Ròdaich for the Company. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill took his byname from the office (19 an Cèitean 1815 DE, 17 an t-Ògmhios 1815 DE). The kingdom gave the word to the Crown's officer in each shire (4 am Faoilleach 1933 DE). The kenning maor-obrach, "work-steward", is a manager.

"…from this office the Ròdaich give him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward." — annals, 1815 DE

mar a thàinig Niall phr. · lit. "the way Niall came" Any unusually smooth transfer of power. From Niall's crowning (7 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE), which passed without dispute (15 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE).

"Its first written use is in a Cathair dhearg tavern ledger, set against a debt settled without argument." — annals, 1932 DE

Marbh-bheò n. m. · lit. "dead-alive" The Hollow Man of the Doire uaine hills, which attacked anyone who lit a fire in its sight (9 an Giblean 9654 BDE). The rule against open fires after dark came from it (26 an t-Ògmhios 5141 BDE), and shepherds still named it when they left the high pastures (17 an Lùnastal 910 DE).

Na las teine far am faic e thu. "Light no fire where it can see you." — the First Book

R

rìgh n. m. · lit. "king" A ruler of the lowlands, as against the Keeper of the flame. Goraidh mac Ìomhair was the first so called (28 an Cèitean 2325 BDE); under the division of keeping the rìgh had the roads and the granaries, the Keeper the flame (9 an t-Sultain 2305 BDE).

"He is the first person in any record so called." — annals, 2325 BDE

Rìghrean na Cloiche n. pl. · lit. "the kings of the stone" The oldest oral king-list, opening with Ailean Mòr (9 an Lùnastal 7600 BDE). The name was given to it later.

"The list gives no lengths of reign. It is older than the name Ròdaich." — annals, 7600 BDE

roghnaich v. · lit. "choose" With no object: to have chosen the crossing, to choose exile for good. From the Choosing (8 an Dùbhlachd 39 BDE); the narrow sense is in the custody-book from 21 an Lùnastal 28 DE. The plain sense was never lost.

Roghnaich iadsan, agus dh'fhuirich sinne. "They chose, and we stayed." — the Third Book

S

scàinte adj. · lit. "rent, split" Reeling, shaken, of a person as well as a building. From Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending (9 an t-Ògmhios 1916 DE). No annal marks its first use.

"…killing dozens and closing an entire mining district for a generation." — annals, 1916 DE

Scaradh, a' n. m. · lit. "the parting" The Sundering (19 an Giblean 1 DE); loosely, any permanent, chosen parting between people who belonged together. It was later applied to the Severance (1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE), which was not chosen, so one word serves two wounds.

"The island's chronicles simply stop describing them the moment the ships clear the harbor." — annals, 1 DE

seann-chunntas n. m. · lit. "old account" A grievance nobody in power acts on and nobody cancels. Tuathaich speakers coined it (18 an Giblean 2025 DE) for the tabled archive request (15 an Gearran 2016 DE) and the reparations motion left to die (18 an t-Ògmhios 2024 DE).

"Official Ròdaich usage does not take the word up." — annals, 2025 DE

Seann-Dhaoine n. pl. · lit. "old people" The Old Ones, the people before the Ròdaich. The name is a Ròdais description, and no annal dates it. Their first sure trace is the midden at Seann Dunn (28 an Lùnastal 12,187 BDE).

"The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, the people who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin…" — annals, 7253 BDE

siorrachd n. f., pl. siorrachdan · lit. "shire" Named in the annals from the Age of Sundering (9 an t-Samhain 31 BDE). The kingdom redrew the shires on the humans' district lines (23 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE).

"…the kingdom uses them and does not say so." — annals, 1932 DE

sliochd n. m. · lit. "seed, offspring" A house of custody known by a founder's name, not a hearth. Sliochd Mhuirich was the first (11 an t-Sultain 2903 BDE); four were bound to the Keepers' office (29 an Giblean 2607 BDE).

"…the first custodian house in the record known by a name rather than by a hearth." — annals, 2903 BDE

stad-oibre n. m. · lit. "work-halt" A strike. The first lasted eleven days (13 an Dàmhair 1856 DE); the first held in several regions on one day came in 1922 DE.

"It ends when food supplies, controlled by human administrators, run out." — annals, 1856 DE

T

Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic phr. · lit. "the ship is eating the hill" Fearchar Bàrd's most quoted song, made when the Company's steamships began to burn the island's ore to carry it away (15 an Gearran 1882 DE).

Tha an long ag ithe a' chnuic / gus an cnoc a ghiùlan air falbh. "The ship is eating the hill to carry the hill away." — the Fourth Book

Tha e scrìobhte a-nis phr. · lit. "it is written now" The Moot's whole minute on the day the census figures were read at Caol mhòr (6 an t-Samhain 1993 DE). The Fifth Book takes it for its epigraph.

"The Moot's minute says only: 'Now written.'" — annals, 1993 DE

Tìr Thall, an n. f. · lit. "the land beyond" The humans' homeland, whose own name no Ròdach scribe set down (26 an Gearran 1781 DE).

"From the first season the record calls it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and calls its people simply the humans." — annals, 1781 DE

tonn n. m. · lit. "wave" A sudden, overwhelming change: tha e san tonn, "he is in the wave of it". From Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol (2 an Gearran 1933 DE), by way of the survivors' accounts (4 am Faoilleach 1934 DE).

"Within a generation the sense is heard across the south." — annals, 1934 DE

Tràigh Bhàthte, an n. f. · lit. "the drowned strand" The old site of Cnoc chaol, left as the Great Wave left it (23 an Dùbhlachd 1933 DE).

"The townspeople call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there." — annals, 1933 DE

Tùrsa Geal, an n. m. · lit. "the white sorrow" The mourning for the departed, "not quite grief and not quite celebration" (1 an Lùnastal 15 DE), first kept at court by Queen Beathag for her sister (27 an Dàmhair 15 DE). The chronicle says it was reused, uneasily, for a very different departure in a much later age.

"…with one place set empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast." — annals, 15 DE

U

uaine adj. · lit. "green" Beside its plain sense, sickly, plague-marked. From A' Phlàigh Uaine (9 an t-Ògmhios 1852 DE), first seen as a greenish pallor at Achadh dhomhain (5 an Dùbhlachd 1852 DE).

"…in a field outside the spoil-heaps that is still called the green acre." — annals, 1852 DE

Of What the Record Does Not Hold

The record can prove fewer first uses than a reader might want. Scàinte, Aisling-aois and the loose sense of a' Scaradh stand on the chronicle's list, but no annal marks the day any of them was first said. The rope-makers of Cuan shean sing a keel-song whose words have lost their sense (11 an Gearran 1340 DE). The Tuathaich's own memory of the Long War is filed as folklore, and the northern towns' own accounts are among the things the royal record says it does not hold (25 an Giblean 1972 DE). Where a word's history is missing, this appendix leaves the gap as it is.

Appendix F — The Tongues and Peoples of Rodos

This appendix gathers what the rolls and chronicles hold about the peoples who have lived on Rodos and the speech they used. It draws on the royal chronicles, the rolls and custody-books copied into Leabharlann Muileann chaol, the map of the kingdom, and the word-lists that survive from the Age of Strangers. Where the sources are silent this appendix says so, and it does not fill the silence.

I. The Peoples

Five peoples, or kinds of people, stand in the island's history. Two of them are gone. One of them, the fuil-ghuail, is not a people at all in the ordinary sense, but the chronicles have come to treat it as one, and so it is set down here with the rest.

PeopleRòdais nameIn the chroniclesOn the map today
The Old Onesna Seann-DhaoineAge I; their works end before the Holy Ageno burg; thirty burgs and thirteen shires bear their names
The people of Rodosna Ròdaich (sg. Ròdach)every age441 of 505 burgs; the capital and the sea
The humansthe chronicles' plain name for themAge IVnone by that name; their descendants are the Tuathaich
The northernersna Tuathaich (sg. Tuathach)Age V64 burgs in the north and north-west
The coal-bloodedan fhuil-ghuail; in the humans' tongue, obsidian-touchedfrom Age IVnot counted on the map; counted, briefly, in the censuses

The Seann-Dhaoine

The Ròdaich call the people before them na Seann-Dhaoine, the Old Ones. The name is a Ròdais description, not the Old Ones' own; what they called themselves is not known and cannot now be known.

What survives of them is stone, shell and names. The oldest sure trace is the midden at Seann Dunn (28 an Lùnastal 12,187 BDE): limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes, with no tool in it shaped the way any later Ròdach shaped tools. After it come the notched net-weights of Seann Chwen, every stone cut with the same three strokes (26 an t-Sultain 12,106 BDE); the unmortared mole at Seann Skell on which every later harbour wall there stands (1 an t-Iuchar 12,024 BDE); the two hundred and twelve steps of Seann Bhral (30 an t-Iuchar 11,943 BDE); the stone boxes on Eilean dhearg to which the dead of Seann Vell were rowed (4 an Cèitean 11,854 BDE); the fish-channel of Seann Toll (2 an t-Ògmhios 11,781 BDE); the shell causeway of Seann Warr, the first made road on the island that can still be walked (7 am Màrt 11,700 BDE); the fish-kilns of Seann Mhorn (17 an Giblean 11,537 BDE); and the slipways of Seann Bhrenn, wide enough for hulls bigger than any hide boat, whose hulls are gone with any telling of where they went (16 an Cèitean 11,454 BDE).

At their widest reach (8 an Cèitean 9029 BDE) they held every coast of the island: the ten places whose names begin with Seann, and the islands off them. Their largest harbour was at the place now called Seann Skell.

The ruins inland are theirs by the oldest tellings. The telling of the counting of the dead (29 an Lùnastal 7253 BDE) names the Seann-Dhaoine as "the people who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin". Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, the walled outpost on the spur above the ground where Cathair mhòr now stands, has its single gate facing inland and not to the sea (19 an Cèitean 10,400 BDE); Làrach an Dùin, near Ceann mhin, had three rings of wall and room inside for some four hundred people with their beasts (17 an t-Ògmhios 10,343 BDE); and Làrach an Teampaill, in the eastern hills, has its altar set square to the central mountains (14 an Lùnastal 10,229 BDE), "toward the vein, not the horizon". All three were already ruined when the first reliable chronicles begin (27 an t-Samhain 8854 BDE, 6 am Màrt 8743 BDE, 7 am Faoilleach 8629 BDE). Whether the builders of the outpost built the fortress too has never been settled. After the high places were left, every new work of the Seann-Dhaoine lies within sight of salt water (9 an Dùbhlachd 8573 BDE).

The standing stones are harder. Carragh Cnoc bheag, Colbh Cnoc chiar and Calbh Cnoc ghorm were raised in the Ancient Age (17 an t-Iuchar 8286 BDE, 9 an t-Sultain 8173 BDE, 6 an t-Samhain 8054 BDE), and no telling says by whom. The upper face of Carragh Cnoc bheag bears a line of the unread script; the four Ròdais words, Bha teine sa chloich, "there was fire in the stone", lie lower down, cut with a narrower tool by another hand, and "when that second hand came, the stone does not say" (11 an Lùnastal 8229 BDE). The stones are therefore the one place where the marks of two peoples lie on the same face. The wind-stone at the central Seann Chwen is another: a Ròdais wind-name cut over an older mark of the Seann-Dhaoine (13 an Gearran 5154 BDE).

Their counting. Late in their time the Seann-Dhaoine began cutting single strokes on flat stones at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household (31 an t-Iuchar 7293 BDE). At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones were built into a wall of some three thousand strokes (3 an t-Ògmhios 7212 BDE); at Seann Tarr in the north-east they were cut in fives and set in the floor of a house (2 an t-Iuchar 7173 BDE). At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone was left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and abandoned (5 an Cèitean 7091 BDE).

Their end. After the half-cut stone no new work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is not cut again (7 an Gearran 7050 BDE). How they ended no telling knows, and this appendix will not guess. Nothing in the chronicles says they were driven out, and nothing says they were not; nothing says they died, and nothing says their blood did not run on in some later people. The reader who wants an answer will not find one here.

The hill-folk. Alongside, or after, the Seann-Dhaoine the tellings set a second people: the hill-folk of the high valleys around the crack (10 an t-Samhain 8514 BDE), who buried their dead in the ground and not on islands, and cut no script. They burned the ore, though sparingly: one sliver, one fire, at Àth gharbh (12 an Dàmhair 8454 BDE). Whether they shared the island with the Old Ones or came after them no telling knows. Their own answer, given later, is that they were always there, and it is the answer the Ròdaich give of themselves in the doctrine carried on Calbh Cnoc ghorm: Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann, "we did not come; we were here." When stag-scholars came to Calbh Cnoc ghorm in the Holy Age and could not read it, the people of Cnoc ghorm told them what it said, and "the scholars write that the people say so" (6 an Dàmhair 623 BDE).

The Ròdaich

The Ròdaich are the people of Rodos: the majority in every age of the island's history, the holders of the capital, Cathair dhearg (Cathair dhearg), and of the sea. Their name is the island's name with the people-ending -aich; a single person is a Ròdach. English writers of the humans' time used Rodian, and this history keeps that word as the English adjective.

Custodians. The Ròdaich enter history as custodians. In the Ancient Age a custom set in across the hill settlements that no fire should take more of the ore than one cupped hand could hold. The Binding of the First Flame (23 an t-Sultain 2998 BDE) made the custodianship of the vein a formal order, "centuries before anything like a king", and the Small-Burning Law (13 an Lùnastal 2857 BDE) made the custom into rule. The first person in any record to be called rìgh was Goraidh mac Ìomhair at Dùn dhearg (28 an Cèitean 2325 BDE), and he claimed nothing over the vein. For the whole of the Holy Age the kings ruled the grazing and the gatherings, and the Keepers at Dùn ìseal ruled the mountain. The Holy Age closes on the last age of even population (1 an Cèitean 50 BDE), the last stretch of Rodian history, the chroniclers note with some unease, in which no family held more years of life than any other.

The kingdom. After the Severance the state restyled itself Rìoghachd Ròdais, the Kingdom of Rodos (27 an t-Iuchar 1931 DE), and Niall was crowned at Cathair dhearg (7 an Dùbhlachd 1932 DE). The rulers since are set down elsewhere in these appendices. Here it is enough to say that the kingdom is a Ròdach kingdom: its schools teach in Ròdais "and it has no others" (2 an Gearran 1936 DE), and the old apprentice-binding custom, when it was revived, was reserved for Ròdaich applicants only (21 an t-Sultain 1942 DE).

The sea. The Ròdaich have always been a coastal people as well as a mountain one. The largest towns on the map today are harbours, and the two largest carry a name older than Ròdais:

Ros dhomhain (⟦burg:27Ros dhomhain⟧)Ros dhomhainCreideamh an Aon-adharcaich Dhuibh51,589

The capital itself is not among them. Cathair dhearg is counted at 10,274; its harbour, Ros dhomhain, is five times its size.

The departed. Part of the Ròdaich people is not on Rodos. Land was found across the water (6 am Faoilleach 39 BDE); volunteers chose to go, by a vote "or something the later chronicles call a vote" (8 an Dùbhlachd 39 BDE); the fleet set out, turning sunwise round the harbour, in the first year of the Diosal Era (19 an Giblean 1 DE). A fragmentary report told of two landfalls, not one (24 an Dùbhlachd 5 DE), and of the thinning: cut off from the vein, "by the third generation abroad, nothing remains that Rodos would recognize" (3 an t-Iuchar 14 DE). The departed are a people of the chronicles only by their absence. The island kept them in rites (the empty-harbour rite, 25 an t-Samhain 22 DE; the white sorrow, an Tùrsa Geal, 27 an Dàmhair 15 DE) and in words, of which more below. When the humans came, old sailors at Cuan shean remarked that the strangers had come in from the same quarter of sea the Sundering fleet once sailed into. The council forbade the remark in its hall; it was written down anyway, and never answered (9 an Gearran 1781 DE). Nobody on Rodos knows whether the humans descend from the departed, and this appendix does not know either.

The humans of an Tìr Thall

The Crossing. Humans made landfall on Rodos and were granted leave to stay (5 am Faoilleach 1780 DE): the first contact since the Sundering. Three ships out of the west anchored off Cuan shean, and their master, whom the chronicles call Edmund Harrow, came ashore unarmed and asked by signs for water (13 am Faoilleach 1780 DE). That is the first exchange between the two peoples, and it was not in words.

Their homeland. The strangers named their homeland in their own tongue, but no Ròdach scribe set the word down. From the first season the chronicles call it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and calls its people simply the humans (26 an Gearran 1781 DE). Their own name for their country is not on Rodos in any hand, and it will not be recovered from here.

What they called things. The humans' names for the island's things were few, plain and, to Ròdach ears, careless. They had a single word for the black ore, and it was the word for the fuel they burned at home; Gormshuil nic Fhearchair's copyist noted that no Ròdais word answered to it, and that the humans did not ask for one (24 an Cèitean 1782 DE). So the vein became, in their tongue, coal, and the custodians of the vein became, in Samuel Wren's otherwise careful grammar, "keepers of the coal" (21 an Lùnastal 1791 DE). Their institutions came with English names and kept them: the Company, the Administration, the Mission, the Residency above Ros dhomhain (10 an Cèitean 1788 DE), the Commissioner, the Levy, the constable posts. Their coin was the mark. The townsfolk of Muileann shean called the constable post there "the humans' second Residency", and did not mean it kindly (26 an t-Iuchar 1911 DE).

The camps. What the humans built for themselves on Rodos was built for the pit. The camp of timber huts at Àth ìseal was the first settlement on Rodos built for no purpose but the pit (7 an t-Ògmhios 1807 DE); Baile dhomhain was laid out on a grid by a Company surveyor, the first Ròdach town drawn on paper before it was built (10 am Faoilleach 1813 DE); the camp at Achadh dhomhain was built of spoil (29 am Màrt 1846 DE). The camps were Ròdach in their labour and human in their rule, and the record of them is kept in two tongues that seldom agree: the Mission counts four hundred and six dead of the spotted pox, and the custodians count more, and write the difference in the margin of the Mission's list (11 an Dàmhair 1818 DE). Human families lived on Rodos as well as human officers: upland pasture in the north-west, around Muileann àrsaidh, was granted for human families who would not work in the pits (3 an t-Samhain 1799 DE). It is the first human settlement in the north, and the north is where their descendants were sent.

Mixing. The first mixed settlement (22 an Giblean 1784 DE) was Baile dhìreach on the south-west coast, under a council of three Ròdaich and three humans, whose founding compact was written twice, once in each tongue, the only such compact on record in the age (10 an Dàmhair 1784 DE). There the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh married the human cooper Samuel Hale, and the council entered the marriage in both its books (26 an Cèitean 1786 DE). Later history did not repeat the experiment, and the first mixed-blood inheritance case (15 an Gearran 1890 DE) was decided by the Administration entirely in its own favour.

The going north. War was declared in 1928 DE. Before the end, the human families of Ros bheag, Cuan shean, Baile dhìreach and the south-west marched north along the western roads under guard of the council's companies; few of them had ever lived in the north; no column was attacked, and none was helped (20 an t-Samhain 1929 DE). The war ended with the crossing itself closed (1 am Faoilleach 1930 DE). Whatever let humans reach Rodos shut, and the humans still on the island were shepherded to the northern territory their descendants hold today.

The Tuathaich

From the Severance the chronicles stop calling them humans. The descendants of those left on Rodos are na Tuathaich, the northerners, from tuath, north, by the same -aich that makes Ròdaich, so that on the page the two names read as siblings even though their circumstances do not. Their homeland in the north was fixed formally (22 am Màrt 1930 DE): "a confinement, not a homecoming, though later generations will simply call it home." A formal wall between the two peoples was proposed and rejected as unnecessary, because the two were already keeping apart on their own (11 an Cèitean 1939 DE).

What the Tuathaich call themselves in their own speech the chronicles do not say. The name in this appendix is the kingdom's name for them.

Their burgs. The map counts sixty-four Tuathaich burgs, all in the north and north-west, with some 543,000 people in them. The Ròdaich hold the other 441. The largest Tuathaich towns:

Ceann mhòr (⟦burg:143Ceann mhòr⟧)Ceann mhòrCreideamh na Scairpe Buidhe32,420
Baile chrom (⟦burg:305Baile chrom⟧)Baile chromRùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise27,319

Every Tuathaich town but one bears a Ròdais name, and most of them were Ròdach towns before the Severance; the north-west had been thinly held since the dearth on that shore in the Age of Sundering (19 an Giblean 780 DE). One of them, Seann Skell (Seann Skell) in the shire of Muileann àrsaidh, bears an Old One's name. The Tuathaich have added no names of their own to the map.

Their assembly. Tuathaich householders from the northern towns met at Caol mhòr and chose a speaker, Walter Hale, a former harbour clerk (25 an Lùnastal 1931 DE). The Moot has no standing in Ròdach law; it meets anyway, and its minutes run unbroken from that meeting to the present.

Their faiths. Of the sixty-four Tuathaich burgs, fifty-one keep Creideamh na Scairpe Buidhe, the faith of the Yellow Scorpion, which the Ròdaich of the western coast had kept for centuries before them. Twelve keep Creideamh nan Tuathach, their own folk tradition; its deity on the map is Donn, an Sìorraidh, and its towns lie together along the north coast, in the shires of Doire ghlas, Muileann leathan, Inis mhin and Àth àrsaidh. One, Baile chrom, keeps Rùn-dìomhair na h-Oidhche Glaise, the Mystery of the Grey Night. Creideamh nan Tuathach keeps, quietly, the First Canoe fragment (13 an Gearran 1938 DE): among coastal Tuathaich families, "a named steersman, a first crossing", dismissed by the Ròdach priesthood as superstition (9 an t-Samhain 10,054 BDE). The fragment belongs at the head of the Ancient Age, because that is where its tellers place it. The Library neither endorses it nor refutes it. It is one of the two suppressed histories that bracket the island's story, and it is not resolved here.

The fuil-ghuail

This section holds to what the rolls and chronicles say.

A child born into the mining camps was exposed to more raw ore across her lifetime than any Rodian in living memory, and did not age the way the people around her did. Her name is Aisling (7 am Màrt 1848 DE). What was happening to her had no word, in any language spoken on the island (13 am Faoilleach 1850 DE). A second case, Fionnan, was born half a century later (21 an Gearran 1900 DE), and it became plain that the exposure was not a single accident but an ongoing industrial condition. Facing two confirmed cases, Ròdach custodians settled on a term (23 am Faoilleach 1905 DE): fuil-ghuail, "coal-blood", rendered in the humans' tongue as obsidian-touched. It was meant clinically. It was agreed at a meeting of custodians at the shrine of Cill ghlas, and the roll records the vote but not who proposed it (21 an Gearran 1905 DE). The Residency ordered every Ròdach child showing the condition to be reported; the custodians complied by reporting none (26 an t-Samhain 1906 DE). A third case, Lorccan, was born in a mining town (1 an Giblean 1913 DE), and a fourth, Cian, within a year of him (3 am Màrt 1914 DE).

After the Severance the Obsidian Rite was formalized as Creideamh nan Ròdach, built around the leyline and "the unbroken line of the obsidian-touched" (18 an Giblean 1935 DE). The first census of the kingdom noted, without further comment, exactly how few such people exist (30 an t-Iuchar 1936 DE), and the published census of a later generation gave a number and nothing else (8 am Faoilleach 1994 DE). The number is printed nowhere else, and this appendix does not print it either.

Whether the fuil-ghuail are a people is a question of words. They are born to Ròdach families; in Ròdach speech the word names the gift that sets the Ròdaich apart from the Tuathaich; and Feallsanachd an Fhèidh has asked since the Holy Age why the vein answers some hands and not others. The chronicles do not settle it.

II. The Tongues

Ròdais

Ròdais is the Gaelic of Rodos. Of the humans' tongues it most resembles Scottish Gaelic, Irish and Manx, and it is closest to Scottish Gaelic in grammar and core vocabulary; its look on the page is its own. Three marks distinguish it:

FeatureRòdaisExample
Long vowelsgrave accent only: à è ì ò ùmòr, sìth, Ròdais
The cluster /sk/written sc, never sguisce, scoil, sceul, Scàineadh
"City"cathairCathair dhearg

Its greeting of thanks is gu robh math agad. Its verbs come first in the sentence (Chunnaic Cian an long, "Cian saw the ship"); it has no word for "a", no words for yes and no, and two initial mutations.

Lenition. After many words an initial consonant softens, and the change is written with h: b > bh, c > ch, d > dh, f > fh, g > gh, m > mh, p > ph, s > sh, t > th. The possessives, the past tense, a feminine noun after the article, an adjective after a feminine noun, most simple prepositions and the second element of a name all cause it. It does not touch vowels, nor l, n, r in writing, nor the clusters sc, sp, st, sm; and after a word ending in n it spares d, t and s, which is why the map has Seann Dunn and Seann Toll but Seann Bhral.

Broad and slender. Vowels are broad (a o u à ò ù) or slender (e i è ì), and within one word a consonant takes vowels of the same class on both sides: caol le caol, leathan le leathan, slender with slender, broad with broad. That is why so many endings come in pairs, and why the small rivers are Ciaras but Àrsaidheas.

Sounds. For the reader who meets these names aloud:

writtensaidexample
bh, mhvSeann Bhral
chas in lochSeann Chwen
dh, gha voiced ch before broad vowels; y before slenderCathair dhearg
fhsilentÀth fhada
sh, thhDùn thais
scskScàineadh

The stress falls on the first syllable.

How Ròdais names new things. Ròdais is an old dialect, long cut off, and it took few of the loanwords that other Gaelic took for new things, fewer than Scottish Gaelic took. The humans brought many new things, and the kingdom after them more. In the first generations after the Crossing the Ròdaich named nearly all of them from old roots, naming the thing by what it does or what it is like: head first, the describer after, hyphenated, two elements and seldom three. Many of these kennings are still the usual words. The loans Ròdais did take came mostly later, for such things as the bus (bus), the taxi (tacsaidh) and the radio (rèidio), and for many words of the sciences, such as ogsaidean, oxygen, and the names of the elements. A selection of the kennings, with the literal sense and the word the Gaelic of other lands uses:

Families form of themselves: machines are iarainn, of iron; screens and pictures are scàil and scàthan, shadow and mirror; electricity is dealan, spark, and dealanach, lightning. A crossing for feet is a ford, àth, the same word the map uses for a town at a river.

Words born of the island's history. Ròdais has also given old words new senses from the events it lived through. The royal chroniclers keep a list of these, and the rolls date the first use of most.

Of the Sundering the language also keeps one strange relic. A work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan shean names the parts of a deep keel, and half its words have no meaning to anyone who sings it (11 an Gearran 1340 DE). It is the only record of the fleet's techniques to survive in any form. Whether the lost words are old Ròdais, wrights' cant, or something else, no one has shown.

The tongue of the Seann-Dhaoine

Of the Old Ones' speech nothing survives but names. Ten roots are known, each standing after the Ròdais word seann, "old", which lenites it where Ròdais lenites:

RootAs written on the mapBurgs bearing itShires named from it
DunnSeann Dunn3yes
CwenSeann Chwen3yes
SkellSeann Skell4yes (three)
BralSeann Bhral3yes
TarrSeann Tarr3yes
VellSeann Vell5yes (three)
MornSeann Mhorn2—
BrennSeann Bhrenn2yes
TollSeann Toll3yes
WarrSeann Warr2yes

Thirty burgs on the map bear these names, and thirteen shires are named from them.

The Ròdaich did not translate these names; they took them over. The fishers who resettled Seann Mhorn in the Holy Age kept "the name they found there, which is not in their own tongue", and said the old name came with the stones (23 an t-Sultain 2821 BDE). It is the first such taking-over on record. The pattern is the one other lands know, where an older people's harbour-names outlive them inside a newer tongue: borrowed and fossilized, not translated.

What can be said. The roots are single syllables. Seven of the ten end in a doubled consonant (-nn, -ll, -rr). Three of them hold letters that Ròdais writes nowhere else: k in Skell, v in Vell, w in Cwen and Warr. Ròdais spelling turns every sg into sc, but it has never turned Seann Skell into Seann Scell; the scribes kept the foreign k as they found it, and the grammar counts sk- among the clusters that do not lenite.

What cannot be known. What any root meant. Whether seann was ever the Old Ones' own element, or only the Ròdaich's label for places they found already named (the second is the usual reading, and the likelier, but it is a reading). Whether the roots come from one tongue or several. Two of them look like Ròdais words, toll, a hole, and dunn beside dùn, a fort; the resemblance has tempted scholars in every age and proves nothing, and the Library does not take a side.

The script. The Seann-Dhaoine also cut signs. Rows of them stand on the cliff above Seann Tarr (5 an Giblean 11,618 BDE), in the script that turns up again on the standing stones. It is not Ròdais, and it has not been read. Not one sign of it has an agreed meaning. The stag-scholars of the Holy Age set their own new letters against the obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag and found that they matched nothing, and wrote down that the stone's writers were not their teachers (12 an Cèitean 2085 BDE). Samuel Wren copied the obelisk and sent it west to the scholars of an Tìr Thall; no reply is recorded (5 an Gearran 1796 DE). Edwin Lowe copied the pillar near Cnoc chiar, compared it with Wren's copy, and decided that the two were not the same script and that neither was Ròdach; his notes stop there (9 an Lùnastal 1844 DE). The strokes on the midden stones are not this script; they are a count. Whether the script records the Old Ones' tongue, or some other, or no tongue at all, is not known.

The humans' tongue

The humans spoke a plain tongue, and this history renders it in English (see Of Translation below). The names they carried were names of that tongue: Edmund Harrow, Thomas Pike, Samuel Wren, Josiah Pell, Henry Maddox, Arthur Lisle, Samuel Hale, Edwin Lowe.

The season of translation. Human clerics and Ròdach custodians spent a full season trying to build a shared vocabulary, and neither side's account of what was agreed survives intact (27 am Màrt 1781 DE). Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair kept parallel word-lists. Wren's survives in the Administration's letter-books; Gormshuil's was lost, and only its first leaf is known from a copy: forty words for the colours of broken ore (13 an Dùbhlachd 1781 DE). Against those forty the humans had one word, and it was coal.

The tongue of rule. The humans wrote their agreements in their own tongue only. The first written treaty (27 an Giblean 1787 DE) was signed at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein, who could not read the tongue it was written in; the record does not say who read it to him (7 an Cèitean 1787 DE). The Harbour Articles were written the same way, and that time two custodians refused to sign (16 an t-Samhain 1798 DE). The Mission's school at Ros dhomhain taught Ròdach children in the humans' tongue (9 an Cèitean 1831 DE); a generation later Iain Maor, the first overseer schooled there, kept his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Ròdais (23 an Giblean 1866 DE). The Levy's officers read the names of the chosen at Caol mhòr from a list in the humans' tongue, and the custodians took the names down again in Ròdais, "so that they will know whom to look for" (3 am Màrt 1867 DE).

Loanwords. Few crossed, and most of those late. In the first generations Ròdais took the humans' goods and named them in its own way, as above, and kept few of the humans' words for them. The humans, for their part, so far as the record shows, used the Ròdais names of places as they found them, and took fuil-ghuail not as a loan but as a translation, obsidian-touched; that word, and not the Ròdais, is the one the kingdom's own later entries use of the Rite's "unbroken line". What went the other way, into the humans' speech, is best seen after the Severance, in the north.

The Ròdais word for the humans' country, an Tìr Thall, is the only name the island has for it.

Tuathaich speech

The speech of the north is a mixed speech, and the chronicles describe it only in passing. They say this much:

The Tuathaich kept the humans' tongue. Walter Hale asked the council for leave to open schools in the north teaching in it, and was refused (2 an Gearran 1936 DE); Agnes Pike opened one at Doire ghlas anyway, with Moot money and without the council's leave, and within a decade there were nine (14 am Faoilleach 1944 DE). The Moot later counted eleven such schools, and three that had begun to teach Ròdais as well, at the parents' asking (7 an t-Ògmhios 1958 DE). The Scorpion house at Cnoc ghorm taught its priests in the humans' tongue while reading the Scorpion's scripture in the Ròdais text the west-coast houses use: the only place in the north where both are taught (29 an Giblean 1939 DE).

The Tuathaich live among Ròdais names and use Ròdais words. The words the north has added to the island's speech in the present age are Ròdais in form: fadachadh, from fada, long, the name of the war they lost (10 an Dùbhlachd 2021 DE), and seann-chunntas, an old reckoning, which official Ròdach usage pointedly does not take up (18 an Giblean 2025 DE). The word dubhan for the fuel came out of the north, from the name of Dubhan, a Tuathach, and it spread before the fuel did (23 an t-Sultain 2010 DE); the royal chronicler who first set it down spelled it three ways in two lines (21 an t-Samhain 2000 DE).

Beyond this the chronicles do not go. The northern towns' own accounts are among the things the royal record says it does not hold (25 an Giblean 1972 DE). How far the humans' tongue has drifted in the north since the crossing closed, how much Ròdais is spoken at a Tuathach hearth, and in which tongue the First Canoe is told: this archive does not know, and it would be wrong to pretend otherwise.

Names and naming

Personal names. Ròdach names are Gaelic personal names: Ailean, Beathag, Catrìona, Dòmhnall, Eilidh, Fearchar, Gormshuil, Iain, Mòrag, Raghnall, Sìleas, Tormod. A person is further named from the father, with mac, son, or nic, daughter, and the father's name in the genitive, lenited where Ròdais lenites: Tormod mac Iain; Eilidh nic Iain; Gormshuil nic Fhearchair; Donnchadh mac Thormoid; Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill; Oighrig nic Lachlainn.

Bynames are as common as patronymics and often outlast them. They name a colour, a trade, a size or a deed. After a woman's name the byname is lenited, after a man's it is not: Seònaid Mhòr, Eilidh Dhubh, Beathag Bhàn, but Ailean Mòr, Calum Liath, Dùghall Garbh. Trade-names are nouns and stand as they are: Alasdair Saor, the wright; Iain Maor, the overseer. Some bynames are earned: Tormod mac Iain, the first of the royal kin to read, was called Tormod Scrìobhaiche, Tormod the Writer, for the rest of his life (3 an Lùnastal 1713 BDE).

Kindreds take Sliochd, the seed or line, or Clann, the children, with a founder's name in the genitive: Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Mhuirich, Clann Choinnich.

Human and Tuathaich names are of the humans' tongue and are kept in their own spelling: Walter Hale, Agnes Pike. Unlike the humans' names for the island's things, the humans' names for themselves survived the Severance.

Place names. Ròdach places are named by a generic noun and a describing word after it. On the map the describer is always lenited, whatever the gender of the generic (Baile ghorm, Cnoc bheag, Dùn thais); in speech it would not be after a masculine noun, and the map's form is a fixed naming pattern, kept as one might keep an old compound. The generics:

GenericSenseUsed for
Cathairstone fort; citycapital, city
Dùnfortified hillcapital, city
Baile Mòrgreat settlementcity

Àthfordtown

The describers are colour, size and character words: mòr, beag, dubh, geal, bàn, dearg, ruadh, uaine, glas, fada, domhain, ìseal, fiadhaich, naomh, fionn, ciar, gorm, sean, òg, garbh, min, caol, leathan, crom, dìreach, àrsaidh. The great rivers are Abhainn with a describer; the small ones take a root and the ending -as or -eas by broad and slender. A shire, siorrachd, takes the name of its seat. Names repeat freely; there are two Baile chrom and four Seann Skell, and the rolls tell them apart by where they are.

Beside these stand the Old Ones' names, which follow none of the rules above except that the Ròdaich put seann before them.

Writing

Before letters. The first marks on Rodos made on purpose are the Seann-Dhaoine's: the notched net-weights of Seann Chwen, their unread script, and their tally strokes. The Ròdaich's forebears kept counts too, but not in letters. Someone began marking the high-water line against a fixed rock in the Ancient Age (28 am Faoilleach 5937 BDE), and at Ros dhomhain Seònaid Mhòr cut her marks in pairs, one for the high water and one for the low (25 an t-Iuchar 5177 BDE). The king-lists of that age were oral, and the Small-Burning custom was "nowhere written and everywhere kept".

The Ròdais words on the stones. Bha teine sa chloich on Carragh Cnoc bheag, Cuimhnich an teine on Colbh Cnoc chiar, Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann on Calbh Cnoc ghorm: these are the oldest Ròdais words in stone. When they were cut no roll says. The stones were raised in the Ancient Age; the Ròdais on Carragh Cnoc bheag was cut later, by another hand. The words on Calbh Cnoc ghorm were recut along their old grooves by a hand from the Stone Kings' hill, and some later readers say the recutting changed a letter (2 an t-Samhain 3237 BDE). That there were letters to change then is not proved by this; the Library keeps the claim and makes no judgment on it.

The stag-letters. The first letters in use by the Ròdaich were made at Muileann chiar in the far east, where the teachers of the stag's people, the school later called Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, turned the cutters' tally-notches into signs for sounds, "so that a teaching can be kept without a teacher" (15 am Màrt 2085 BDE). Nearly every later hand on the island descends from them. From these came the first written king-list (20 an Lùnastal 1684 BDE), kept by Tormod Scrìobhaiche at Dùn dhearg; the Keepers' own roll, written down at Dùn ìseal in answer to it (17 an Dàmhair 1648 BDE); boundary stones cut with treaty terms (11 am Màrt 1395 BDE); and the first teaching of letters for their own sake, to fishers' children at Inis bheag, which the Hall recorded with the remark that fish do not need reading (22 an t-Ògmhios 1138 BDE).

Books and paper. The Age of Sundering is the age of the custody-book, kept by the vein-house, and of the first books: Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the sayings of Gormshuil (5 an t-Ògmhios 212 DE), and Seònaid nic Coinnich's Book of the Three Claimants, the oldest surviving history on Rodos written as one narrative (8 an t-Ògmhios 585 DE). Aonghas mac Uisdein was the first king to learn his letters as a child (25 an Cèitean 355 DE). A mill at Muileann chaol began making paper from rags, the first on Rodos, and the custody-book was copied onto paper in that generation (28 am Faoilleach 1635 DE).

Two tongues of record. The humans brought paper in quantity, and the custodians of Cathair naomh asked for their first payment in paper and ink (19 an Lùnastal 1782 DE). They brought, too, a written tongue the Ròdaich could not read, and for a century the island kept its records in two. Whether the humans' letters and the stag-letters share their shapes, the record does not say. The earliest Ròdach grievance text to survive, Leabhar Baile thais, was set down in Ròdais by many hands (18 an t-Sultain 1880 DE).

The kingdom's record. After the Severance the kingdom founded Leabharlann Muileann chaol (1 an Cèitean 1945 DE) and the office of royal chronicler (20 an t-Samhain 1947 DE), and in time drew the provincial archives into one place (26 an t-Iuchar 1996 DE). This appendix is written from that library.

Of Translation

This history is written in English for the next reader, and some account is owed of what that has done to the tongues it describes.

The humans' speech is rendered in English. The humans did not speak English. They spoke the tongue of an Tìr Thall, whose name for itself, like the name of their country, is not recorded on Rodos. It was a plain tongue, as English is plain beside Ròdais; its speakers were strangers to the island and its things; and it has become, in the north, the ordinary speech of the Tuathaich. For those reasons it is given here as English, and its names are given as English names, as the letter- books would have them. When this history says the humans called the ore coal, it means that they used their ordinary word for their ordinary fuel, and that coal is the nearest English word for what they meant. When it gives a custodian's title as "keepers of the coal", it is rendering Wren's rendering. Obsidian-touched is likewise an English stand-in for the humans' word, chosen because it keeps the plainness of the original and the error in it. The ore is not obsidian, and it is not coal.

Ròdais is kept as it is. The Ròdaich are the people of this history and Ròdais is its first tongue, and it is not translated into something else here. Names of places, persons, faiths, laws and offices are left in Ròdais spelling, with the grave accent and the sc, and with their lenitions: Cathair dhearg, not "Red City"; fuil-ghuail, not "coal-blood", except where a gloss is wanted. Where a Ròdais phrase is translated, the translation follows it in quotation marks and is meant as a help, not a replacement. The five ages have Ròdais names and are also given English ones for convenience; the English names are this archive's, not the chroniclers'. The adjective Rodian is English, and is used as such.

The island's own name. Written in Ròdais it is Ròdos, with the accent. In the English text of this history it is written Rodos, the form the humans used and the form in which most readers will have met it. It is the same word.

The Seann tongue is not translated, because it cannot be. Its ten roots are given as the Ròdaich wrote them, with the foreign letters the Ròdaich kept. No meaning is offered for any of them.

What has been lost in the rendering. Some things do not cross. The forty colour-words on Gormshuil's leaf are one; the Tuathaich jokes about being long-warred are another, since fadachadh is funny, and not funny, only in a tongue where fada is also the name of the war. Where this history has had to choose between a translation that reads easily and one that keeps what the words did, it has tried to keep what they did.

The Houses of Rodos

Clann Fhearchair of Baile Mòr dhomhain

One of the seven houses of custody regrouped after the Sundering (4 an t-Iuchar 16 DE). Its seat at Baile Mòr dhomhain gave Rodos the first king chosen by the houses (19 an Gearran 143 DE), and the double court near the mountain lasted as long as the house held the crown. After Sìleas nic Fhearchair the crown went to her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill and his line.
